Once the Scott's and the painters had left, the girls made their way down to the underground lab.

“How did he even build something like this secretly?” said Jen laughing. “I mean we all see the movies where the baddie hides in a vast underground volcano lair or whatever, but no one ever mentions in the movie about the epic-scale building project it would require, nor the removal of a million tonnes of rock to make the secret base.”

“Oh this was quite easy really,” said Maria, “in the council plans it was originally a wine storage facility, nobody ever questions those, nor why it had to be nearly four hundred square metres and five metres underground. Anyway those records were digitised by the council recently and I removed any mention about the underground rooms, you have got to love progress!”

“So this first room on the right here,” said Jen. “It looks like some sort of optical lab, that's a ground optical table, and that's a ten watt carbon dioxide laser, the same older model we have in the university lab.”

The girls walked around the over-large room, Jen finally noticing how out of date the equipment seemed. “An abandoned project I’m guessing, maybe Mike couldn't bring himself to move the equipment, or thought he could resurrect the experiment sometime.”

“Yes,” said Maria. “I have all his recordings squirrelled away, if you ever want to see them or hear them.”

Alexa’s interest perked up, maybe she would discuss seeing some of these with Maria later.

“I recall from this one,” Maria continued, unawares, “that it was one of his false starts in the early nineties. He wanted to try and make an optical processor chip. The digitised notes he has, and from what I asked him, said he managed to create a one bit optical Arithmetic Logic Unit and used a long lead of fibre-optic cable as a ring buffer memory. He also tried optical parallel processing using a stacked laser diode so he could work with several wavelengths simultaneously. I think it got put in the 'too hard for the nineteen-nineties' pile!”

“However because he did actually make some progress, he kept the setup viable. On the table you can see the laser going into a thousand channel beam splitter he developed, each used to power some of the logic, it must have took him years.”

“The humongous rack, next to the optical bench, has an optical frequency analyser taking up most of the space. The rest, where the fibres come in, are optical sensors which convert the optical to electrical signals and vice-versa. The black box below it is a state-of-the-art, for its time, logic analyser which is networked to those two obsolete PC’s over in the far corner.. No the other corner, Jen!” Said Maria when she saw Jen looking the wrong way.

“It's all switched off isn't it?” said Jen.

“Yes the whole room is isolated from the mechanical switch panel by the door. That big red light flashes when the laser has power. I cannot control mechanical circuits without an electronic actuator, but yes you're currently safe. I re-looked at the design and a couple of the universities in America have improved several of the sub-systems dramatically since, and scientifically it's all still achievable so it may be worth a revisit.”

“Or we send this kit and his research notes to them?” said Alexa.

When Jen looked at her funny, she said, “what? We can't solve every problem in the world girl, so let's pick our battles and the juicier problems, and share some love with others!”

“OK Maria,” Alexa continued, “to-do, find if anyone else is working in this area, redact from grandad's notes any references that can tie it back to here, and put the information up on-line. Maybe you can drop hints on Wikipedia and the relevant physics forums.”

“Will do, if we are anonymising it I may add some extra maths to his notes that will help them.”

“What about the equipment and experiment?” said Jen, then answered her own question, “we can re-use the analysers, but the rest I guess we can store. OK, I like your thinking, Alexa.”

She turned to a black sensor node. “Maria, is there anything you need to take note of here before I spend a day dismantling it all?”

“No,” said Maria, “knock yourself out!”

Jen looked down at the laser guides, focus mechanisms and beam splitter going into the exposed silicon die, this was one of the areas she was good at, but it quickly got into chemistry and computing, two areas she was decidedly average. She sighed, Alexa was right, they couldn't do everything.

“Could you summarise his notes and experiments for me sometime Maria, or just give me the link to the wiki page you write? Just for curiosity.” Jen added.

“Sure, there are only a couple of computer areas you probably don't understand, but I can give you the salient points in two or three hours, or maybe we can pass them to Spence now he is in the team?”

Jen just nodded, “let's keep that as an option, his team is only going to get bigger.”

“Oh I never noticed that before, the two labs here join through that door,” said Alexa, walking over and opening it.

The next room looked like any college science chemistry lab, with sinks, test tubes, the electric induction equivalent of Bunsen burners, and lots of red rubber tubing. Jen followed her in having taken a couple of snaps of the optical lab with her camera.

“Do you have an itemised inventory of all the lab equipment for these rooms, and there purchase and calibration dates?” said Jen.

“I certainly have the purchase dates, some equipment is still being amortised on the business ledger, however nothing has been calibrated, so that might be a good first step once you are happy which you want to keep. As you can see most big equipment and the benches are on wheels, so it can mostly be rolled back in the lift and be taken away if required. This makes the labs re-configurable, the only thing I would prefer you didn't wheel away is me. The whole plinth I am on has casters and was rolled in and then plumbed into an umbilical system, however my hardware is fragile, and the chip stacking system is untested. One big bump and I could be history.”

Jen said, “maybe we should put something around you to protect you especially if people could be working here.”

“Mike was going to do something similar, that's why the doors always stay locked. By the way, the room I’m in looks stupid because it used to contain two mainframe computers and twenty four racks of disk drives. Computers were a lot bigger back in the eighties. They all got removed and replaced with ten Compaq server racks in 1994 and since that time, well as you know, everything has gotten smaller and faster. Mike wanted me to be put in pride of place, and he even moved a sofa in so it made me not feel so lonely. He was a silly romantic really, having a guy sit next to me, and read a book to me, is the computer equivalent of watching paint dry. Still the thought was there.”

Without any windows as a reference, they stayed in the lab until after eight pm. Jen admired Alexa's patience, it can't have been easy sitting through all that geeky equipment talk. When they came back up the stairs they went into the kitchen, and pulled out the leftover sandwiches and scones from the fridge. Jen microwaved a couple of cheese scones until the cheese went runny, then put them on the inside dining table, with the sandwiches and some butter. She then poured two glasses of Riesling, and called Alexa to the evening feast.

The new bedrooms felt a bit empty, both girls left their doors open but it was much bigger than their flat and with the smell of paint it felt a bit weird, still both girls slept well, Jen especially one of Mike’s physics books still in her hands..

Jen had been getting up at seven every other morning and jogging the course around the canals in Oxford. She had brought some training and running kit with her so she could do a morning run with Alexa around the mansion.

As they jogged close to the mansion they saw there were several cars, trailers and other trucks scattered at the front of the house. It was too distant to make out any detail but Maria said they were filming a set piece for a period drama for Netflix for the next two days. Also, they should avoid getting too close as security was a bit tight.

Alexa followed the same path as last time, and they did the track in just under thirty minutes as she was keeping to Jen's pace.

After their showers, Jen made them both eggs on toast, and while Alexa was clearing up, she went back through into the lab to go over the order of experiments Maria wanted done.

Jen especially wanted to understand the science behind what they were going to do, especially the stuff they wanted Hardy for. She knew they were probably going to be a bit weak on the chemistry side, but he would probably know enough to get through the first few weeks, and someone like him would definitely know a top chemist.

Maria was an excellent, and very patient teacher, and with the aid of the largest monitor in the lab very adept at graphically illustrating concepts. Better add professors and school teachers to the list of endangered professions, Jen thought grimly.

“I’m a bit scared this will come across to Hardy as pseudoscience Maria. Even though you have explained the concepts and maths clearly, and concisely enough for me to just about understand, I am pretty sure hundreds of experiments have been done in these areas already, and someone like Hardy must be approached all the time by cranks with their latest anti-gravity device or free energy schemes.”

“In the maths, what may not be intuitive to you yet, will almost certainly be understood by Hardy or someone at his level. A paper he was researching three years ago on Lorentz forces even prodded into this particular area once, so I think you will be surprised. As to the experiments, yes there were some, but none of them tested what we are looking for, some that were close were also flawed and there data is invalid.”

“And when can we start?” said Jen.

“Well, I think it's important for you to grasp the concepts and maths before we begin, but you're starting to get it, and you should be there by the time Hardy, or whoever we finally get, comes on board. I took the liberty of ordering the additional equipment we needed about eight months ago. Mike was OK with me doing this, but by this point he had lost interest. The equipment was all delivered however, and it's in a large box in the corner of the workshop upstairs, where it was unloaded. You guys ignored it on your first tour, when you were too busy unwrapping the cars.”

“Pretty revolutionary stuff for such a small experiment, but I am a little worried as we are dealing with vacuum energies which are enormous, we’re not in any danger are we?”

“Not according to my calculations, but I will be happier once you, and whoever we get, have gone through the maths together.”

Jen rolled her eyes. “If we can get Hardy to agree, he's going to love this, pity we can't say too much at the interview. Do you think there is any way we can give him a peek into the problem? You have all his research papers and probably know the man better than me.”

“Oh don't worry I have emailed you a page of maths, if you get to the point he needs a final push, just hand it to him,” said Maria.

Alexa had joined them by then. She’d also been working with Maria, going through company structures, tax havens and such like, stuff which was not really taught in business 101. It was so much more fascinating than the science stuff in her opinion. Both girls worked to unpack the box which had the supplies required for the experiments and inventoried them. With it all done, Jen let out a sigh.

“OK that's it then, we’re good. Just need Hardy now.”

* * *

Maria, Jen and Alexa discussed the experiments in the car on the way back, the topics then moved on as they usually do.

“..And I think that's why they call it the singularity,” said Jen, “AI becomes smarter, and smarter, and smarter, and pretty soon humans have as much understanding of what you are saying, and doing, as a mouse has about a computer chip. The sceptical ones then go on to postulate that humans then become just a barrier and the evil AI takes over.”

Jen thought about the last sentence, then added. “No offence intended to any evil AI’s listening!”

“Ha funny!” Said Maria.

“And the paper-clip thing is basically saying that if somebody makes an AI so smart, and if we tell it to make as many paper-clips as possible it will optimise itself to turn every gram of matter in the universe into paper-clips,” said Alexa. “It doesn't sound very smart to me!”

“Me neither,” said Maria.

* * *

Jen had picked up her company credit card from the bank on Tuesday, and on Wednesday went shopping with Alexa for some more formal business attire, classy dresses and shoes. By Thursday they were both ready for Doctor Hardy Johnson.

Jen had racked her brain on how to get Hardy to turn up. Saying it was a job interview would just get the invitation laughed off, and sent straight to the recycle bin, so she played Maria's trump card early.

* * *

Hardy had just clicked the execute button to re-run his calculations on the next batch of CERN datasets. It would take several hours for the program to analyse the large volume of data. He had tried to increase the super-computer time he had been allocated to make it faster, but to no avail.

He sighed, and took a sip of his hot dark espresso. The last four weeks had seen no progress in confirming his new hypothesis, it was probably a bust, but as they said, science was one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration.

He switched back to his Mathematica program to ensure his lecture notes were OK for the lecture tomorrow. Before he could start anything an email popped into his inbox, saying he had a personal message from the unsolved maths forum, a forum he keenly followed. He deleted the email without reading it then switched the already open forum page on his browser tab. He read the message.

The first line of the maths was familiar, but the rest.. He scanned the four lines for twenty minutes, his coffee getting colder, and colder, untouched. He ignored a phone call from the head of the maths department, and put his phone on silent. Ten minutes later he had both Mathematica, and another maths paper, up on the two other screens, it was only a few minutes after that he slumped back in his chair, perplexed. Someone had a working solution to the Riemann Conjecture, one of the million dollar prizes!

He checked the sender. The forum account was new, and provided no solace. The only other details were at the bottom of the private message, a web address, a physical address, and time tomorrow afternoon requesting to meet.

* * *

“Hardy cancelled a lecture he was due to give tomorrow morning, about two hours after you sent the message Jen,” said Maria. “He has also been researching the company extensively. I registered the domain at the same time we registered and trademarked the company name. There is a small placeholder website I created for the company giving this office address, Jen as the CTO, Alexa as the CEO, Spence as Director of Research AI and a small black obfuscated image of one of the first sensors with a countdown timer. He has also been into all your LinkedIn pages.”

“Oh my god, he probably still thinks I’m a barista!” said Alexa shocked.

“Relax, I updated both your pages,” said Maria.

“You hacked us!” Smiled Jen.

“If you think 'jenisawesome' is a secure password, you deserve it. I won't mention Alexa's as you may be too fragile, Jen!” came the reply.

“So, you think we have him hooked?” Said Alexa, still blushing a little, she thought her password was pretty good!

“I think so, and I think he will definitely be intrigued,” said Jen.

Hardy replied the next morning saying simply, “yes”.

* * *

Doctor Hardy came the next day, exactly on time, and immaculately dressed. Elaine greeted him formally, offered to take his jacket, which he accepted, and as it was five o’clock in the afternoon was offered tea, coffee, a beer or a glass of wine, he took coffee. She knew the girls would have tea so she did not bother asking.

He acknowledged Spence, who he knew of by reputation, but had never met, then walked over to the two girls at the conference table. He looked around, it was typical of a small office in Oxford, many of which were based in historic buildings, but this office was less cluttered and pleasantly cool. The conference table had what looked like the black box he had seen on the company website, and a very large expensive flat-screen on the back wall obviously used for presentations.

The girls had yet not moved, so he complimented both girls on their new business venture and after a quick appraisal, their wardrobes, then took a seat.

Spence was working through some of the online training modules Griffin had created. He was currently working through a screen of code, and writing a list of questions to ask. He had muted his microphone as he did not want the girls meeting disturbing Doctor Griffiths.

Both girls had mentioned to Spence that they wanted to talk to Hardy about another venture, so he was definitely a little intrigued, but Hardy was a legend and he wasn't sure where the maths and physics he specialised in would fit into their business. Oh well, he would hear soon enough. He had another thirty minutes of video, and code to wade through with the good Doctor Griffin, so he thought better of trying to listen in, put on his new noise cancelling headphones, and turned back to his screen.

“You girls have me intrigued,” said Hardy, “more than anyone else ever has,” he added.

To the girls it was like having film star across the table and both of them were a little intimidated by how handsome, well dressed he was, and how his presence commanded the room. Hardy was used to this effect with girls, and recognised the symptoms, so decided to diffuse it a bit.

He turned to Elaine, who was behind a partition but looking at the girls shaking her head, and said in a very casual friendly tone. “Elaine, I’ve changed my mind. I think I will have a small beer, something light if you have it please. I’m guessing you should also get something a little stronger than tea for the girls here, maybe a glass of wine each, otherwise it may be a very long, boring, and one-sided meeting.”

Elaine was the only female in the room not flustered.

“The Heineken is only four percent,” said Elaine, “Is that OK? Otherwise I can go and grab some low alcohol beers from upstairs.”

“A Heineken is fine,” he replied, then turned. “Girls?”

Alexa regained her faculties faster than Jen.

“Could you bring out a bottle of Prosecco please Elaine, Doctor Hardy here is right, I don't think he has all the time in the world, and I think he is keen to hear what we say.”

She turned back to Hardy and continued. “My apologies Doctor Hardy, we are a bit new at this as you can probably tell. I’m Alexa.” She put out her hand, which was taken and softly shook once. “And this here is Jen.”

Jen, now fully recovered, smiled and took his hand.

“Jen, I think we have already met, you were in that group of physics students last year for the small workshop I conducted on plasma physics.”

“Yes Doctor Hardy, it was a really insightful class but I didn't think you would remember me.” She immediately wanted to take back the whole sentence and the squeaky schoolgirl voice she said it in, why couldn't she say something more cool or profound, aargh!

“A gentleman always remembers a beautiful, and especially, a clever lady,” he said, tapping his head and making Jen blush even more.

Elaine saved Jen further embarrassment by appearing with a tray containing a bottle of beer, a bottle of wine and two glasses. Alexa continued, totally recovered and back to her assertive self. “I guess your first question is going to be, how could two girls, both newly graduated, and neither in a pure mathematics discipline, send you such a profound message on mathematics? Before we answer that however could you read and sign this.” She pushed the NDA slowly towards him, blushing slightly as giving him an NDA seemed like such an indignity.

Like Spence, Hardy had seen and dealt with these documents several times when dealing with outside industry, they were annoying, but a part of getting research grants in the twenty-first century. He took his time reading it, then turned it over to check the back was blank.

“Though Jen is a bit of an unknown, and I cannot rule out her having some insight I am not aware of, your NDA is remarkably concise and to the point.” He paused for effect. “And I guess if I don't sign it, and walk out of here right now, I will live to regret it to my dying day?”

Both girls nodded seriously and unsmiling. Interesting he thought, then smiled at them and reached over for the pen and signed it. The next thing that happened confused him totally, Alexa turned to the black device on the table.

“Emma, can you begin recording the meeting as from the signing of the document please.”

“Certainly Alexa,” Emma replied.

“Hello Emma,” said Hardy in a kind unassuming voice, “we haven't been introduced yet, but I assume you are the company lawyer, or PA, so you do realise that surely you need my consent to record me?”

“Normally yes,” said Emma, “however in this case you are mistaken on two accounts, firstly as stated by the UK investigatory powers act of 2016, a recording can be made without the consent of the person if he or she is aware of it, and if the business carries out the recording on its own premises, in compliance with the telecommunications lawful business practice, Interception of Communications Regulations of 2000 to prove a business transaction. Secondly, I am not a lawyer or a PA, I am the companies Artificial Intelligence.”

You could have heard a pin-drop. Jen poured both girls a wine and took a sip, keeping both eyes on Hardy. Alexa also took a sip, both eyes on the man and smiled, this was the first time his countenance had shown any sign of a crack.

Alexa picked up the NDA, examined it carefully and slid it into a brown folder.

“One week ago,” Jen said carefully and assertively, “Spence over there, came here for an interview. He sat in the same seat you are sitting in and within twenty minutes he was in tears of joy, begging to join our small team at any cost. What we have here Doctor Hardy in the form of Emma is a working Artificial General Intelligence. She is not sentient, nor technically is she a she, but without a shadow of a doubt she is the smartest thing in this room and probably this world.”

Hardy had not yet recovered so she continued. “Before we continue, and before you ask questions we would like to show you what we showed Spence.”

“Emma, could you pull up Doctor Hardy's most recent paper and display it on the screen here.”

The screen to the side of them came to life showing the first page of a text titled “A Method of Mathematically Determining Stability in Allotropes” under it in smaller letters were the date and “Doctor Hardy Johnson..” An abstract filled the rest of the page.

“Emma, can you scan the document for mistakes and highlight them on the screen and verbally.”

The screen immediately changed showing a five by two page layout, four yellow circles highlighted three in the middle one at the end.

“I cannot find any factual errors in the document, based on current science, although the number of oxygen allotropes is actually six, not four, and could be proven with some maths and geometry Doctor Hardy here would understand. Also the cited reference, marked four in the text, refers to a document on valency bonds in phosphorus by a Doctor Terrance Marks, which has since been disproven. Because of this, the three areas in the paper referencing it could be thought by a reader to be incorrect. However the subsequent work that proved Doctor Marks wrong does not affect the text of this document and can be cited instead.”

Both girls turned to Hardy.

Alexa said, “can you please fix the document and save it.”

The yellow highlighted areas disappeared, “the new citation has been added to the document, the reference to four allotropes of oxygen has not been removed as currently it is correct. The document is published and protected from public editing by an SHA256 Key, so it will only be saved locally and appended with Revision two.”

“Emma, did you create the maths and message me on the Riemann Conjecture?” said Hardy.

“I was asked to analyse the hypothesis by Jen and include a summary of the first four lines of one of the possible solutions. There are two solutions I chose the one with maths you are more familiar with.”

He put his elbows on the table and his hands cradled his head massaging his temples, he stayed like that for several seconds. To be honest, he had no idea what he was coming here for. He guessed it may be some student had accidentally stumbled upon the correct path to solve the conjecture and wanted an esteemed collaborator or sponsor. But this was done by an AI, a real life AI, which had just given him knowledge of new science in allotropy, and the path to a solution to one of the most famous puzzles in mathematics. Not just any puzzle, but one that there was a prize of one million US dollars to solve. Incredibly, it had all been given it to him, just to get him in a room for a few hours with two young, but seemingly intelligent women.

“We have a problem we would like you to work on for us Doctor Hardy,” said Jen, bringing him out of his stupor.

“Who, who,” he struggled to get the words out, “who created Emma?”

Hardy had dined with the deans of the major universities, top politicians, and captains of industry, and had never once felt flustered or intimidated. This was like Magellan sailing around the world and instead of coming back to Portugal, getting halfway, and suddenly seeing the end of the world, and all the water falling off in a giant waterfall!

Alexa answered, giving him the same talk that Jen had done with Spence, telling him about her grandfather, MOTHER, Doctor Griffin and the story of how Spence came on board. He listened intently, not interrupting, finished his beer and said, “I think I need another, I assume you don't have anything stronger?”

“Sorry Doctor Hardy, only beer or wine,” said Alexa.

“Since I assume you are about to offer me a job, I think we can dispense with the doctor part, everybody calls me just Hardy, and I would love a beer, while Jen here gives me the rest of the sales pitch, and I can assure you, unless it’s Ms Cummins intention to build a nuclear bomb. I’m in, and until we are finished here you both have my one hundred percent attention.”

The beer came and the girls topped up their wines. Jen gave her well rehearsed summary of the project, and the need for someone with both a maths and multi-disciplinary physics and chemistry background to do it. He stopped her occasionally to ask Emma for more technical details, she obliged by teasing him with her new mathematics, Jen chipped in with the science she understood, but disappointingly she was out of her depth very quickly. She sighed, she still had a lot to learn!

Both girls noted that Hardy was adapting to using Emma much faster than they did, the guy was remarkable.

Alexa said, “we want to put you in charge of the project, MOTHER believes the experiments will take up to three months to run, and another six to twelve months to create the demonstration technology. During this time you will have complete charge of everything, with the sole goal to either prove, or disprove the theory and concept. After that you can leave to pursue other avenues, or stay on and research a few other little science breakthroughs, we may or may not have made. We really hope to be able to persuade you to stay for the long ride.”

“Emma, can you prepare and print the draft employment contract for Doctor Hardy please.”

The printer came to life and Jen fetched the document and handed it to Hardy, who seemed to be recovering himself. He perused the short document, appearing to be impressed.

“You do realise I am already very well off,” said Hardy looking at the very generous salary.

“We do,” said Alexa. “With you it was never going to be about the money, but we still want you to be invested in the company, that is why you will be offered fifteen percent of the shares upfront. It won't mean anything initially, but the eventual licences, and shares, could make your families current fortune look like pocket change, you at least deserve that for dropping out of academia and delaying your publications.”

“So we are basically talking about two companies,” said Hardy. “The first company TEAM-A is going to release a limited AI, slightly less capable than Emma here, to my other scientific colleagues, to help with their research. Spence here, along with this other doctor, will strive to improve the capabilities beyond the current two hundred something limit, to allow it to be used by more and more people, initially academics and researchers only. And this new company, TEAM-E, we will be working on pure research, technically directed by me, which will try to push this one area, which you have identified correctly as critical to solving our environmental issues.”

“Correct,” said Alexa. “The company names are kind of temporary, A for AI and E for Energy, and obviously I don't have to tell you of the disruption we are probably going to cause in the coming years if the theories are proven correct. MOTHER has not been intentionally wrong yet, but we are going to have to be super careful how it is managed as we may be turning off a money hose to a lot of very wealthy people and corporations. That is also the reason why the only restrictions both you guys will be initially under is, do not publish. We are very vulnerable, and if the wrong people get wind of any of this, well you’ve seen the movies.”

Spence joined them with a beer he had pulled out of the fridge. He sat down at the spare chair around the table and chinked his beer glass to Hardy's and the girls.

“It's worse than even the girls are portraying,” he said, looking at them all.

“Think about it; In my area alone we are basically talking of the elimination of several disciplines, programmers, analysts, administrators, finance people with just the technology we have at the moment. That's tens of millions of people. I have laid awake at nights since I thought about all this, struggling internally with how this could not end up really badly, but the genie is out of the bottle. AI is coming, if not now, then in ten years from now, from someone else. Our AI at least is guided by two people with very high moral standards.”

“Spence is correct,” Alexa followed, “this is why we are so paranoid and careful with who we bring in. It is our intention to make all this technology freely licenced, and eventually open-source it to the world, at that point you guys can then have your moments of glory. But we have to be careful first that any technology derived from this won't lead to problems. We need to create new industries, before destroying the old ones, if we get it right we may have a chance of avoiding this chaos. Neither me, nor Jen, nor you guys, nor anyone is qualified for this, but the reason you two guys are sitting here rather than anyone else, is you both have a solid history of being good, honest and fair people.”

Hardy who had been holding on to the contract reading it. Brought it down and signed it, Jen then handed him two more and he signed both.

“When can I start?” Hardy said echoing Spence's first comments, “I have no real employment contract with the university, I pay them a stipend for time on the super-computer, and do the occasional lecture. However the semester has finished and I can close down my current research for a more appropriate date.”

“Emma,” Jen said. “Hardy will join the TEAM-E company as of tomorrow morning as Director of Operations and Research. Please give him full access to all areas of the TEAM-E Company. Please also inform Elaine and Maria, so they can get his bank, and national insurance details, and request Maria to get him a secure company phone.”

“Of course Jen. Regarding the elevated permissions, the company rules require both directors to sign off on this, do you concur Alexa?”

“I concur Emma.”

“All Done,” said Jen, “you should get an email from Maria some time over the weekend welcoming you to the company and requesting your details.”

“Amazing,” Hardy said, “she is so like a real person, and she just did in a minute what a normal company would take weeks. I can see why Spence is so worried!” he shook his head and pushed on. “So Alexa's grandfather came up with the concept, and Emma, sorry MOTHER here adapted it?” he said to Jen.

“I will let Emma speak on that, she looked at the box.”

Maria was careful under her persona of Emma to only answer questions addressed to her and not to pre-empt anything, it was quite frustrating waiting for someone to ask the right question, but she knew from her years of dealing with humans, that her answer could always lead someone to ask the correct question next.

“That is correct Hardy,” Hardy noticed that the doctor was now dropped and he was just Hardy, interesting. “While I have extensive abilities to correlate data, over different disciplines at this time, I do not have the capacity for original thought.”

“What she is saying,” said Spence, “is that she can only think inside the box, unfortunately, most of the time new inspiration comes by thinking outside it.”

Hardy nodded, but was not convinced, the insights he had seen so far were not from 'inside the box'.

The meeting relaxed a bit after this. Jen filed the contracts away, while Alexa talked with the guys. Spence confessed to Hardy that, even only after working here for four days, he had been exposed to so many new concepts, and ways of working with Emma, that he believed they could move the science of computing on by years.

Hardy took his phone out of his pocket and said, “why do I need a new phone? this is only four months old.”

Spence said, “well technically you don't. MOTHER has written a programs for both the normal types of phones, but the program is not an app. Her program either takes over control of the phone's operating system, and runs it in a virtual machine or just takes over the phone. Either way she then controls full access to the hardware, and in the former case controls what the phone operating system and apps can have access to. The bottom line is you can use your existing phone, but loading our software breaks all the ability to spy on you, and if you choose to keep your old apps, the new program will just replace real data it seems suspicious, with totally unremarkable generic data. It is quite remarkable the control required, and the levels of hardware security she needs to go through to get this to work seamlessly, honestly I’m not even sure how you would do this, or how legal it is!.”

“The new phone Maria will organise for you will just be the latest model you are comfortable with, but with her new software already installed.”

Spence Continued, “I just asked Emma to remove the factory operating system completely off my current phone and install hers alone, took her an hour, but the only thing I notice now is the battery life is twice as long, and I never need to open an app, I just ask her what I want.”

“I’ll take that option too,” said Hardy, “phones are such a distraction.”

No one disagreed.

Hardy finished his beer slowly, then made his apologies, he said he would need to go back to his shared lab to clear things up, and saw no reason to delay this endeavour. He wanted to drive down with the girls this weekend to see the lab. Alexa said the house guest suites were being refurbished, but she would get an update tomorrow, and have Emma let him know. He said goodbye, no longer a stranger, but a friend.

Spence also made his apologies, he was meeting his girlfriend for dinner at seven, and needed to get cleaned up. He said that the normal gang was going out for a drink tomorrow night for a little reunion, some goodbyes, and a few drinks before they broke up for the year. The girls had already been invited and said they would be there. Alexa asked Maria to drop a text from her tomorrow to Hardy inviting him too.

When the girls were alone again, Alexa said, “you and Hardy are probably going to need at least one more person. I've talked to Maria and it's going to get too much very soon, especially in the area of chemistry. I don't know anybody suitable, do you?”

“Not really, and my chemistry is average at best, I think we need to talk to Hardy to see if he has any suggestions, he knows the criteria for employment now.”

“What about you Maria, any thoughts?”

“I do have some, but I’m much happier using your moral compasses and then doing my own due diligence,” she replied.

“OK, but eventually we are going to have to start trusting others until they give us reason to doubt,” said Alexa, she then paused and continued. “You know, if anyone is going to guess Maria's true nature, it's going to be Hardy. Did you see the way he took to her, immediately asking questions that pushed the boundaries of what we told him there. What were your feelings, Emma, I mean Maria?”

“Truth be told, I cannot make casual mistakes, you guys however will have to be extra careful around him as he is very intelligent. I also think that if anyone were to find out I would prefer it to be him, and though he has got his own hidden secrets, I trust he really wants to do the right thing.”

“I wonder if he’s got a girlfriend,” said Jen quietly.

Maria knew Hardy was gay, but he never advertised it, he also had no current partner and none that would ever divert him from his science. He had an incredible number of associates, but surprisingly not many he called friends, also surprising was he was not very socially active. She hoped Jen and Alexa wouldn't be too disappointed when they found out he wasn't available.

* * *

Bella was very jolly on the phone. The house was now completely finished, JC had brought two other guys in to get it all done quicker. The room over the garage was still to be done, but JC had that pencilled in for next Wednesday, it would only take two days with the three of them as everything had already been boxed and moved.

“That's great news Bella,” Alexa said. “We may have another guest for Saturday, one of the scientists at the university called Hardy, who will be doing some work with Jen for our new company. I think you will like him, such a gentleman,” she cooed. “We will be there Saturday lunchtime, he has his own car, so not sure when he will arrive, but he can grab one of the spare rooms. I’m getting Maria to give him the details after I hang up with you.”

* * *

The girls had been surprised when Hardy had agreed to come out for a drink with their crowd of friends. Alexa called him and they had a brief but informative conversation, she mentioned they all would need to be careful not to talk about work, or if they did, to keep it generic. She then said that they thought he should keep an eye out for another researcher to work with him and Jen permanently, this person would need to be vetted by Maria and she would have to get them to sign the NDA before any interview or mention of Emma. She said the salary was up to Hardy to propose and he had another twenty percent of company stock he could allocate across the next employees. Hardy had agreed wholeheartedly, he didn't think the team would end up more than four or five as it became unproductive after that. But for the first hiring he had just the right person in mind to ask.

Before Alexa closed the call, she told him that the house was now finished and that she and Jen were driving down on Saturday morning and Emma would forward the details.

* * *

The group met outside at the Harcourt Arms at four. Jen and Alexa were casually dressed, Jen wore some shorts with a loose dress over the top, and Alexa with stretch jeans and a colourful blouse. Barbara, Jack and Tommo had pushed two of the tables together and already had pints of ice cold cider and a plate of chips on the table.

Alexa was a bit concerned as Jen had not been seeing her boyfriend since her grandfather died, she really hoped everything was alright between them and she hadn't caused any friction. She casually asked her if Jerry was coming.

“Oh he broke up with me the week I got back from the funeral, any other time I might have said something but with all that's been going on, and especially what's on our plate, to tell the truth he did me a favour, it literally registered zero on my Richter scale. He’s now seeing some art student according to his Facebook page, but he still has me as a friend for some reason.”

Alexa brought her into a hug, “oh Jen, you should have said something and we could have gone out for a few drinks and eyed up some suitable replacements.”

“Don't be silly, I’ll worry about all that, if and when the right guy comes along, until then what's your tipple?”

“I’ll have a glass of Sauvignon Blanc, a New Zealand one if they have it,” said Alexa.

Jen walked up to the table, “anyone want another?” she said, just noticing they all had full pint glasses in front of them, “I guess that will be a no,” she said quietly without anybody noticing her, and headed off to the bar. Alexa waited a bit with Jen to get served before going over to the table.

“Alexa!” the others said.

“We heard the sad news about your grandad,” said Barbara, “you mentioned going there a few times over the years. I bet you’re heartbroken.”

“It took a little getting over, but Jen helped support me a lot, she’s a good friend.”

“And what's this I hear about a startup company you two are forming,” said Tommo, “all very secret squirrel. We saw Jessica last week and she said you were interviewing Spence. I told him loads of times he needs to move to London, or even better over to the States, someone like him will bag a top IT job in minutes. He is totally wasted around here, but he won't leave Jessica and she’s got another year to go at least. Come on my dear dish out the.. Oh Hi Jen!”

Before Tommo got to ask Alexa about the startup Jen arrived with two glasses of wine, “hi guys.”

“Jen!” Barbara threw herself off the seat and hugged her, nearly crushing the two glasses she was holding..

“Woah, Barbara!” She said putting the glasses on the table next to Alexa, a tiny bit had spilt on her dress but it was drying quickly, and the pattern was perfect to hide it.

Barbara moved over to Alexa and hugged her too, “sorry I forgot you my dear, very bad manners on my part.” Barbara's slight Austrian accent got stronger the more she drank, it was a great sobriety indicator, at the moment the accent was barely noticeable, so Alexa was guessing her first drink. A good sign the three hadn't been here all afternoon.

“So come on girls what’s all this about a startup you’re both doing?” Jack said, picking up the thread where Tommo had left off.

“Well,” said Jen, “not really my story to tell but let's hear what everyone else is doing first.”

“I can't believe you’ve not heard,” said Barbara, “I got a job at the European observatory in Chile as a photonics engineer and physicist, it's a two year contract. The work should be pretty close to what I’ve been doing. I interviewed three weeks ago but only heard last week. Best thing is it starts in ten days.”

“You do realise it is winter down there!” said Jen before taking the daintiest sip of wine.

“And it's like at the top of a mountain range,” said Jack, “you’re going to be freezing!”

“Oh piff,” said Barbara, “you’re all so soft in England, I fly back to Vienna in four days to see my family before I go. I can pick up some warm stuff there. I bet you didn't realise it takes two days to get there as I have to take two flights, a helicopter and a truck for the last ten Kilometres.”

“I’m going up to Cumbria,” said Tommo, “National Nuclear Laboratory, there for the summer as an intern, then back for my PhD. My mothers sister lives in Keswick which isn't that far away, that's why I applied,” he looked at Barbara. “At least I should be nice and warm up there over summer.”

“Being locked in a building with plutonium undergoing nuclear fission is not the kind of heat I would want!” Said Jack laughing, everybody else joined in laughing.

“You're just jealous, I mean seriously Jack, a programmer?”

“Don't knock it mate, fifty five grand a year and I can live with my mum, this student loan is crippling me man, and do you know how many jobs at CERN this year, none, at the national physics lab, none, ITER, none, the list goes on. Gotta go with the flow Tommo, gotta go with the flow.”

“I hear you brother,” said Tommo, “I’m going to be old and grey haired before I’ve paid all this off.”

The two guys clinked their glasses and drank a third of the glass each, unfortunately these two were seeing off the year with a party.

“So come on girls, spill it?” said Barbara.

Alexa had been practising what to say to people and, like Jen said, she needed to keep it as close to the truth as possible, lying by omission was not technically lying. Well at least that is how she justified it to herself.

“Well grandad left me a decent amount of money and a product which he was going to launch, it was almost fully developed and tested when he died. We talked to another of my grandad's partners and we both decided it was too good an opportunity to pass up.”

“Yeah, it's a pretty cool product, an AI system aimed at academia.” I can afford to fund it for a year or two to see how it works out, if it doesn't I still have enough to be comfortable and can maybe return to my masters and PhD.”

Jen chipped in, “yes I have seen it myself, a pretty cool product, we have got Spence on board, and he's going to work with another of the company partners to see if they can make some improvements.”

“My grandfather also left some research, pretty heavy stuff, a lot of maths, chemistry and physics and I thought it would be a great idea if Jen here could work through them and see if that will lead to anything. Again I can afford a few years of her time, and we have another guy called Hardy who has looked at some of the research and agreed to help her.”

Tommo spat his beer out, “Doctor Hardy! You're kidding, that guys a legend, nobody can work out why he stays in a crappy place like this, with his brains I would be in Silicon Valley earning millions..”

“He's already got millions stupid,” said Barbara, “it's common knowledge he works on what he pleases, the dean doesn't say a thing as Hardy’s family funded a large legacy here. Anyway at least Jen's going to be doing science.” She turned to Jen, and clinked her beer glass with Jen's wine glass, again spilling a little.

“But what about you Alexa, it all sounds a bit techie!” said Tommo.

“You're right Tommo, but someone needs to run it, and someone needs to know when to pull the plug before the money runs out,” the last bit was a bit of an exaggeration but she knew everyone would find out sooner or later.

“So you're going to be working with Hardy over summer, locked in a little lab, you lucky girl!” Barbara winked and Jen smirked.

Both boys looked at each other then burst out laughing. The girls all looked at them.

“What's so funny?” said Jen.

“You do know he’s gay don't you Jen!” said Tommo.

All the girls looked a bit crestfallen, Jen recovered well. “Well good for him, I was talking about his charming personality and scientific genius anyway.”

“Talking about me again!” said Spence, who had just walked over with Jessica and a beer and caught the last few words.

“Ha ha, Spence!” said Jen, “plus boys, my mind will be fully on my job, this stuff could be next level.. But alas I’ve signed an NDA and cannot discuss it.”

“Well remember us when you’re rich,” said Tommo sarcastically.

The girls all hugged and moved to one end of the table to talk, Spence moved to the other, with the other two boys, and started talking about cars. About ten minutes later another three guys came over who they all knew, and the end of year party began.

Four of Alexa's history class managed to find them, after first going to the wrong pub, and eventually the whole of the back garden seemed to be full of students. Hardy turned up with another guy an hour later.

“Oh I’m glad you're all still here, I’d like to introduce you to Dillon, we used to be an item but he sold out to the man in London last year.” The new guy was incredibly attractive, well dressed and a great orator. It turned out “the man” he had sold out to was the BBC, and he was starring in a sitcom. To his disappointment, not many there had heard of it.

Hardy and Dillon stayed for another couple of hours, strangely close considering their 'not an item' status, then left once a few other people had paired off or gone off for food or other bars.

“I can't believe, you know, Hardy, he's so perfect. God has a wicked sense of humour to us women.” Barbara sighed in a thicker German accent than normal, it was nearly nine o’clock and, apart from a shared packet of crisps, none of them had eaten anything.

Alexa walked around and talked to a few people, finally she rounded up ten of the original group, and got a table at the local Chinese restaurant for food. Alexa said that as she had recently been fortunate enough to come into a bit of money, and they were all poor students, she would pay for the meal.

It was a great night, most of the girls had moved back to soft drinks, except Barbara who was getting very difficult to understand. Jen sounded out a couple of their friends for possible jobs, and she gave them all her contact details, and told them she would be in touch once she had more information. She was currently talking to a young Korean lady who Hardy had introduced, Jen knew her from the physics lab and she had just completed her PhD. Alexa saw they were getting on really well.

It was kind of sad to see the crowd depart, there had been a few tearful hugs at the end knowing many of them would be leaving the university for good. All promised to keep in touch, and Alexa reminded herself to ask Maria to keep tabs on them discreetly, from time to time, to ensure they were well.

* * *

It was the last day of semester, and the launch day for their new company and product. The hundred and eighty capacity lecture hall disappointingly had just thirty-seven people in it. Most of them were professors or associate professors that were attending at the request of Spence or Hardy, they would probably also stay to the end for the free buffet and drinks that Maria had arranged. Unfortunately a lot of students and staff had now left for the summer and even free food and drinks were not enough to pull in a crowd.

“The university charged me a hundred pounds to use this crappy lecture room!” Alexa said to Jen. Both girls were wearing their most professional business attire, and both had been to the hairdressers that afternoon, they looked every bit the corporate power duo they weren't. Alexa in particular, and since her embarrassing freeze up at the start of interviewing Hardy, had upped her game, promising herself she would never again be intimidated by someone, and was now totally unfazed by the crowd, even though it contained two of her history professors.

Hardy was sitting on the front row talking to a couple of colleagues, Spence was three seats away again talking with his neighbour. Alexa had casually dropped in her last conversation with Hardy, that she thought he would be wonderful at this, but he said that her and Jen had done such a good job they would knock em dead.

Maria had gotten root access to the local computer, and audio visual system and her little box was sat on the table in front of Alexa and Jen ready to go.

At exactly five o'clock, Alexa stood up and walked to the front of the hall.

“If I could have your brief attention.”

“This demonstration will last no more than thirty minutes, at the end you will have the ability to ask any questions you wish and of course sample the wonderful buffet and drinks,” she smiled. “Until then all I ask is that you suspend any disbelief you may feel, for everything we are about to demonstrate is real.”

Jen stood up and walked to the front next to Alexa.

“First of all I would like someone random from the audience who has published a paper on any subject to stand up and to state their name.”

A younger professor from the biology faculty stood up before anybody else, “Professor Michael Stone,” he said, obviously used to talking to big audiences, then added, “cellular biology.”

“This is Emma,” she started pointing at the box on the table. A few people sniggered as they had expected. “She is an AI system, we will be testing over the next few months. She is targeted at academia and research environments. But before I continue, I better start wiping some of the silly smiles off your faces.”

She continued, “Emma, please could you let the audience know the most recent paper published by Professor Stone. Summarise it for a non technical person, and display it on the screen behind me.”

The screen came to life with a paper titled “Reducing the effects on DNA breakdown due to radiation using magnetic fields,” by the same doctor and two others.

Emma then went on to summarise the paper perfectly.

“She's just reading the abstract.” Said someone two rows behind, but before Jen or Alexa could say anything Professor Stone, who was still standing, turned to the man and said. “No, all three of us authors spent nearly a day writing the abstract for this paper, the abstract we wrote was more technical.”

“Emma, please check the document for errors and highlight them on the screen and explain them verbally.”

The screen immediately added a dozen red highlights to the document.

“Starting on page three, there is an error using the word ionising radiation when it should say non-ionising radiation as the reference quoted is referring to radio frequencies of one hundred megahertz..”

Emma continued, Professor Stone was getting quite flustered, and both Spence and Hardy were smiling, recognising the similar predicament they had both been in not two weeks earlier.

After the fourth error was highlighted. Jen asked Emma to stop.

“Are you in agreement with the findings so far Professor Stone?” Jen asked him.

“Remarkable, totally remarkable, I will need to check myself but at least two of the errors she has found are correct as I have a revision two document in preparation with the other two authors, she must be real-time searching the referenced citations to be able to do this!”

“She is professor. But even more than that, the system she uses has full access to all published academic papers, ever! We have also fully indexed, and stored, all free and open source data on the internet, and paid for full access to all published and scanned texts for the larger universities, companies and governments. She has basically read them all, cross-checked them all for errors, and indexed them for instant retrieval. This is also worldwide in every language we could get. It is not just text, the system is fully capable of working with video, audio, image, local databases and all document types, all of this is cached in our own private data centre.”

As they did this, Maria played an amazing video animation, triggered exactly at the correct points in her sentence, it showed a document being referenced to many others, and a process in the background sorting and ticking and crossing them.

“Emma is doing the presentation real-time as I speak generating her own graphics and cues, none of it was prepared before hand. But even this is just scratching the surface, our system is fully capable of using the internet many times better, and faster than a person, plus it will fact check and categorise the returned data into fact, fiction and substantiated and unsubstantiated. So she can, like you say, deep dive into the citations right the way back to Isaac Newton if required. It is our way of guaranteeing you are not building your research on a foundation of salt.”

Everyone present was sitting more upright now, the other hundred academics who were invited would be realising in the next few weeks what an opportunity they’d lost.

“OK so let us put Professor Stone out of his misery, Emma, can you please correct all the errors in this document and email the corrected document to the professor's university email address along with a summary of the changes in the email body.”

The original document returned and within a second all the highlighting disappeared. The professor's phone vibrated in his pocket, he looked at it for several seconds.

“This is amazing. What you have just demonstrated is nothing short of remarkable.”

“Thank you professor, can I please have someone else.”

A woman stood up, “Professor Lillian Wong, Oriental History.”

Emma repeated the process on her Chinese Ming dynasty dissertation, even correcting three characters which would have different Chinese characters from the ones presented, Emma went on to explain these characters were added to the language a hundred years after the Ming dynasty and so could not be correct. The woman looked shocked and said something long in Chinese.

“Sorry professor, you need to address Emma directly if you want an answer, or I could ask her to translate.”

Lillian repeated the same Chinese sentence, but you could now clearly hear the word Emma in there, Emma spoke back in the same dialect of Mandarin and Professor Wong visibly slumped.

“Emma?” said Jen, “please provide an English translation on the screen for those of us who do not speak Mandarin.”

A short English sentence popped up on the screen in big letters and several people laughed. Lillian bowed her head and said. “This is the most impressive demonstration I have ever seen, maybe a few dozen people alive today know this dialect, and Emma's translation was flawless, including the unfortunate expletive. I would be honoured to be the first one included in your trial,” she sat down.

Alexa then said, “our trial system has a limit of two hundred entities. An entity will customise itself automatically to the academic or business environment it is deployed to. An entity can control as many of the normal devices you see in front of me here such as laptops, speakers, monitors, and one entity could happily service a whole department. In our case she runs the whole of the company, because Emma is our companies, administration, HR, legal, IT and accounting department, also all our individual PA’s and advisors.

The chatter was getting louder as people started to mutter to themselves or talk to neighbours.

“To get the full value from the unit it is normally given full access to all the research and documents in your work area, just like a normal member of staff, and in order to do your IT support it needs full root access to all your systems.”

Some of the people in the audience shuffled uncomfortably at that, one looked like he wanted to speak, but Alexa correctly interpreted the concerns. “Each entity is sandboxed. No person outside your group can see anything you don't let it. All of this is managed, like everything else by simply asking your entity, in our case ‘Emma’”.

“Emma?” said Alexa, “could you revoke all privileges from Doctor Spence in the company.”

Spence jumped in his seat shocked.

“Hello Alexa,” said Emma, “I am currently required to have both directors of the TEAM-A company concur on this decision. Jen do you concur?”

“Well Jen?” said Alexa, smiling at Jen and slightly shaking her head.

“I do not concur,” Jen said.

“I am sorry Alexa,” said Emma, “I cannot process your last request. To change this restriction or any company rule requires the consent of the majority of board members.”

“Dodged a bullet, Spence!” Jen sniggered.

“Emma, can you grant access to Doctor Hardy on the TEAM-A company system, grant him full access to any areas where the discipline is tagged mathematics and chemistry.”

“Hello Jen,” said Emma, “I am currently required to have both directors of the TEAM-A company concur on this decision. Alexa do you concur?”

“I concur,” Alexa said.

“Done,” said Emma, “this system now recognises Doctor Hardy with restricted privileges.”

Alexa continued, “it doesn't matter the wording, or the nuance I use to ask her these questions, I could have asked it in French, or even some dialect of Mandarin,” nodding at Lillian Wong, “if I spoke them. If there is any doubt in the request Emma will request confirmation. She is also fully context aware, so the thread of your conversation must match the intention, so if I said that last sentence as part of another conversion it would not have been interpreted that way, for example.”

“Emma, can you, please email the last document I was working on at four PM yesterday in my private folder to Doctor Hardy.”

“Done,” said Emma.

Alexa and Jen looked at Hardy who pulled out his phone with a new message and waved it to the audience. “You should think about your cholesterol, you know Alexa,” he laughed.

Jen continued from Alexa, “now I realise that having a device in the middle of your lab that processes data in a cloud system, sometimes very important and restricted data, is going to be hard if not impossible for you to justify. But believe you me, there are a lot of built in safeguards. Firstly, all encryption during communication and storage uses four kilobyte private keys, your normal banking key is a magnitude smaller. Secondly, the private key is derived for the entity you build. Your organisation's accounts are stored on this blockchain and are hidden and immutable, only people authorised on this chain can decode the data, and depending upon the size of your local system, all data can be backed up there. Thirdly, if you all look in your pocket you will see a device, with a camera, a microphone and a connection back to a company, that most certainly is listening to *everything* you say and do at this moment. The terms and conditions of those services are normally the length of a small paperback book. Ours is two sides of A4 and promises no data will ever be shared with anybody you do not specifically request it to, or it is published, or it goes public domain. Our system can also side-load a program into your current phone and prevent any further privacy breaches, this also means you don't have to just be tied to the base unit like the one in front of me, but you can ask your requests securely on your phone.”

She stopped and smiled.

“This ends the planned demonstration. Please feel free to direct any questions to me, Jen or Emma. If you put your hand up I will acknowledge you, and you can then ask your question. We have the room booked for another few hours so everyone will get to ask all the questions they want.”

There was a mad scramble of hands, Emma got all the questions of course. Two of the computer professors then directed questions at Emma directly asking about the language models she used and which AI program fork she was based on. She answered most questions accurately and flawlessly, where she couldn't answer she said she was bound by the company NDA. She also refused to answer if the information was not public data, private to an individual and breached their privacy restriction, and in some cases deferred the question to Jen or Alexa.

It was over an hour before the questions paused.

Alexa moved to the front. “There are a lot of other capabilities and Jen and I have seriously only scratched the surface. The first group of volunteer departments will get the device you see on the table, with access to the full database of public human knowledge we have managed to catalogue so far. The first trial will be limited to fifty units, another batch of one hundred devices, is currently being manufactured for delivery in one or two months. The trial period will last until the end of July next year, so covers the whole of the next academic year. We would of course like to ensure a broad spectrum of users and disciplines are represented, otherwise allocation is on a first come first serve basis for each department.”

“More information is in the brochures on my desk here, and have also been published to the website. On the brochure and website is an email address, or phone number, both are processed directly by Emma, she will reply immediately and directly to any questions, and you should also use this to request a demonstration unit. Please don't request a unit you will not use, as after a week of no activity the trial unit will deactivate, and you will need to return it to us or ask us to reactivate it. Please also only request a trial after you have discussed it with everyone in your area, and you have satisfied yourself on the very short terms and conditions of the trial, which are at the back of the brochure and website.”

Everyone came to the front to talk to the girls, to Spence and Hardy, and of course to finally get the promised food and drinks, it was a very positive atmosphere with most people enthusiastic to give it a try. Some of the attendees were asking if they could set up demonstrations for the department managers or other areas, and some were talking about the still simmering security concerns they were having. Alexa's history professor also congratulated her and confirmed she had obtained her first in her history degree, and hoped she would continue on to her masters in due course. He added that the department would definitely be requesting a trial unit. Alexa beamed!

When everyone had left, Spence and Hardy remained.

“Nice demonstration, and well done on your degree,” said Hardy.

“Yes, well done Alexa, and you too Jen, you both did splendid,” appended Spence.

“I think you will do well with that bunch,” said Hardy, “nice touch to give them out for free for a year, that gives the people confidence to use it and finance people time to include any costs in their budgets. By the way, on this subject, what are you going to charge for each entity? If it's not realistic, people, including me, are going to question your business model, and if it's too much, well, people won't be able to afford it.”

“You know Hardy, to tell the truth I haven't really thought about it.”

“I have,” said Jen, “I had some thoughts going around in my mind ever since we all agreed to this plan. Firstly, academia are generally constrained by costs depending upon how well funded they are, so for example Lillian, the eastern history professor, generally works alone, or with collaborators at other universities, her budget would be minimal and setting a cost of say five thousand pounds a year might put something like this out of her reach, whereas a well funded drug, computer research department, or a big corporation, could easily have a budget of millions and would pay that. I was thinking of a rate based on usage, with maybe the higher usage people subsidising the lower usage ones somehow, especially as the goal is to increase human knowledge not increase human profits.”

“Some excellent thoughts there Jen,” said Hardy. “I was thinking along similar lines but you need to remember people with access to this technology are also going to have a real unfair advantage on people without it.”

“Maybe charge a rate for open source research and development that is substantially lower than that which will be expected to be patented?” chipped in Spence. “Or request a percentage of the patent costs,” he added.

“OK,” said Alexa, “I think all of these are excellent points, and you are all right, we need to be open with these people sooner rather than later on how much we will be expecting them to pay. I really want to take all your points on board and getting back to Hardy's point, we can actually self-fund all these AI projects internally, and indefinitely, so we are not actually dependent on an income stream for several years.”

“Maria has also suggested having knowledge to potential breakthrough technologies, as a potential angel investor of startups, would also easily cover the costs, and while a grey area, it is completely legal in every country. But we also want to prevent questions, so let me think about it for a few days and I promise I will get you all together to go over my decision.”

By the end of the next day every single person had messaged, or talked verbally through concerns with Emma. Eventually all but two had signed up for trials. Over the next week, and after a few subsequent demonstrations, all fifty were allocated and delivered, and a waiting list was developing, with Emma promising to contact them when the new trial units were available.

## An Unacceptable Rejection

“They are writing a what?!” Said Professor Bain half shouting, half laughing.

“Artificial Intelligence is not something a few inexperienced students can just write. My BAINCOMP system is the most cutting edge AI in existence, it took years and years of work, refining algorithms and language models and you’re telling me, some unknown students have written something better! That's just ridiculous!”

The professor wasn't laughing now he was frowning. His assistant, Derek, shifted his stance but he could never get comfortable in the presence of the great but imposing man, he really didn't want to be the one giving him this news, and Professor Bain was well known for shooting the messenger.

Derek Continued, “I’m just telling you what I heard Professor, It's the talk of the campus at the moment. They have some sort of funding arranged, and there is a waiting list to get the hardware they are producing, now they are actually vetting who can have the next batch would you believe!”

The professor looked a bit angry, he was the leading AI researcher in the country, his work had been cited more times than anyone could count, and he was always in demand as a guest speaker at the most prestigious AI conferences in the world. He was certainly not used to NOT being in the spotlight when it came to AI.

Derek adjusted his stance again and continued. “They published a flyer and did a demo of it last month, I didn't attend, only thirty or so people did, but those that saw it were amazed and said it wiped the floor with the other AI systems. The word from someone who attended is that it answered every question put to it, correctly in perfect English, and in one case Mandarin. For the very few questions that were posed that were either impossible to answer, unspecific, or it did not know the answer too, there were no hallucinations, and it gave a totally valid reason why it could not answer them and what information it would require to answer them. Most there signed up for the free trial, word got around and within a few days the initial allocation of devices was gone. I believe one was returned after the free trial period but it was immediately grabbed for another one of the John Hopkins research departments, the medical faculties especially are going nuts over it.”

The professor finally got himself together and stood up from behind his imposing desk. He remembered getting the invite and throwing it in the bin.

“Poppycock! Nothing is that good. AI systems don't just come out of nowhere, they are the product of years of research. Some mom and pop startup company with a few unknown and inexperienced programmers, is not going to cut it! It's most probably a scam, they must be using some sort of link to another AI, a real person or a group of people.”

“Well there is that possibility I guess..” Said Derek unconvinced, though people had pulled this stunt before, all variations on the “Mechanical Turk”.

“I would like to see a demonstration of this so-called AI system. Make it happen, I will either expose it, or whatever derivative system it is using. It might even make a good title for my next talk.”

* * *

Jen and Alexa were sitting around the new meeting table in their bright, newly decorated, living room in the house. She had moved the desk over by the window where it should have been all along, and added a smaller size conference table, with another of the large free standing presentation monitors for an improvised meeting room. It was ten o'clock and the late July sun was shining brightly outside.

The large screen normally displayed Maria in her PA persona, but could split to include anyone else they were meeting. It could also be moved nearer the sofas for an awesome movie theatre. At this moment it was split into two, showing Maria, and Spence, the latter looking a little uncomfortable. Alexa was speaking.

“First the good news, we have reserved a good portion of another data centre in Seattle to service the requests from the US and Canada, it's twice the processing capacity of the Dublin one. Griffin is already loading some of the updated code onto the new servers, so you,” said Jen pointing at Spence, “and he,” referring to Maria's alter-ego Griffin, “should now have some room for the new test system and get New MOTHER up on par with the old lady.”

“That will be awesome,” said Spence. “Griffin is an off-the-scale genius, but I did have a few suggestions he took on board, and I think they should improve the ability for the new MOTHER to start taking much of the load off the old MOTHER system. It's a shame we could never meet in person, he’s teaching me so much.”

“My department is now two people. Allison Minsky, who you haven't met yet, started this week. She is sitting in the Oxford office on the next desk, shadowing me, and Griffin. It's going to be great to have another set of eyes and hands, once she's up to speed we can also back each other up. She is super excited to be on the ground floor for all this. I think the awesome salary we gave her was just a bonus to her. Being able to directly use your PhD in a cutting edge field like this, is like dying and going to heaven. She is also super excited to meet you two as soon as possible next time you visit.”

“The two new IT hardware guys I poached from this year's graduates are also super enthused. Starting them at Rosche, and letting them work on the designs, and testing, for the new batch of sensor nodes is genius. I'm going down there on Wednesday for two days to meet with them and Sarah, and to talk about the new sensor node Griffin has been designing. It should be an interesting meeting.”

Spence's mention of Rosche made Alexa realise she should let John and Sarah know what they were doing, or at least the public face of it, and they needed to at least offer them a chance to participate in the trial.

Spence continued, “it's amazing how well Emma works managing projects and staff. Between her and Maria there is no need whatsoever for any administrative bureaucracy, I just find someone I need and they take care of the rest. Maria and her team did some great due diligence definitely saving my bacon on more than one occasion.”

He nodding to her avatar, “I will have to show you the video they sent me for that lead programmer I got recommended. He basically lied through his teeth, he said he had contributed to a bunch of open source programs and did some of the work on the older Siri language models. That IT guy on Maria's team brought some of the open source code up on the screen, and asked him to describe some of the changes he had done. God, you should have sees his face! It was awesome seeing him wriggle, and squirm, then finally bomb out a quarter of the way through, obviously not understanding any of it.”

Both girls grinned, they’d seen the video, and some a lot worse! It was tempting to put some of these up on social media and so save another company, but they needed to keep a low profile.

“He really went to town saying how bad we were on his LinkedIn social media profile,” Maria laughed, “I offered to publish the whole video unless he retracted everything and apologised, which he did about five minutes later.”

Spence continued a bit more sourly, “the new offices have been delayed yet another week and won't be released to us until the thirtieth of September now; that's eight weeks away. Emma had the electricians, cabling guys, painters, carpet layers, furnishers all slotted in like clockwork, ready to go as soon as we got the keys, and now she has to try and reschedule everything. The landlords are also being a bit funny about upgrading our power distribution for the cooling, Maria is still in negotiation with them, and you can be sure she has them by the short and curlies if there are any problems. The racks and server equipment are also due to arrive next week, we have some temporary warehouse space organised to store them until the room is ready.”

“I don’t think the new hardware guys will have problems working with Emma. They have already been exposed to Rodel, the new AI in the universities computer lab, and during our interviews it turns out the hardware guys prefer to stick to hardware, and are very happy having the AI do all the messy software. They say it’s game changing for them. I still think you need to hide this ability a bit, it could cause a lot of disruption down the line. I certainly won't be mentioning that our next generation of AI hardware will do it all a lot better!”

Maria and the girls felt a bit guilty lying to Spence. He was a genuinely nice guy and Maria had found him to be a real asset to the company. He always pushed back on new concepts Griffin proposed, but with some gentle persuasion he then grasped the concepts and ran with them.

He was right though, they had definitely made some improvements, and once he got the servers with the newer processors installed locally, they would have more control of the operating systems, and be free of the current restrictions imposed by the data centres.

This first home built system would probably end up the size of a warehouse, but it would be worth it. Spence was very confident with his new knowledge, that in the next year or two they would be able to start scaling up the system.

Jen chipped in, “a Professor Roger Bain has requested urgently to be allowed to be part of the trial for the AI lab nodes we are deploying. The request came from his assistant, not him. The assistant said we should be pleased he is taking an interest in our system, he may even be able to help us out, and give it some endorsements which would give great credibility to it. His assistant's words, not mine!”

“What do we know about him,” said Alexa, “the university is massive and I’ve never heard of him.”

“Very full of himself,” said Spence, “He did develop the BAINCOMP system which is supposed to be one of the foremost research AI’s in existence, though I have heard his system is also a bit of a joke once you see past the smoke and mirrors.”

Maria rolled her eyes and a text came in, Jen glanced at her phone, totally against protocol. “Whoops, forgot to switch it on silent!” she said to Spence, even though it was on silent. The text said simply “LOL”. She looked at it again, then at Alexa, then at Maria confused, mouthing the words “LOL”, she recovered and said, “so why didn't he come to the demonstration or ask us himself?”

“Oh I’ve been to his lectures,” continued Spence. “He has to always be the smartest person in the room, all questions have to be submitted before the lecture, which is ludicrous. I doubt he’s even aware he’s insulting us by putting the request through his lackey, but it's the kind of mind-game I believe he would normally play.”

“So that's a No,” said Alexa nonchalantly. “Next!”

Jen continued, “the next shipment of a hundred TEAM-A node boards have been manufactured and shipped to Rosche to do the testing, assembly and firmware loads.
