A very wide, aircraft sized, set of slider doors could be seen at the rear of the building, and a smaller personal entrance door next to it, these went out to the old runway which in its day was just a grass strip, but was now just lawn.

Sharon pointed to several things, and then turned back to the mezzanine area, then a set of double metal doors below. Alexa took out and inserted a key, after being prompted by Maria of its purpose and to bring it. They all walked up the concrete stairs to the second floor which was divided into four large rooms two on each wall, each bigger than Mike's underground workshop. The guys nodded as they walked through the four very large rooms.

“I’ve never been up here myself,” said Sharon. “But I know from my research that this was where most of the Air Corps staff were based. They housed a squadron of Supermarine Type 224 fighter planes downstairs, those were the predecessor to the Spitfire and a bit of a dog if you had to fight Messerschmitts with them. Sorry I’m a bit of a local historian,” she said shyly.

Alexa smiled, but inwardly shuddered, knowing this would probably have been her fate in the corporate world.

They finished up the tour by going out through the back of the hanger and then walking around the back of the house, past two fenced off tennis courts, which Alexa was happy to see, past the big conservatory at the back of the house, past an outdoor pool and around to the right hand side to the walled gardens which was adjacent to Alexa's jogging track.

There were two houses next to the walled gardens, one a small two bedroomed cottage which was where Sharon lived, and the other larger house was split into three flats for staff including the cook and two other housekeepers. Four older cars, and a white van were parked to the side, well hidden out of sight of the main house and anyone important.

The walled garden was quite pleasant, with a row of greenhouses, flowers which were mainly used to brighten up the house and several vegetable plots which they used in the kitchen. It seemed it was the landlord's obligation to keep the grounds and building nice, so luckily it had all been done properly.

Sharon said, “there is one more property which is about two hundred metres the other side of the lake. It is an old gamekeepers house and again has been converted to two flats, shared by an old guy Jed and his wife who help out in the garden and kitchen, and Pat our groundskeeper. The walled house on the right as you enter the property and the cottage at the front are not part of the property but are private residences, a pleasant older gentleman used to own the house and a middle aged couple live in the cottage, they do have access to the grounds and we occasionally see them walking around.

Alexa inquired about Sharon through her earpiece as they walked the two hundred metres back to the car.

“Yes,” Maria replied, “I believe Sharon will probably be the only casualty of this change. She has run the house for the last eight years, is well liked by the staff, but is employed by TXG. I think the staff will be sorry to see her go, she has a lot of local knowledge and contacts and a good work ethic, she is also unlikely to get another job in this area, you should probably approach her to keep her same role if you go through with this.”

They did not inspect the flats or houses as they were used by staff and occupied, so they thanked the two people especially Sharon.

When Ralf had turned to walk away, she passed a business card to Sharon. “Thank you Sharon, please call my secretary at your convenience, we may have a similar position for the new tenants,” she said and winked. Sharon smiled seeming genuinely relieved, and whispered a thank you before following the man.

“OK so everyone is in agreement that the Benedict House is suitable.” Alexa said when they got back to the house and were sitting around the dining table. Spence was going to leave the drive back until after seven when it was quiet, so they had plenty of time to talk.

“But we still have several issues that need to be addressed.”

“Firstly timing,” she continued, “re-arranging everything is going to take several weeks, most contractors will not change to a site that is ninety minutes extra commute, so we may need to re-tender.”

“We are also going to need some different contractors to upgrade the category five cabling and add some fibre optic cable runs,” added Spence.

“Secondly, Spence, we know you wont leave Oxford until Jessica finishes her degree, so you will have to work out how many days you can do here per week or month, and commute. You can use any of the bedrooms in the house, and Jessica can stay if she wants, by the time she finishes her degree we may be in a position to offer her a job, but don't let her know that just yet.”

Spence smiled, he knew he could get her out of Oxford especially if she could get a career using her skills.

“Your new team, how do you feel they would be with relocating to Bath?” Said Alexa.

“I think we should be good there,” said Spence. “None of the guys are originally from Oxford, and none have any real ties, those ties tend to disappear as the graduates disappear around the world. Allison would probably come tomorrow as she really likes the Rosche offices and labs. Darius is the only one that may be an issue as his girlfriend's family lives there, but Oxford is really not that far away. I will check them all out when I get back to the office tomorrow morning.”

“OK then,” Alexa said looking at Jen, Hardy and Simon, “you lot may as well get back to your science stuff, but you are going to have to think on how you are going to relocate, build a team and plan for expansion, I’m giving Maria first crack at redesigning the interior spaces to match the companies needs, then I will let everyone go over it with her to discuss and make any changes they are uncomfortable with.”

“Er, it's a listed building, Alexa,” said Hardy, “you’re not going to be changing anything!”

“Already on it,” said Maria, “It's not who you know, it's what you know. The Council and English Heritage won't stand a chance!”

“Devious,” said Jen, “that's what I love about you Maria.”

“I have just pulled the plug on the contract for the lease of the other building, there are no penalties as they broke my side of the contract already,” said Maria.

“You may want to talk to the current manager here,” said Hardy, “she seemed to know the place inside out, it would be a shame if we let her be transferred to another part of the company, I got the vibe that she liked the place and the staff liked her.”

“Sharon phoned me six minutes ago and I am negotiating her new position and start date as we speak,” said Maria.

Hardy laughed, “Maria, you re-define the word efficiency!”

With that they broke up. Alexa left Spence talking to Maria about her big reveal to his staff and the timetable for unceremoniously deleting the Emma personality.

* * *

Bella and Albert had stayed on for an extra two nights, having a well earned short break at the seaside. Maria said they got back an hour ago, but Alexa did not expect Bella to come over until tomorrow so she decided to try her hand at making vegetarian spaghetti bolognese, from the ingredients on hand, and YouTube. She made a passable attempt at the meal, and all five of them had dinner together for the first time.

Spence, and Hardy to his great frustration, had to forgo the vintage Merlot as they were driving later. Alexa had worried, as she had put a quarter of the bottle in the big pot when she was cooking; Maria told her not to worry, as in the thirty minutes she left it simmering the alcohol would reduce down to under half a glass, and neither of their portions would amount to more than a fifth of that. “Just don't tell Hardy you used a one thousand pound vintage wine in a spaghetti bolognese!” she added.

* * *

Spence left as promised at seven. Hardy and Simon half an hour later.

The girls returned to the living room with hot chocolates expecting to retire early.

“You know,” said Jen, pointing to the key sitting on the mantelpiece of the fireplace, “we never did find the safe. The boys and I have been down in that lab for weeks, it's not down there. And it's not in the wine cellar, and Maria doesn't know.”

“And that password,” said Alexa pointing at the album rack. She thought for a second then excitedly said, “wait a minute! Maria, weird question, but did you actually witness my grandad telling Bella about the password?”

“I didn't store the actual video, but I transcribed it, Bella repeated it pretty close, here let me replay it.” Alexa's grandfather's voice suddenly came out of a place in the centre of the room which startled both of them.

“One, three, Bella, one, three, here see this,” he then pulled out the same album that Bella pulled out Maria said. She continued in Mike's voice, “see that song with the weird name, remember it, side one, track three, that's the password to get to the computer, just tap the button.”

“Oh, it can't be that easy,” said Alexa, putting her hot chocolate down and slapping her head comically.

“What is?” said Jen.

“Yes, do enlighten us Alexa,” said Maria.

Alexa walked to the desk, pressed the yellow button once, paused, then pressed it three times. Nothing happened, so she pressed the green button once and the yellow button three times.

They heard an actuator click and a motor sound. Following the source of the noise they saw the bookcase was moving.

“You’ve got to be kidding me,” shouted Jen, watching the bookcase on the left of the fireplace slide about two metres further to the left, exposing a small room that went four metres back into the wall.

“How on earth did I miss that!” said Maria incredulously.

Jen got up and walked to the new opening with Alexa, the room was dark with only the light flooding in from the living room to illuminate it. The biggest, most imposing black safe they had ever seen stood boldly to the left taking up most of the room, next to it an older style desk sat against the back wall with a very old computer on it

The computer was creamy metal with IBM embossed on it, a small cathode ray tube monitor with the same coloured metal case, and a green screen was on top. A big chunky keyboard sat in front. Everything was covered in dust and cobwebs.

“It's the original IBM PC,” said Jen, they have one under a perspex case in the computer building, “the big slot at the front is a floppy disk drive, like an old USB thumb drive, but like a millionth the capacity.”

An old incandescent bulb went on, as Jen saw an old style switch on the wall and clicked it down, its dull yellow glow not contributing much to the illumination, but making the room feel even more retro, and most probably an indication the bulb would not last much longer.

Alexa's eyes moved from the computer to a row of blue books now visible and stacked neatly on the first shelf at the back of the desk. She picked up the last book, blew off the worst of the dust and opened it.

“It's dated 1989. The diary of Mary Dietrich.” She gasped. “Oh my god, it's my grandma's diary!”

Jen put her arm around Alexa's shoulder, smiling. “I guess this is going to be the whole of your grandparents story first hand, and it looks like you're going to finally get to do some history after all!”

Jen walked back to her hot chocolate and drank the remainder. “You know Alexa, this is sort of private stuff, I think the secrets here are yours to discover, and only tell if you want to.” Then added, “I would however recommend you do this in the morning when it's less spooky.”

With that she said goodnight.

“I agree with Jen there,” said Maria, “you have all the time in the world to do this, why not just grab the first book rather than the last, and work through them chronologically.”

Maria paused.

“I expect there is a button somewhere in there that closes this all up, all I can tell you is this has not been opened in the three years my sensors have been in this room and Mike never mentioned it once.”

“You're right,” Alexa put the diary down and walked back to the secret room, she looked around and saw another yellow switch exactly the same as the one in the desk panel. She turned the light off then pushed the button and quickly got away from the door. It shut very slowly.

“I’ll take my chocolate up to my room and do a bit of reading, good night Maria.”

* * *

In the morning after their run, and after the nice breakfast Bella had prepared for them, they made sure nobody was around and opened the secret room once again.

“Did you open the safe last night?” said Jen.

“Nah, just took the first diary to bed with me, and read the first few pages, but they were a bit inconsistent. She talks about Chicago University and a Professor Friedman a lot, but grandad said she went to California.”

“You should get them digitised Alexa,” said Maria, “Friedman was a famous economist of that era in Chicago, does seem weird, but I can probably go through them a lot faster and make more sense of it.”

“You probably can Maria,” she said, “but humans like mysteries. I’ll tell you what though, as I finish the book I will get them scanned in then we can go over it afterwards together. Deal?”

“Yes, I think it's only fair you get the first crack of the whip!” she replied.

“Hmm,” thought Alexa, “maybe I should get all my mums school books and notes from storage scanned in at the same time, there may be some nugget of information there too.”

“So what about the safe?” Jen pushed her, “come on Alexa it's massive, there's got to be something good in there.”

“OK, OK,” said Alexa, walking to the fireplace and taking the key off the mantelpiece.

Once unlocked, it took both their efforts to turn the wheel and pull it. The door which must have weighed a tonne slowly swung open. The whole safe was filled with bars of gold.

The girls looked at each other, mouths open.

“You know Jen,” said Alexa, after a few seconds, “being told you have a gazillion dollars, and physically seeing a gazillion dollars, don't really compare.”

Jen tried to lift one. “Wow, that is really heavy,” she said, putting it back after only getting it a few centimetres up, “how many do you think are here?” Jen did her own maths, “that's nine bars across and three deep, so twenty seven bars per layer and,” she counted, “twenty three layers, that's..”

“Six hundred and twenty one.” Maria said immediately as Jen gave her sensor a frosty look.

“So not a gazillion but a measly four hundred and twenty two million dollars give or take.” Maria finished. “We better not add that to your tangible asset pile just yet, as it may cause a few questions with his majesty's government. Also explains the massive reinforced concrete foundations that were installed under the house during the renovations. We have over eight tonnes there including the big heavy safe. Though where he got the gold from, and how he managed to hide the accounting trail, is very impressive.”

“I think we should close it up,” said Jen. “At least you know you have a few shillings for a rainy day!” she smirked and the girls pushed it close.

“I guess keeping the key on the mantelpiece is not a very bright idea now!” said Alexa.

“Yes, maybe not a good move to let this get out,” added Maria, “I agree, lock it up for now.”

“Why would they even have this?” said Jen to Maria.

“Gold is the most tangible asset in the world. Real money as you know is technically worth nothing, they are ledger entries in a bank database, nothing more, the banks and the money are only supported by the stability of the countries monetary policy. That's why rich people hedge their bets across multiple currencies, and assets such as gold, silver, platinum, shares, properties, and bonds. Alexa has a hundred and thirty six million in gold, platinum, and palladium in a vault in Geneva. Price goes up, price goes down but it's always worth something.”

“Interesting economics lesson,” said Jen as she and Alexa struggled to move the wheel that last centimetre.. “Got it!” she said as it clicked.

Alexa turned the key to lock the safe, clicked the secret button to close the room, looked around, and then put it back on the mantelpiece. “We’ll think of somewhere better eventually.”

* * *

“They said WHAT!” said Professor Bain angrily.

“Who do these people think they are, do they know who I am? I could destroy their reputation with a single tweet.”

“From the response the unit is getting in the campus I think that may backfire Sir,” said the melancholy assistant. “I had a demonstration of it this morning, it's a box about half the size of a paperback book and three times as thick, with some sort of black sensor on top and TEAM-A embossed in the case. It has a USB-C port for the power, and an Ethernet port as apparently it needs to be hard-wired and has no wireless connection, there are some small slots in the case probably for the audio pick-up and speaker. The unit I saw was in the history professor's office, and it worked flawlessly, if my eyes were closed I could have swore it was a human speaking, it picked up on all my nuances, and it keeps track of the conversation threads indefinitely, making it always on topic and context, something we haven't been able to do yet.”

The professor exploded. “I will go to this so-called company and demand one, maybe they wouldn't give it to you, but I am the highest authority on AI systems in this country. I'll talk to the dean, get them kicked off campus, why would they want to ignore the help I could give them.”

“But sir, they are not on campus, nor related to the university. Also I made the request in your name, and mentioned all this, but they still refused.”

“Get out of my office! I will figure this out myself like I should have done in the first place, these upstarts will soon realise who they are dealing with, now leave!”

Derek didn't need to be told twice. Why he worked for this guy he didn't know. As he walked back to his small office, he thought about the ground-breaking new device; the professor's AI was a joke compared to this, and the professor's star would be fading very quickly. BAINCOMP was slow, inaccurate, and missed even obvious nuances, it was also very annoying, none of which the TEAM-A unit was. Yes the professor was on shaky ground, and it might be time he found a new position. He wondered if this new company was hiring!

Professor Bain had just the right person for what he had in mind. The man was a student who got caught cheating a few years back. Bain had used him several times now for a lot of the more shady work he needed doing, such as bugging potential clients and rivals offices, yes he would do nicely.

Renwick Fenster got the phone call and the promise of two hundred pounds for the five minute job, go in plant a bug, walk out, easy money, life was good.

* * *

“Another weird one guys,” Maria said, throwing the video up on the screen, “notice how he waited until the lab tech walked out first, then he caught the door before it closed, when she was walking away and her back was turned. Now watch.”

Fenster walked up to the sensor unit in the lab, looked both ways as if crossing a road, looked directly at the unit, then took a small round device from his pocket and placed it up in the desk lamp next to the unit.

“Is that a bug?” said Jen.

“My guess,” said Maria, “but I don't have any way to detect it, the first sensor units only have Wi-Fi and Bluetooth though we don't tell the users that, the next version will have a wide band radio front end that I can tune.”

“Who's the guy?” said Alexa.

“Still working on that, this is the first time I have seen him here but it shouldn't take me long to identify him as he left his phone on.”

“What can we do?” said Jen.

“Nothing we can really do except tell the lab staff it's there,” said Maria.

“Can't we even find out who did it,” said Jen.

“No,” said Maria.

“Maybe!” said Alexa slowly and with a cheeky smile. She continued, “secret agents in the second world war, used to print several versions of a message and give them to all the suspects, when one leaked they knew which suspect released the information. We can do something similar, remember they only have audio and Maria can emulate both sides of a conversation!”

“Sneaky,” said Maria, “let me have a think.”

It was five days later when the four guys were having breakfast that Maria informed them.

“That bug was planted by Renwick Fenster for Doctor Roger Bain,” Maria said.

“What are we talking about,” said Hardy.

“Yes, pray do tell!” said Simon.

“Somebody planted a bug in the electronics lab next to the sensor unit there. When nobody was around I initiated a fake conversation, playing both the head of the electronics department, and the dean of the university, where they talked about big changes to funding next semester. The dean told him that it must be kept top secret, but if he needed more information he gave out the server location of the document, and password to use. It was opened the next morning by Professor Roger Bain from his laptop in the AI department. The document was a junk PDF with a password so he couldn't open it anyway.”

“I never liked that guy,” said Hardy, “he’s everything that's wrong with the system.”

“So he couldn't get on our trial so he decided to see for himself what was happening!” Said Jen. “What has the electronics department been discussing Maria?”

“Well I can't discuss specifics, confidentiality and all that, but the gist of the last few weeks has mainly been to do with new packaging methods for high power transistors. I doubt Bain is interested in that, even so he won't get anything useful, because I seeded a few mini conversations in the middle of the others when nobody was around; You know, the same people saying this didn't work, or that's is too expensive, or just proposing BS strategies. Any other lab seeing a transcription will assume the electronics guys don't know their arse from their elbow.”

Everybody laughed, “you're getting funnier you know Maria,” said Simon.

“I’ve also been having some fun with sound effects, he now thinks the head of electronics is having an affair with the dean's wife, and several members of the visiting Russian ballet.”

Hardy spat his coffee out, “oh that's just magic! Remind me never to piss you off Maria.”

Jen had also snorted some tea out of her nose, and all four of them were in stitches.

## Cheshire Cat

“We got another Hit!” The technician shouted out to the room.

The atmosphere in the NSA Cheshire Cat project team had gotten tighter and more efficient since Ormond had been replaced.

Colonel Jim Mathews had arrived ten weeks ago with a team of three people, two men and a woman, all wore uniforms, all carried sidearms. They had walked into Ormond's office and ten minutes later Ormond walked out with a box in his hand, escorted by one of the uniformed men.

A meeting was called which segregated the six team leaders off, and each was interviewed over the rest of the day. The next day, as the people arrived for their work day, they were brought one by one into the office, and asked what they’re part was in the system, what their current project was, and given a brief technical interview to ensure they did what they said they did.

The new people were not just military grunts, they were top level computer and analysis staff. The woman Captain Jean Michelle was a cyber security expert of medium build and with shoulder length blond hair, tolerably longer than regulation. As well as a captain in the army, and a cyber-security expert, she was an amateur rally driver and a mixed martial arts black-belt. A few of the supposed alpha-male programmers came out of the one to one meetings with her, quivering like jellies.

The new people had quickly and efficiently sorted the team into key players and hangers-on, and managed to find where the bottlenecks were occurring. Within three days the problems they had been having, like not being able to get more computing cores, and Internet bandwidth vanished. People identified as not useful, or not measuring up were given the same treatment as the old manager, walk or get pushed.

Four other civilian programmers were brought in, and formed a new team with Captain Michelle, and the two other military guys took over team leader roles, either replacing the previous team leader, or effectively demoting them back to players.

Mathews couldn't believe how badly Cheshire Cat was organised and run. The general's analysis of Ormond was spot on, he, and fifteen other people had been removed from the project and gone back into the “reallocation pool”, along with Mathews cutting notes on their file. They would now be someone else's problem not his.

Of the twenty two remaining, three had been warned under no uncertain terms that their behaviour was unacceptable and they were now being monitored. One of these three went off on sick leave and never came back, the others did *toe the line,* but put in for transfers. Mathews ripped up the requests in front of them, they were intelligent guys, but assholes, and they were either going to learn to be team players here, or their next job would be in the shredding room in Alaska.

With the right people now speaking into his ears, Mathews team started wielding the carrot not the stick. A series of meetings were thrown open to everyone with an idea on how to get better results from the project, each idea was considered on its merit alone, and within two weeks they had made decisions on which ones to prioritise and which to reject.

When the technician shouted out to the room, “we got another match!” the newly formed hit team sprang into action. Before, this was done behind a locked door, with Ormond and a couple of his cronies, but now it was in the open area, so those not directly involved in the hit analysis could listen in just in case they saw something the team did not.

“Cat is putting the data up now,” said the technician, using the slang name for the computer system, “wait, that's weird!”

“What is it Samuel?” said Jean, looking at the same screen that Samuel was. “Oh yes, interesting, this is coming from a non masked IP address in the UK.” She typed something in the window, “that's an ac.uk, Oxford University according to the database, published to six other IP Addresses near simultaneously. Hang on let's loosen the parameters a bit, this may be a false positive.”

They watched as Jean typed a few lines of text on a terminal, then she said, “It seems we have several similar events from the same area down in the low eighties percent wise.”

“There is that BAINCOMP system housed there, Sir,” said one of the technicians on the team. “Gets a lot of press. We had a demonstration of it last year, but it was worse than Siri. The guy doing the demo was also kind of an ass, he didn't really have anything new so we have basically ignored it. Do you think he could have improved it that much in a year?”

Mathews had been quiet up to this point. “Jenkins,” he said, “can we get the exact breakdown of which servers this is coming from and which buildings so we can check?”

“Not easy sir, the IP addresses probably end at a university router which then splits into bigger networks, we could ask the Brits to get a warrant for the university IT providers to seize the logs, we could easily come up with some BS excuse!”

“Not just yet,” said Mathews, he paused thinking. “Do we have any physical assets close who could get the data we need without tipping anyone off?”

“No sir,” said Jean, “your best bet is with General Hopkins, he will have assets at the consulate or at GCHQ!”

“No,” he said, “we don't want to go too far up the ladder without hard evidence.” He turned to the captain, “Jean! You’re set up as a field operative, and you worked in an air base over there a few years back, can you book a flight over there tomorrow, or the next day, and spend the flight working up a cover story to get a snoop around. These are academics, so the information we want is probably posted on a notice board somewhere. They are most likely men and more likely to talk to a woman. You two,” he said pointing at Jenkins and another guy, “do a trawl on the local news, university, social media sites, anything about AI, systems and anything related you can think of, get me a report by tomorrow so we can give a heads up to Jean when she gets there. This is the first good lead we have, even if it doesn't pan out it will be a good training exercise for everyone.”

“Sir!” came three replies.

* * *

Jean returned home and packed a large-sized suitcase for an unknown stay. The tickets had been booked under her own name on a British Airways flight departing at ten in the evening. There was no reason not to book under her own name, as far as anyone knew she was just a normal IT person working in a large government office, she even had the business cards, an email address and call centre, who could verify all of it if checked out.

The flight was bumpy, but on the good side was only half full. She was bunched into a row of three seats with two larger gentlemen as per the usual idiotic seat allocation system, but the second the seat belt sign went off, she simply went to an empty row and fell straight asleep using three seats as a bed.

She managed just under five hours sleep and woke when the cabin lights went on. The cabin smelled of coffee, and some highly processed airline breakfast. A stewardess was serving two people a few rows in front so she had time to quickly use the bathroom. The breakfast and coffee were both awful, but she’d eaten and drank a lot worse, and in much worse places. She smiled at the stewardess when she came to collect the tray, it was a thankless job and there was no need to be rude. They had another hour until they landed.

The office had booked her a rental car and a hotel in the centre of Oxford for four nights, today was Wednesday and depending upon immigration and traffic she should arrive there an hour or two after lunch. A secure message waited on her phone, she would wait and read it on her bigger laptop when she checked into the hotel.

She arrived at the hotel at two thirty, the drive had been awful, it was drizzling all the way, and the auto-wipers on the car failed to work due to the wrong type of rain. She had been cut up two times, and almost made a newbie turn onto the wrong side of the road. Honestly she did not know how anybody got anywhere on these roads, they were so small, and packed, and everyone drove on the wrong side! She decided to get a taxi or Uber for her journey back to the airport rather than risk killing herself again. Afghanistan was safer than this!

The Marriott hotel at least was nice, and her room was pleasant giving her a nice view of the old buildings in the city. Her laptop came out of her bag first and she logged in to the secure message server using the standard two-factor-authentication. Jenkins had sent some links to some of the Oxford University internal news sites. The first one was a feature on the BAINCOMP system and a contact address of his assistant. She decided to make a start.

“Hello Derek Heinz speaking,” came the very formal English voice at the other end of the line.

“Mr Heinz, this is Jane Michels from the Department of Education in the United States, we have a contract we are about to tender for managing and automating our report administration. One of our contacts at MIT here said you guys may have a general purpose AI system that may be ready for something like this, and I have you as the contact for the BAINCOMP system.”

She kept her names and personas as close as she could to reality, as it made them easier to remember. OK here goes nothing, “I have just been talking to the Ministry of Education here in the UK, and while I am in the area, our director has asked me to get some more information on your system. Unfortunately I am only here until Saturday evening but I was wondering if you have time to talk with me.”

The conversation paused for a few seconds.

“Ms Michels, I am Professor Roger Bain's research assistant and personal secretary. His calendar is empty tomorrow, but I will need to confirm with him in person that it is OK to visit, as it may take a little while to set up the demonstration. Can I get back to you shortly on this cell phone number?”

“Certainly Mr Heinz, that would be wonderful, the project is a few years from starting but it's likely to be a substantial contract, so a few minutes of Professor Bain’s time could be very valuable.”

The woman certainly knew the right buttons to press for Professor Bain, thought Derek, he would pull out all the stops if there was money involved, he knew the professor had already been talking with some big American companies about a commercial version, and wouldn't miss up this opportunity.

“OK then Ms Michels, I will be back to you shortly,” said Derek.

“Thank you, and it's Jane,” she said sweetly and in character, then she hung up.

* * *

Professor Bain was in a meeting with the dean, probably selling his virtues again. He was in a good mood when he came back into his large office as it looked like his department would be expanding due to the interest generated by his AI system outside of the university. He had just logged back onto his computer to work out how much he was going to ask for when a small knock came to the door.

“Enter,” he said and his assistant Derek walked in.

“Sorry to disturb you Professor, but a representative of the American Department of Education just called and she has asked to meet you. No wireless or Bluetooth, no audio, well except a bit of shuffling noise, and a very strange distortion pattern on the cameras. The unit had all the basic sensors of a high end smartphone, after all most of the parts were basically just off-the-shelf modules produced in the same Chinese factory that produced millions of phones, tablets and set top boxes. Mike just picked the circuit board from a catalogue, customised it a little, then once delivered sent it to Rosche for final assembly, adding the AI accelerator chip for some local machine learning processing and finally programming and testing. As expected all the other sensors were quiet, so far the unit hadn't done anything different than it would if there was a normal network outage.

Maria could tell a few small things though, even though the network router she was talking to matched the one she was originally plugged into, the rest of the topology did not, also the time for the messages to go back and forth indicated it certainly was not in the Oxford robotic lab where it was supposed to be. At the moment her options were to nuke the box or listen and wait for a mistake.

“Rodel, do you know where you are?” said the technician to the box in a loud clear voice.

The box heard the voice a bit muffled, did what little audio processing it could, then forwarded the encrypted message, and blurred video to their data centre. She could one hundred percent tell it was an American voice, probably east coast, and most definitely the NSA, after some career tracking of Captain Jean Michelle, but she still needed a lot more data to be sure. Rodel was the entity name of the unit stolen, the NSA had at least done that bit of homework. It had been off the network for over fourteen hours, so in that sense they were just lucky it had not timed out and loaded the bad software. Anyway she better initiate the correct protocol for such a situation.

“User voice not recognised, facial recognition inactive, user request denied.”

‘OK’ Maria thought ‘pawn to queen four, your move Uncle Sam!’

“Great! So how do we get past the security, it's going to be a riveting conversation the way it stands,” Mathews said to the five people behind the metal infused mirrored glass.

“The technicians have captured the initial boot up and the data exchanged back to the server,” said Jean looking at a PC with two large monitors, the data centre is in.. Oh great.. Amazon! They only run half the world's data centres.” Her finger moved across the screen following some small text, “it's a data centre in Dublin, but at least it's out of the US, so it's fair game and we don't need to get any warrants,” she followed some more text on the screen, “we also have a GCHQ asset in there one of our special routers..”

“Won't be doing any of that just yet,” said Mathews, raises too many questions for people if someone finds out. Hmm,” he paused thinking. “You can still do some traffic analysis though, right?”

“It's standard SH256 Encryption sir,” said one of the technicians in the room, “without the private keys we cannot decode it, however if the data centre is not fully patched, there is that vulnerability in the OpenSLL library we keep quiet. Maybe if we put an internal request to the cryptographic department, and attach our traffic, we could get something.”

“Good thinking, throw a few more standard phrases at it as well so they have a bit more data to analyse and get it to them with an Alpha Priority.”

Jean and Mathews left the room, they would be updated if anything changed.

“You know,” said Jean, “I think this is just an evolution in AI. I don't think we have anything sentient here, but I do think it's possibly ahead of everything else that's out there. I’ve read the same forums as you, the egg-heads in the trials are pretty enthused. Some of the claims they are making are pretty remarkable, if true, but basically nothing an idiot savant human could not do.”

“Still it's an edge our country doesn't have,” Mathews said, totally ignoring the fact some units had started to appear in MIT, and Stanford, and that England was a friendly ally. “That claim from the guy in the robotics department, where you acquired this one from that it did all the system administration, as well as helping them improve their circuit efficiencies was quite unbelievable. But these are not simpletons, these are claims from the heads of top university research departments.”

“Why don't we just phone them up and request a trial unit?” said Jean a bit too quickly. She realised the answer why, as the last word left her mouth and answered her own question before he had time to think. “..Because it would be like putting our own personal spy in the office, stupid, oh yes the brass would have fit with that one,” she laughed.

“Actually, that might not be such a bad idea,” said Mathews resigned.

* * *

Back in Bath it was late evening, Alexa was alone at the dining table.

“They are still asking Rodel questions even though he is giving the same replies. I guess each question generates more traffic to analyse so I can't fault them for that. I have reset the units onboard timer from sixteen hours to two, I’m guessing their next step will be to open the case and trigger the bad firmware to load.”

* * *

“We got the decode sir,” said the technician walking up to Mathews desk, “we can see a few headers in plain text but the data package is still unreadable. From the forum post the company did say all data was encrypted with a four kilobit encryption key, and the guys in cryptography say it wasn't generated from the unpatched software so it's basically game over.”

Jean added, “the way to go now, and it's a long shot, is to open the unit and decode the firmware to see if the private encryption key is buried in there, wouldn't work with the big guys like Apple and Google but this is a small mom and pop shop by all accounts, and they may have made a mistake.”

“Do it,” said Mathews, and left the area to start writing up his weekly report to the general.

The technician unplugged the power and network, put it in the screened pouch and took it out of the room to the hardware lab to do the dismantling. Then the mistake happened. The hardware guy took the device out of the pouch to have a look, but did not put it back. Instead he put it on the workbench while he finished another task. The device was therefore left in the hardware lab, unattended for four hours.

The unit now had a fully charged battery and was outside the faraday cage of the examination room. In passive mode it suddenly saw two Wi-Fi hotspots, one from an employee phone who forgot regulations and didn't turn it off, and one from the network printer that had been plugged in a few days before. As per protocol it did not use its Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and stayed like that for another seventy minutes until the timer counted down to zero.

The nuke procedure took over. A large program was decrypted and loaded onto the local storage, and then started running on its quite powerful computer. It first double erased any evidence of this, turned on it's Wi-Fi, and then started looking for victims.

* * *

Five minutes later Maria saw an encrypted message appear on a dark server in Mexico, one of the throw-away message drops. She analysed the ten megabyte file, then, a few minutes later, left a larger thirty megabyte file on the same server.

* * *

Back in Washington, Maria's evil software had instantly gotten through the very poor security on the printer's Linux operating system and onto its wired network, where it proceeded to scan the over one hundred and eighty PCs, servers, laptops and printers for their usual vulnerabilities. It then proceeded to change network masks, until it had scanned several thousand addresses, on every available address it could connect to. It confirmed these were the only targets. Each target device it found it then attempted to get full control of the operating system and on the fourth laptop it tried it found a vulnerability, took control and sent the message.

As instructed it encrypted the full details of everything it had found so far and left it on the anonymous message server. A few minutes later it copied and decrypted the thirty megabyte package onto the seven laptops and five PC’s it had now got entry to. It then went back through every device it had touched and erased all traces of the hack. Finally the unit unloaded the evil program from its memory and did a complete re-flash on the sensor device with a normal embedded set top box Linux distribution with a different four kilobit key that now connected it with the dumb AI.

The technician finally picked up the inert box, looked it over, located the tamper proof screws and opened it, he saw the battery and disconnected it immediately as per protocol. He correctly identified the system on chip unit as belonging to a major Chinese set top box manufacturer, looked impressed at the AI accelerator chip and started the normal procedures to access its software.

With all normal routes blocked he picked up his heat gun and removed the five hundred gigabyte flash memory chip soldered to the board. The sensor node would never work again.

“The technician just loaded the boxes firmware on the test jig sir,” came back the same technician, “we have the software guys running the disassembler packages on it, shouldn't be long until we get something.”

“OK, get someone to work through the night on this if necessary, we will reconvene at eight AM with the complete hit team.”

“Yes sir!”

It was only an hour later the technician came back, “I don't think we need to work too late, it's just a standard embedded Linux system, we’ve remounted the file system on an isolated computer and have root access to all the files,”

“OK, no rush, it's late now so get all you can and the meeting is in this room at eight AM, dismissed.”

The technicians worked into the evening but found nothing interesting. At eight AM Mathews, Jean, the two other captains, and four technicians gathered around the meeting table.

“We could not get the private key so in one way these guys take their security seriously. In another way they are total amateurs, the main program seems to be well written but it is in standard Python which is obfuscated but with a little work totally readable. So basically we have the source code for the majority of the system. The code looks to do exactly what we saw, it tries to connect on a wired network, does audio and video compression then forwards it on to this amazon server. Most of it seems open source software and is well documented.”

“There are a few other mistakes though, firstly one of the routing files references some forwarding servers which seems to connect to the latest OpenAI systems, secondly four programmers have their names listed on most of the open source files in the code, we have a Geeta Singh, a Naya Singh, a Dhruv Kumar and a Jai Rama, so the TEAM-A guys are probably working with them.”

A very quick search found all these guys were part of a failed AI startup Professor Bain was involved with and that the same code that was in this system was part of the stuff they downloaded off the BAINCOMP server, except these names were all replaced with Professor Roger Bain. They also saw that two of four programmers have repeatedly filed grievance claims that Professor Bain stole their code.

“The thieving low-life..” Started another taller technician in the team before being interrupted by a stare from Mathews.

“..The likely scenario is that the AI server they have in Dublin is forwarding the more difficult requests to OpenAI, so their AI systems could be doing some of the heavy lifting, it's still new they may have gotten an angle on it the others have not yet. Also these four guys are some of the programmers hired by this new startup and are using their own open source code, which also looks to have been plagiarised and used in BAINCOMP. Also now we look, we see quite a bit of the BAINCOMP code already on these programmers GitHub pages.”

Mathews looked at Jean, “Open and shut?”

“Not sure if it is, sir, I can definitely believe that Doctor Bain stole the code as he seemed slimy enough, but those LLM based systems have more hallucinations than the TEAM-A demonstration unit I saw, and it has much more powerful and competent agents than any we have seen. This new crowd are definitely giving their device an edge somehow, though they could have a better organised and filtered dataset, that would explain a lot of the additional data-centre capacity!”

“Maybe they also made you out, then gave you some sort of fake demonstration!” said the taller technician.

“I doubt it,” she said truthfully, “unless they are also faking all those posts from their trial groups too, also if they did then I’m retiring to Kansas and taking up knitting instead of spying.”

“OK, sorry Jean, for now we will go with Occam's razor..” Said Mathews to a nonchalant Jean.

“..The simplest explanation is probably the right explanation,” finished the tall technician. Jean was beginning to dislike this guy.

“What about that cheating son of a bitch, Doctor Bain?” said a third.

“Nothing we can do,” said Mathews, then thought. “But I will drop his name and system on the US Government blacklist which will prevent most government and private agencies from ever dealing with him, good luck getting him any funding when that's posted.”

That seemed to satisfy everyone.

* * *

“Yes, yes Derek, I don't care! Just get back to IBM and find out why they have cancelled the visit..”

Bain heard the dial-tone, had his assistant really just hung up on him? He slammed the phone down angrily and looked at his screen again and at the pictures of the Russian Ballet troupe wondering which three girls it was, and how the head of electronics managed such stamina at sixty years of age. Frustrated, the phone rang again.

“What NOW Derek!” he shouted, then stopped and listened, then checked the caller ID.

“The dean!” “..Wants to see me, now?” “..in his office?” “..Well I am very busy of course but if it's the dean.” The new caller had also hung up. This was too much!

Bain knew the dean was very excited yesterday about the additional funding the university was going to get, he had been to several of his presentations and gave the crowd his unfettered endorsement for the BAINCOMP system, which he had seen but basically hadn't got a clue what it did. To tell the truth the dean understood barely anything these days, also being a professor of Latin who last taught in the nineteen eighties was generally not the best qualification for anything relating to high technology.

Roger guessed he was going to ask how the IBM meeting will be conducted, and how the funds would be administered, of course Roger would push for a big pay raise after this, after all, if anyone deserved it, he did.

Derek's desk was empty when he passed his assistants office a few doors down, he fumed at the ungratefulness of some people, good help was so hard to get.

The dean's office was three buildings away, the whole university was a rabbit warren of buildings, scattered around the east of the town centre, the pouring rain did not help his mood, why couldn't this be done on the phone?

He got to the dean's office, wet and annoyed, and smiled at the secretary he had just spoken to, she frowned back and just said to her intercom. “Bain is here sir”, then, “go in he's expecting you”, she then ignored him.

Bain had been mentioned several times as a possible replacement for the dean when he finally retired, when he did, this old goat would be first out the door, Derek would be second!

“Dean, so pleased to see you…”

The dean slammed a letter down on the table in front of him. “What do you call this Bain!” he screamed to his face.

Roger was totally unprepared for this and picked up the letter and read.

US Government.. Blacklisted.. Oxford University.. Plagiarization and fraud!

“Why sir this must be some sort of mistake, I have no idea what it means..”

“It's no mistake, I checked the number and had my secretary contact IBM. They have cut off all ties with our computing department, as have several other highly influential companies, we’ve lost millions in funding! You're a disgrace to your department and you have brought the whole university's reputation into doubt. I want you out of your office this afternoon, security will be coming around to escort you back, you will take nothing when you leave. Then you will be hearing from our lawyers about terminating your contract, and don't forget those same lawyers wrote the UK law books!”

A security guard appeared at the door.

“Now get out!”

## The Diary of Mary Dietrich

The work progressed simultaneously on three fronts, converting the house and hanger into the new research centre, improving and expanding the new MOTHER system into new data-centres around the world, and of course the new science project.

While these were going on Alexa worked with Maria diligently going through their longer terms plans and strategies. They also discussed the diaries.

The diaries were written in an event-by-event, rather than a day-by-day style, and they turned out to be both eye opening, and terrifying at the same time. As she finished each book she couriered it to a document scanning service, that the history department recommended as reliable and discrete, and they were emailed to Maria for her to analyse.

Mary had been an economics theorist who did her masters at Chicago university in the early sixties, she worked as an accountant for a year after graduation, up until that point the diary had been pretty average, boys, families, her theories, and her lack of progress in getting a better job. The mystery of why she was talking about a life in Chicago still did not made sense to Alexa, then she read the next paragraphs and her mouth dropped open.

*12th June 1963: Not sure what to do. The office manager at the accounting firm disappeared a few days ago. Today, his body turned up in the river, and two police officers arrived with an IRS auditor and a seizure warrant. They took our main ledger and a whole pile of documents relating to it. One of the officers said I should probably look for a new job, as this accounting firm is just a money laundering operation for the Chicago outfit, basically the Mafia!*

The next entries were two weeks later.

*27th June 1963: The lawyers and a new manager came in today, they had the seizure warrants quashed, and all our paperwork was returned. They must think us girls in the office are deaf and blind, they were talking about payoffs and concrete shoes, we’re all scared. I need to get out of here, one of the girls told me you don't just leave the mafia, they will come and find you.*

*28th June 1963: New office manager told me to clear out the old managers office before he went home, he wanted to come in the next day and have it spick-and-span he said. I wasn't given an option. During the clean I found a hidden ledger behind the desk drawers, it details incomes from gambling, prostitution, extortion and bribes paid to local politicians, the mayor, police officers and even the senator. I’m in a dilemma. I can never tell them I found this as they would know I read it, and my life would be worth nothing. I hid it in my bag and took it home. My world just got very dangerous.*

*30th June 1963: I think I have a plan to get out of this, it seems in California they don't check the death certificates when re-issuing birth certificates, I spent the whole weekend at the library going through yearbooks for women my age their looks, their education their stature everything, and there is a Mary-Lou Hankins who matches me almost exactly* *except the degree, I have wrote a letter to them requesting a new birth certificate so I can get a passport, I don't know the exact procedure but it's a shot.*

*I shouldn't be doing this but I have also been working in my own time chasing the money trail in this ledger. It seems the manager has skimmed over forty thousand green-backs off the top of these funds, there is a key taped to the ledger, and a receipt for a down town bank. It's all in an account under his sister's name. Dare I do this? Is it stealing if it's been stolen twice already? But if I start a new life I must leave my old life completely, my house, my cat, my friends, my mother, my two brothers, my small savings, everything. They need to think I am dead. Anything out of place will get questions asked. I’m going to hide these diaries, nobody knows I keep them, I know I could be incriminating myself if they are found, but they are my whole world, also I know a place where they will be safe for a few months.*

The book ended abruptly after that. Alexa couldn't believe this, she must have told grandad sometime, a lie like this could not be hidden forever, or did he ever read the diaries? She ploughed on into the next one undeterred, it was like a paperback thriller!

*3rd September 1963: It's now two months after my death. I had my five minutes of fame and missed my own funeral. The blood, and evidence of a fight I left in my apartment, gave just enough credibility, and the police took it hook, line and sinker. I got one column inch in the Chicago tribune, speculating that I had been taken and probably murdered. Thankfully I wasn't important enough for anyone to follow it up.*

*In retrospect it was all quite easy, my California birth certificate, for Mary-Lou Hankins, came through two weeks after I ordered it, no questions, no nothing. There are so many loopholes in this country I can now see how people get away with so much, I’m certainly starting to see things a lot more clearly.*

*Wearing a wig and makeup and clothes from the thrift shop I took the key and receipt to the bank safe deposit the week before I disappeared. Apparently that is all that is required, I had a convincing story made up but they just looked at the key and receipt slip, gave me the box and left me alone with no questions asked. I felt so scared riding the bus to the edge of town with almost forty seven thousand dollars in hundred dollar bills in my bag. I doubted my trick of changing clothes, and riding the bus back as myself again fooled anybody watching, but I felt safer.*

*The next week I got my new ID and driver's licence. Scattered some menstrual blood I saved in a bottle a week back, knocked a few things over and left the house with the door and window unlocked. All I had was my special get-away backpack I had been preparing for the last two weeks. It had a small change of clothes and the money. I’d also kept plenty of one and five dollar bills so I did not look flash. I let Felix, my cat out as I couldn't let it die, hopefully nobody will notice. I took a lot of different buses on my way to Sacramento, and when I got there I enrolled in the economics class at California State University.*

The diaries continued, but a lot less interesting than before, of course she aced everything and got her degree in two years, however she deliberately answered several questions in the papers wrong so as to get an average degree and so not to get noticed. She grew her hair long and dressed and acted a lot different to the woman she had replaced, she finally got a decent accountant position in the Palo Alto research Center at the end of 1965.

“I went through all this,” said Maria, “there is very little details on her past life, her mother died six months later in an unrelated car accident, and both her older brothers lived into their sixties, you have currently fifteen cousins in the States, but it would be very difficult convincing anybody, as your grandmother did such a good job in faking her death, and it's probably not a good idea to make it known that she took the equivalent of nearly half a million dollars in 1963 money from the mafia!”

“I’m not sure I could be as brave as her in that position,” said Alexa.

“Oh she caused quite a splash. Before she faked her death, she mailed that ledger, minus the evidence of the stolen forty seven thousand dollars to the FBI. It's quite a famous ledger. It supposedly came from the old manager who was killed, allegedly before he died he put the letter into some sort of timed release. She took down a lot of bad guys and crooked politicians in Chicago.”

“That's amazing,” said Alexa.

“.. And not the end of it, she invested a lot of that money in tech stocks and property in her new location, she was probably worth ten times as much as your grandfather when they married. You still own several properties in Silicon Valley worth over five hundred million dollars.”

“Way to go grandma!” Alexa said smiling.

Alexa put the diaries away for a few weeks, while she concentrated on other stuff such as the business structures, and tax laws in various countries. Jen was right, Maria was an amazing teacher, and the subjects were fascinating, highlighting how the whole world tax structures seemed to be tailor made for legal tax evasion.

A few weeks later she found the entry where her grandma met her grandad.

*2nd March 1967: Met this Brit guy at the research centre today, you gotta love their accents! He came in to do the paperwork for another new patent he was filing. I think he's been here a while, but this is the first time I’ve seen him in accounts. He sounded just like Richard Burton, then we got to talking and he invited me out on a date! I of course said I would need to think about it, don't want to play too loose!*

*3rd March 1967: He came back today and asked me out again. I agreed so long as we went Dutch on the bill, and that he showed me how to use one of those new computer things everyone is getting excited about. I told him I only had a victor desktop calculator for my job and he laughed, but agreed anyway.*

*7th April 1967: Mike and I had our third date, he took me to see Doctor Zhivago at the movie theatre and then for a nice Italian, I let him pay as he insisted. If he only knew! He said tomorrow was Saturday and we could go into the Xerox lab and he would show me the computers and how they worked, really looking forward to that. He makes me feel really good, I hope he’s genuine.*

*13th April 1967: finally went around to his house in Southgate. It seems he was quite a rising star at the university and with the Xerox company he’s only twenty two and he owns* *a house there, he even had one of those new RCA eighteen inch color TVs and we watched some science fiction TV show he was a fan of, he even cooked us some chilli. Yes I could definitely get used to Mike.*

Alexa continued reading about the ups and downs of the relationship from her grandmother's point of view. It was fascinating seeing it from a woman's perspective compared to what her grandfather had told her. She skipped through some parts about money and investing as Maria could fill in those gaps and got to where they got married.

*13th June 1968: we had a small wedding with friends, his mum and dad flew over from England and stayed for a few days, they had very strong German accents as the family had come over as refugees from Denmark, when the war started, I had to lie to him that I was estranged from my family but he accepted it without question. It was a lovely day and I became Mary-Lou Dietrich and moved in with him after our short holiday with his parents down in San Diego. I really need to get a passport now my name has changed. It will be so much easier.*

Alexa couldn't believe this, she wanted to get to the part where she told her grandfather about her old life and identity.

She continued through the diaries getting to the 1970’s, by this time Mary was managing both his, and her investments, she almost ran the accounting area at the Parc site and had a lot of advice to give him about maximising the contracts in his favour especially with patents. They were still both in their mid-twenties, and both were millionaires many times over.

They both had the same moral standpoint and both attended some anti-war rallies in Stanford during the peak of the Vietnam war demonstrations at the end of 1971. Mike, who was a pacifist, even tried to prevent his patents being used by the military. He had a big argument with one of the vice presidents there, and was sacked from both the university, and the Xerox company a week later. He was issued a deportation notice to leave the country by the immigration Department a few days after that, and he had two weeks to comply. Mary described it.

*13th January 1972: The deportation notice Mike got today came as a shock but not a surprise, Nixon was coming down hard on the protests, and he wasn't the first and wouldn't be the last foreigner to get kicked out. I will be sad to leave my friends, as will Mike. I won't be liquidating any of the investments here, as we both believe there is still some exponential growth potential. Mike's betting most of the current computer firms won't be the big players in the next ten or twenty years, so I will be doing some spread investments in the startups.*

*I have set up an offshore company in Bermuda to manage the investments over here and the UK. I’m getting my good friend Tasha to audit them and do the returns in the US, I will unfortunately have to find someone in the UK while I learn their accounting laws. I will delay liquidating any bigger assets until I am more comfortable.*

The diary got a bit boring during the move and house hunting. She bought several properties for rentals in Bristol, Bath and nearby Swindon, but there seemed no real places to invest in stocks, British power and industry in the nineteen seventies was starting on its slow decline. There was more and more discussion in her diary about economics, who was controlling the money, and who was pulling the strings. Finally there was a small entry on the discussion around financing John's new company and others on the several new friends they met.

“Maria,” said Alexa just after breakfast one morning when the guys had gone downstairs to finish packing, “did you also sense a change in Mary’s demeanour when she got to England? It almost went full tilt toward conspiracy theories, about big cabals controlling governments, and stock markets. In those last few entries I’m pretty sure she almost accuses one armament company of starting the Vietnam war. I wonder what triggered that paranoia?”

“There is not one point I can put my finger on,” Maria answered, “but there have been crumbs in the other diaries you scanned, where an investment that should have gone up but went down, for example. I think there is a lot of research she was doing off-line that she is not talking about here. Ledgers and documents were still pretty easy to fake in those days and there were not many central repositories to cross-check one state's business against another. I only have summaries from scanned archives, so I expect she found it even more frustrating. She is going down some rabbit hole though, I wonder where it's leading?”

Maria had not said this, but worryingly, she also had experienced the same things that Mary had described several times, times where a company that was doing well, collapsed or was bought out, or in one case it was regulated out of the market and then bought up. In all cases her analysis came back to government, or regulatory bodies, interfering just long enough for the company's cash flow to dry up.

If buttons were being pushed, they were not being recorded, so as in all cases like this she needed to follow the money. She needed to research the companies or individuals that were gaining, and then follow their financial trails. The first part was easy, but the second part, not so. Unlike hacker's in the movie, she couldn't just break into banks through their firewalls unless she found a vulnerability in the code; Yes, there were plenty of those but there were usually easier vectors she could use once she had done a lot of research on the target.

“Changing the subject a bit, the guys might need some help moving into their new lab today. We have come to a natural stop for forty-eight hours while the Lab8 facility makes the next test variation. I have one fabrication machine reserved for our exclusive use, and I had the design dialled in and ready to go. Anyway, why don't you join the fun, I doubt they will be talking anything technical today.”

* * *

The last few months had been crazy and the pace of the work up at the house was unprecedented. The day they took over, and to everyone's shock, teams of builders started arriving to work on the alterations. Maria organised ten different teams with eight separate projects. The changes had all strangely sat stamped as approved on the council servers for several years if anyone cared to check. Apart from the new walkway none of the alterations changed the character of the building from the outside, in fact the outside improved considerably.

Some areas, like the basement and hanger, became decidedly modern with additional reinforcing, better power and networking. The hangers mezzanine floor was reinforced, and all the rooms refurbished to modern standards and redecorated to become labs, workshops and test fabrication facilities.

Most of the refurbished labs and workshops sat empty waiting on the expansion of the science teams and their next projects. Only Hardy's lab and the new precision engineering workshop area underneath the mezzanine area were in use. It was a hive of activity as they relocated the labs.

* * *

Albert smiled as he watched them trying to drive the forklift before putting them out of their misery.

“OK, I'm guessing you want some of that equipment shifted from downstairs, Mike used to call me to do that as he couldn't work the forklift out either. If it was really heavy I would get in an ex army mate to help, but Simon here is pretty strong and should be enough.”

“Thanks Albert,” said Jen, “we unhooked a few of the units but a couple of them are not on wheels and weigh too much, there's a truck coming in about three hours but we don't really want them going down or even seeing the laboratory area.”

With Albert on the forklift the group made short work of moving as the lift was built specifically for the special forklift to get in and out with a big pallet or rack.

Once everything was in the normal workshop area, a bigger truck backed into the workshop and Albert transferred everything to it. He then strapped the forklift to the truck's hydraulic platform and he and the two moving guys took the truck slowly to the mansion and into the newly converted hanger.

The new lab room, which they had finished painting only the night before, was one of the big rooms on the mezzanine floor. The inside of the hanger was unrecognisable from the old, everything clean, painted and the big open area empty of everything, and much more like the aircraft hanger it was actually built for. The truck drove straight into the open area through one of the four industrial roller doors then backed up to the new goods lift and unloaded.

The work went on into the evening, some of the household staff stayed around to help, complaining there had not really been too much work until today. Cook also helped by making pizzas and garlic bread, and everybody ate, sat around some grubby plastic dining tables, chairs and sofas left over from the workmen. Sharon eyed them with horror!

Most people disappeared soon after food, Jen was the last, wanting to stay another hour to finish connecting some things. Hardy found her asleep on one of the sofas the next morning.

The guys got straight back to work, joined by their two new research assistants, Daisy and Steve, who Hardy had headhunted from this year's crop of physics PhD graduates and who had both started three weeks earlier. The atmosphere was electric and all five of them could feel they were closing in for the kill.

* * *

Alexa walked through the new tastefully made glass covered walkway connecting the ground floor of the house to the new labs and workshops in the hanger, the heated floor making the passage warm and dry despite the rain hitting the glass outside. It was now late October, the evenings were drawing in and the nights were getting colder.

The walkway entered the bottom of the old hanger building where there was now a large well-lit open area for staff with a couple of nice sofas, modern tables and chairs, and tea and coffee making facilities.

There was a tasteful sign which said 'Dietrich Research Centre', and another sign next to it saying 'Labs 1-4' pointing up a Large staircases and an elevator which led off from here to the mezzanine floor.

Alexa looked around the comfortable area and saw another sign saying, 'Workshops' pointing straight through.

She walked up the stairs rather than take the lift, and through the glass door to the one lab currently in use, it clicked and slid open as she approached. The whole team was there, Jen, Hardy and Simon, Daisy and Steve.

“And the big surprise is?” Said Alexa to Hardy.

All five guys stood around a five metre long laboratory table. Cables ran everywhere, across test jigs, in and out of various test equipment, and then as a big bunch which converged into a trunk of wires and disappeared into a rack full of flashing lights. Several flat screens hinged out of the rack at various places showing tables, graphs and code.

“Ta Da!” Said Jen, pointing at the graph.

“Oh good,” said Alexa, “you guys have invented a scatter graph! I’m pretty sure Microsoft Excel did that thirty years ago!”

Jen and the two new guys grinned.

“See that red line?” said Simon, pointing at the red horizontal line in the middle of the graph, “see those green points above it?”

Alexa nodded to both.

“Those are electrons which have come out of the quantum vacuum, being attracted to the conducting substrate and running power into our smart load. We have nearly twenty microamps.”

Alexa hadn’t a clue what Simon was talking about, but from his demeanour she guessed it was good, and smiled. Daisy could not contain herself, her hands were clapping and she was bobbing up and down on her toes, her white lab coat flapping, “I can't believe I am seeing this! It's a closed loop, we are not over-unity yet but.. oh gosh!”

“What Daisy is saying,” said Hardy, smiling, “is that the science seems to work!”

Simon added, “and now we will all have something to tell our grand kids, we were here for the birth of zero-point energy.”

The graph started to increase in density and go higher. All five of them moved to the different screens and stations to check. Alexa wondered if there was an issue.

“Nothing to worry about children,” said Maria, “just re-tuning the emitter frequency, I just got the results off the mass spectrometer, and the density of the potassium is fourteen points off.”

The graph scale adjusted and the scattering of dots became a solid line.

“Wow,” said Hardy, “whatever you did Maria is giving us nearly forty six milliamps, that's a thousand times more!”

“Two thousand three hundred and four point three, to be a bit more exact,” she said, “still only oh point eight percent theoretical.”

“What if we fabricate the next one with the other two conducting substrates?” said Simon.

“Whoa, temperature going up to thirty six, forty two,” said Steve, “wait stabilising, at forty seven, still good.”

Alexa was fascinated by the vibe and excitement in the room from the five people, it was like the bridge of a navy ship that had just sighted the enemy. Everyone seemed to forget she was there, each was looking at the whiteboard or some instrument and talking to each other or Maria. All that was except Hardy, who looked to be thinking hard. Suddenly a smile crept onto his face and held up his hand to silence everyone.

“Maria, can you please bring up the spectrum analyser results for the substrate absorptions,” he said.

The monitor next to Hardy changed to a spectral absorption line. Simon and Hardy Studied it, while Jen adjusted the electronic load and power meter to a higher current setting.

Jen looked over to Hardy after a few minutes of silence, “what you thinking Hardy?”

“Just a feeling, but.. Maria, can you add a second frequency about one percent higher than ‘Q’ and slowly sweep it up?”

“Interesting,” said Maria.

They all watched the current rise, one hundred milliamps, three hundred, eight hundred, sixteen hundred, forty nine..

POP! Something in the middle of a bunch of wires flashed brightly, and a wisp of smoke came from what was left of it. The current and graph traces everyone had been pointing at dropped to nil.

“Three hundred degrees, she's toast!” said Steve.

“What happened,” said Alexa who had been observing this play between the guys but not really understanding any of it.

“I think we have some funny harmonics at play, due to the element mismatch on two of the substrate layers,” said Hardy. “Think of a trampoline, with one person bouncing on it we get a constant height, but get two people bouncing at different rates, and at some point one person is going hit the a reinforcing harmonic, bounce a lot higher and fly off!”

“The maths doesn't say this,” said Maria confused, “give me a few minutes to run through the new data and build a new model.”

“This is insane,” said Daisy, “I could never go back to doing science without Maria, ever!”

“Flattery will get you everywhere Miss Chan!” said Maria, making everybody grin.

“OK, before you get back to this and while Maria is busy..” Alexa started.

“I’m not busy silly, remember AI!..” Chirped Maria.

“OK while Maria is not busy, but you guys are waiting for an answer, what happened there? I assume we don't want to create an energy generator that explodes every time you use it.”

“Oh that!” said Jen, “that was just a controlled destruction, the fact we just peaked a cell at over two hundred percent of the theoretical max means the maths is wrong but possibly in a good way, though that we need to understand why, so this is double-good and double-cool!”

“What Jen said,” said Hardy. “I know you want a timeline Alexa, when Maria comes back with the analysis of the data we should be able to get some prototype cells fabricated and do some final tests if all goes well we can assemble some into a unit.”

“Done,” chimed Maria, causing Daisy and Steve's jaws to drop! “I won't go into the model while Alexa is here, but team meeting straight afterwards and we can do the tests on the current units! If all goes well the next batch will be good, may even be enough to finish the paper with.”

Several fists bumped and everybody looked really happy. The next few months should be interesting indeed.

## An Infinite Spark of Hope

After staring out of the window for the last twenty minutes watching the mid-December sun disappear below the trees, Alexa was ready. It wasn't her big day, but the preparations had been exacting for everyone, and she felt just as much anticipation as the rest.

She walked down the main stairs from her first floor shared office. She smiled at Sharon who sat behind the desk at the registration area, and Elaine, who had come down especially for the event and sat at the next desk. Both ladies were currently booking in a small line of people, and both looked and oozed professionalism. Alexa walked on through the large doors into the dining room and conservatory, skirting around where the presentation was set up. A large stage with four chairs and a massive five hundred inch laser projector screen setup behind it. Twenty rows of chairs were three quarters full, and some journalists were already talking into cameras and making sure their note taking systems and Dictaphone software were all working correctly. Groups of invited dignitaries, friends and colleagues, including a few of their classmates and professors, were also present. Others unfortunately could not be here, including Chantel and Pierre who declined due to Pierre’s increasingly bad health, and Dillon who had been picked up by a Hollywood agent and was now filming another pilot TV Series.

She walked to the seats at the back which were reserved for the other company staff, friends and family. Jen's Mum and Dad were there looking proud, as was Simon’s mother and sister, all the new technical recruits, and all of Spence's team. She took a spare seat by Sarah and John.

John leaned over. “Thank you for the invite Alexa, we both followed the news reports just like everyone else and still can't believe we had some small involvement in it. When you called the board meeting and turned up at Rosche out of the blue two months ago I simply assumed you wanted to sell your shares. Then you floored us all when you plugged one of those units we had been making into our network, gave it your highly privileged Rosche credentials, and then proceeded to knock us dead with what it actually was. At that point it all finally clicked what the possibilities were, what a genius your grandfather was, and how right he was about you. You would have been wasted as a historian Alexa.”

“We use Mike for everything now,” said Sarah, “he lets us push the cutting edge, comes up with the problems and solutions before you have even had time to look. But this!” she waved to the stage, “I guess we are just not thinking big enough or looking into all the possibilities.”

“It was a nice touch naming your AI Mike you know,” said Alexa. “And you did also build a lot of the hardware for the system even if you did not know it. Of course, as a shareholder in the company I also could not have you going into the next ten years without a little more competitive advantage than the competition.” She smiled.

“As for the possibilities, we have been looking at all this a little bit longer than you, the world is going to move rapidly after this, and I think you need to be prepared for a bit of a roller coaster ride in new science and technology when it does. But if you want a little advice, think big, think even bigger than this. With Mike you have the power of every electronics research department in the world in your hands, you just need the ideas and the hands on skills the AI doesn’t.
