Of course you also have the backing of a certain friendly local entrepreneur if you think it's too much to handle.”

The results had now been reproduced by nine international universities and CERN. Simon, Jen, Hardy and Maria had run the experiments on the final prototype units and authored the paper meticulously, there was not one un-dotted i or uncrossed t. Of course several flawless papers had appeared since the new TEAM-A system AI’s had been released, but perfect papers with boring results were still boring. To ensure the paper was properly supported, ten of the experimental units had then been delivered to these institutions the day the paper was published.

There was initially little reaction. The public and academia, used to exaggerated press releases, and tabloid click-bait chose to ignore it as the same. The paper was titled “A pathway to clean energy production from the quantum vacuum,” It was written both for the layman and the scientist, the two pages of mathematics, numerous graphs, diagrams and photographs, all having a well translated human readable part and hyperlinks that could be drilled down on if more details was required, the paper would set the standards for clarity for many years to come.

Then the first experimental reproduction of the result came from MIT, sensational headlines and numerous talking heads followed. People analysed the paper, both praising it, and saying why it was pseudo-science, and could never lead to commercial power production, or even in a few cases could lead to the end of the world. Maria of course monitored all the channels for them, using both herself, and various aliases, putting down the false science and explaining the good science, it worked to an extent.

Then came more positive results a few days later from CERN, then Cambridge, then Stanford, then Bonn and Tokyo helped by a perfectly translated German and Japanese versions, then all the others followed, the world took notice. Maria fielded all the calls and emails in her usual brilliant manner.

Finally at the allotted time, and after everyone had been seated, the three humans got on the stage, and two of them sat down. It had been decided beforehand that they would all have a turn speaking, but the other two were not so used to dealing with such events, and Hardy was both a pro, and the most well known, so would do the majority of the presentation.

Hardy walked to the front and the crowd went quiet. “Friends, colleagues and esteemed members of the press and public. Welcome to the Dietrich Research Centre.” He started in a loud clear voice.

“By now you have all seen or read that all ten worldwide institutions we sent our test apparatus to have reproduced our experimental results and verified our conclusions. The team that wrote this paper are on stage with me now, the rest of the team, who we could not have done this without are either present in the audience over there,” he pointed to the six technicians at the back including Daisy and Steve, “or watching live from our sister research establishments in America, India and Australia.”

Hardy continued, pointing to Simon.

“Doctor Simon Jones, who has been key in working out the chemical processes and fabrication.” Simon got up and bowed as Hardy turned to Jen.

“Miss Jen Cummings who has diligently been working through the experimental physics and mathematics with me,” Jen got up and bowed.

“And me, Hardy Johnson.” Hardy paused, looking at the empty seat.

“But there is a fourth author of the paper, one who sense-checked every line of maths, physics, chemistry, ran, monitored and analysed every byte of experimental data, and fielded every communication between us and you. She was every bit a part of the team as all the people physically here.”

Hardy looked to the screen and Maria's avatar came up in the bottom corner behind the empty fourth desk.

“Please meet Maria!”

Maria’s avatar waved. “Hello.”

Hardy continued. “For any of you living under a rock these past few months, our sister company has been working in secret for the past several years on an AI system focussed on scientific research and development. The original founder of the company Doctor Mike Dietrich, who was extensively published, and who this research centre is named after, made several breakthroughs before his death. The new CEO formed a team of scientists and engineers to continue this work, and a few months ago pushed through a trial program to several local medical institutions and universities, which soon went global.”

“The result you see here is what happens when you allow an AI to amplify the human brain. The timeline for this project is staggering even for me to believe, for the first line of maths was derived in June of this year. Let me repeat that in case someone misquotes it, June of this year, six months ago, not years.”

“So let me get to the paper. As this is mainly a presentation for laymen and laywomen, we will simplify it somewhat, and I will ask you to leave any questions until the end. So I will have Jen come up, introduce herself and explain what we have achieved here.”

Jen got up and moved to the front, Hardy touched her shoulder reassuringly. Jen gave a well researched five minute presentation of the science, one of her old physics professors decided the end of her five minutes was a good time to ask a question about the strong nuclear force preventing this. She stopped him dead with a hand before Hardy could get up.

“Maria can you put up the bonding energy chart, I think it's the second one in the paper,” the correct chart came up, “that's the one, thanks,” she said. “Professor, if you look at the first kink in the chart,” it conveniently highlighted as Maria was already aware what to do, “the strong nuclear force does not affect the electron in the standard model, and the frequency we are using will only produce fermions. No doubt as you are aware under Pauli's exclusion principle no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state.” It was quite an impressive performance, but Jen was not the same student she was six months previous, Hardy, Simon and even Maria could see she had progressed in leaps and bounds.

To his credit her professor said, “my bad Jennifer, it looks like the student has become the teacher, I probably should keep my mouth shut for the rest of the presentation!” several people laughed.

Simon got up and went through the various doping and frequency trials, again calling upon Maria who did her very best to keep sub-sentient. A few more inappropriately timed questions were asked and answered without problems.

A photograph then came up on the monitor, it was a box the size of a toaster with two wires in it. It was a new picture, not in the paper, nor mentioned in the presentation briefing and several journalists immediately took notice.

“Some of you may be wondering what that picture is behind me that Maria just put up. Well, just like every other decadent capitalist company in the world, we do intend to make a small profit from this, but we can only make a small profit if we have something that works!”

Jen and Hardy got up next to Simon, there was a little five second discussion then both Simon and Jen sat down.

“OK, looks like it's up to me then. The device you see behind me is the prototype of a commercial two hundred watt power generation system that requires no fuel to run.”

Several people shuffled in their chairs and a lot of cameras came out, the press stood to attention.

“Two hundred watts may not sound like a lot but there are a few points I would like to make. Firstly, and I think I may have mentioned it already, this device produces excess electrons from the quantum vacuum and it uses NO FUEL, nada, not a drop, no sunlight, no heat, no wind, no nothing, and like normal batteries you can stack these together in series and parallel to produce different voltage and currents.”

“Secondly it is designed to run twenty four seven for its entire lifetime, which we expect to be a minimum of thirty years. We are not too sure about this yet, but you can guarantee Simon is working on the chemistry, and Jen and I are working on the physics, and of course Maria is checking everything.”

“Thirdly there is no pollution of any kind, the unbalancing system produces a small amount of excess heat about ten watts in this unit, but no CO2, no radiation, no noise and nothing detectable in the radio frequencies. You could basically sleep with one in your bed for the next ten years and the only side effect would be your toes would be a bit warm! And of course it cannot be weaponised, there is no version or variation of this technology that could give you more than an electric shock.”

“Lastly and most importantly, cost. This device can be mass produced, and was designed for mass production. The prototype behind me uses twenty of the demonstration units that were sent to your various institutions, there are no special chemicals or metals required that can't be found in a normal microchip or school chemistry lab. Everything is patented but the licence to produce these units will be only three percent of the unit cost, and the unit cost should come down to well under two hundred US dollars once mass production starts.”

“There will also be no restriction on who can buy a licence. Maria will provide full technical support for all manufacturers that participate. We do only have forty prototype units, ten are going to the institutions that helped test our results, the other thirty will be allocated to companies who apply, based on their ability to manufacture and environmental record. We of course expect by this time next year there will be thousands if not millions in circulation. At the end of ten years the licence fee will be waived and we will make the design open source.”

That got a shocked reaction from some of the people in the crowd.

“We of course are Scientists not business people, however our parent company along with Maria are excellent business people, they will be handling all this non-science-stuff, while we get back to the fun stuff.”

Simon walked behind the screen and came back with a tray with a dark black cloth on it, he put it on the centre-most table and took the cloth off, the unit in the picture was on the tray with two wires going to an old style filament bulb. Four similar units were unveiled with less ceremony around the presentation room.

“Oh, and did I say, we have already made some!”

Several people looked stunned.

Maria had sold all Alexa's stocks in anything linked to non-renewable energy companies back in August. In October, when the first milliamps of power trickled out of the clunky test unit, she offloaded everything to do with any energy production, except a couple of fusion companies she thought stood a chance, then she bought shares in the companies she expected to benefit. There were no moral quandaries, she just worked on facts and logic, and she was a businesswoman too.

“So with our small presentation complete, I will now open the floor to questions.”

The questions flooded in. Several people had left already to ensure they were the ones to get the first story out.

A man from the BBC asked if any were going to be manufactured in the UK, Simon pointed to the prototype box on the table and said it was manufactured by a company here in Bath called Rosche-Dynamics Limited and the power chip fabricated in a company in Swindon called Fab8, and there would be no restriction imposed on where manufacturing would take place.

On timescales Jen said, this was up to the licensee’s, they would obviously want to reassure themselves of all the claims, so undoubtedly there would be delays with some, especially if the devices are embedded with other technologies such as batteries.

On the question of can it power my house or car, the answer was yes with a but, the house would be OK but like solar panels it would be fairer to export the excess power back into the grid. However, electric cars require large amounts of instantaneous power which the current device could not provide, but they could provide some self charging ability for the existing batteries if weight and space constraints were overcome, though several of these devices could charge the car completely over the course of a night, and with advances, who knows.

A reporter asked about how this would affect oil and gas producers. To which Simon replied, “probably badly.” There was still currently a need for oil for lubricants and plastics, but the need for diesel and petrol would slowly diminish over time, he said it was one of the reasons he got on board with this project was to help the environment and make the world that little bit cleaner. Hardy sensibly added that there would be a long ramp up to peak production and there were still four or five years before supply exceeded demand, and possibly longer to replace legacy infrastructure, this was plenty of time to allow a business model to adapt, and those that didn't would go the way of the Kodak camera company.

The professor who interrupted Jen, asked what were the implications of the excess electron production. This was a good question, and one on all their minds at the start, but measurements now confirmed there was no mass change from the device, Hardy popped an equation on the screen and highlighted a term which satisfied the professor.

With the question from the CNBC news guy, about what they would do now the project was over, Hardy said the team will stay together and work in the research centre here but re-invest most of their energies into a few new challenges. But with the power of AI systems soon to be everywhere, expect big breakthroughs to happen at every discipline not just science and engineering. He also referred them to the recent breakthrough in room temperature superconductors which were also achieved from a company with an AI system.

“Everything except songwriting,” chirped Alexa quietly.

One person asked Jen how she could go from a graduate physics student to a possible Nobel prize winner in six months, she said it was the hardest six months of her life, but she was in the same room those six months with the three finest brains on the planet, and with Hardy and Maria's help she was easily able to understand the maths and physics and help push the project on with them, Maria was probably the best one on one tutor a person could possibly have.

A few questions were directed at Maria, including the inevitable “Are you Sentient.”

Hardy recognised the serious questions were probably over and concluded the presentation by saying all calls for more information and licencing should be directed to Maria, at the email address on the screen, an email address appeared on the screen, he then invited people up to see or video the demonstration units, there were four other units around the room if it was too busy on the stage.

Alexa sat at the back for the entire presentation and question and answer session, then got up, shook a few peoples hands, hugged a few others then left. She was still anonymous for the time being, but questions were being asked, and her anonymity would not continue for much longer. She walked back through the security door, which having one of Maria's sensors above it, opened automatically. Maria knew all the staff implicitly, who to let in, to where and, mostly, what everyone was doing. Alexa had complete confidence in the building's security.

* * *

The presentation and news of the working physical devices was of course top of all the news broadcasts and influencer videos. The talking heads again either praised or criticised it depending upon their agenda, audience, or who their sponsor was, the negative ones struggling to make any headway against the vast majority of positive ones.

Maria received nineteen requests for licences from six different countries within the first forty-eight hours, further requests and technical questions continued to flood in until by the end of the month Maria had nearly two hundred. She sorted them by their track record in manufacturing, time to market, and environmental policies, moved any companies that did not meet Alexa's or her new moral guidelines to the bottom of the list and bumped up those that would be adversely affected by the changes such as those manufacturing solar panels to the top. The first test units began dispatching to licensees by the end of the week.

The world of manufacturing and production were currently scrambling to work out the effects of the new technology on their businesses; share prices fluctuated wildly in some sectors, all fully anticipated by Maria and enabling her to make considerable gains in her portfolio's.

Calls to legislate the technology soon started to appear from politicians egged on by powerful people with vested interests in oil and gas. But governments moved slowly, the timing of the announcements and presentation was of course deliberate so that it was weeks before the first parliamentary or senate debate could occur. Before that first debate forty licences would be signed, technical specifications released and sample hardware delivered to businesses in fourteen countries. The cat was truly out of the bag.

* * *

It was nearly three weeks after the launch event. Alexa walked from her house to the Research Centre as she did most mornings, wearing her thickest coat to protect her from the still dark cold January morning. Rain was forecast for the afternoon, hopefully she would be home by then, if not Maria would drive the car up. The “Benedict house” sign had now been moved back to the main road, behind a new, and unfortunately required, automatic double gate. The sign below it now read “Dietrich Research Centre” with “Authorised Visitors Only” and a phone number to call for access below.

“So what do you think?” she asked.

“The final diary is certainly interesting,” said Maria into her ear-pods. “My research doesn't see one central organisation like Mary saw, but what I am seeing are four cabals in competition. Of course it has been thirty five years since Mary died, and her final diary was never found in the wreckage, why she was flying to Paris and not back to London is also a mystery we may never solve.”

“So you think the crash was an accident?”

“There are no indications it was anything more than a structural failure as reported, although only parts of the wreckage were recovered, and the black box was never found.”

“So are we safe?”

“Tricky question, and I can't really answer it as I am missing many pieces of the puzzle. All four of these organisations were definitely blind-sided by your announcement, their public facing companies are big investors in armaments, banking and petrochemicals, and one of those has just taken a major hit. I can guess questions are being asked, and they will ultimately link this with us and try and exert influence. The fact is we need to tread a lot more carefully especially as they can buy and sell political favours in most geopolitical areas including the UK.”

“These organisations are unfortunately well protected and I am having a hard time getting information, the inner circles, it seems, are very paranoid about IT. We do have the channels open still in the NSA, and I am treading very lightly with my monitoring. I have gotten some information on what they know, unfortunately it is not a lot, but more worryingly there are signs of cabal activity at the higher levels there too. I think they have the power to act against us any time, but they need more information as we are still an enigma to them, a very public and well liked one. The attempts to get access to our systems have gone up a thousand fold since the announcement, and unfortunately I expect physical penetration attempts soon, that's why I have developed and deployed those newer drones and cameras.”

Maria paused, “Ironically it may be safer for you, and the company to step further out into the light.”

Maria's statements about physical safety worried Alexa more than anything else. The physical safety of her friends and employees was something she was not prepared to compromise.

“Thanks Maria, I know you are doing your best here, and if there is any way to deflect these guys attention away from us we should do it.” She sighed heavily, “I suppose I'd better start brushing up on my CEO presentation and people skills.”

She walked into the Research Centre up the stone stairs, through the imposing double doors into reception, which was never manned unless they were expecting visitors. Jen was waiting, a little more worldly and mature but still the same girl Alexa knew.

“Hey sis!” said Jen, giving her a small hug. Jen sometimes slept overnight in one of the spare rooms if she’d been working late, Maria didn't discourage the practice as she knew it was sometimes necessary. She always kept a four bedded room free for girls and another for boys if required, managing the bookings as required.

“I’ve been looking forward to this for months.” Jen said.

“Me too,” said Alexa, “when Maria woke me this morning I wanted to drive here immediately, but she said you were just getting in the shower so I decided to walk. You ready?”

There would be little activity until at least eight thirty, staff tended to start and work later in winter. The two companies had now been merged in to just the Dietrich Research Centre, they had thirty eight staff here at Benedict house and another ninety at their other research centres. The push now was to get their AI system to as many schools, colleges and universities as possible around the world. It was a first step, but nobody could think of a better goal than pushing education and research.

The two girls walked through the security doors on the ground floor of the main house into the old TEAM-A work area, now just called AI Research and Development, and turned into the first lab. Walking past the empty workstations, science stations, and electronics benches of the open plan area, the girls continued through into one of the restricted server rooms, being two of only eight people currently allowed access.

“I’ve not been down here for weeks since Spence and Allison started the installation,” Alexa said to Jen as they both walked through the cool room, the ten servers, storage racks, fans, and a million blinking LEDs, contrasting with the eerie neatness, and silence in the rest of the house. At the back of the room, and not that prominent, was another double metal door. This door had a sign next to it saying “Access To Switching Room” and “No Entry at any time”, someone had also added “Beware of the Tigers!” below it, they both grinned, IT staff had weird senses of humour. There was no button or key to enter but as they walked up to it the doors slid open into a normal sized lift, one you could have found in any office. This lift also had no buttons or indicators, just the normal AI sensor, which was now fitted everywhere in the house and grounds, except for private areas.

When both girls had stepped in, the doors shut and it went down three levels, opening into a quiet eight by ten metre room. In the middle of the room were two plinths, almost the same as Maria's back at the house, but with vastly improved connectivity.

On top of each plinth was a black cube.

“How are they?” said Alexa, both girls slightly concerned by the lack of sound and light from them.

“Why don't you ask them yourself..” Maria said happily.

“April, Helena. I would like you both to meet Auntie Alexa, and Auntie Jen!”

# Book 2: Singularity

*In technology, the singularity describes a hypothetical future where technology growth is out of control and irreversible. A period where intelligent and powerful technologies will radically and unpredictably transform our reality.*

## Blind Sided

“Were we blind-sided?” said Mathews in a resigned voice from behind his coffee mug. “It's the question I keep asking myself over and over again.”

Jean, the target of his friendly tirade, was sitting on the other side of his utilitarian government desk, hugging her own mug of the bitter coffee. Mathews propensity for leaving his window open meant the room was a good deal colder than the normally balmy temperatures in the rest of the building, and the heat from her mug was far more satisfying than its contents.

Jean looked around the very familiar spartan battleship grey room, the two black filing cabinets she knew were empty except for the one top drawer, the large old fashioned wall clock, the whiteboard with today's date the third of March 2026 written on the top, the neatly arranged folders on his desk, the single large monitor, keyboard and mouse on the desk. She then looked at the man attired in his usual camo fatigues wearing in big letters ‘Mathews’ on the breast like a badge of honour. Jean was similarly attired and tagged. She felt no real need to wear her black business suit and she felt the military garb differentiated her as someone who actually worked for a living rather than pushing a desk. She sat there seemingly relaxed, but her thoughts were actually as distant, and as muddled as his.

Mathews shifted position and the squeak from his chair brought Jean back to attention, her eyes meeting his. “We saw a lot of this activity play out last year,” he continued, “and now, only a few months after I made the call, the world seems to be in an AI meltdown.”

The squeaking of his chair continued for a few seconds until he also became aware of it. He frowned then stopped moving and the silence of the room returned, both heads now turned to the sound of the ticking clock on the wall and both people smiled. Mathews finally decided to take a sip of the coffee he had also been holding for the last five minutes, his dark eyes closed and opened, then his posture relaxed some, “and yet nowhere in all this are we seeing any concrete signs of sentience, or is that some sort of ruse as well?”

Jean could tell that Mathews was in a bit of a dilemma, still trying to understand if the perceived failure of the project he had taken over last year laid with him or not. The once bustling operations area of the NSA’s Cheshire-Cat project was shut down and silent pending a technical evaluation. The hundreds of new ‘AI signals’ it was detecting daily made it basically untenable, and Mathews had finally made the call to shut the operation down. The area was now a ghost town of empty workstations, with a skeleton staff of three analysts reviewing the data and logs and seeing if anything could be saved. From what they could tell it didn’t look promising, and both Jean and Mathews expected reassignment in the next few weeks.

Through Mathews monologue Jean just smiled, content to listen and sipping her coffee. They were good enough friends that a few moments of silence every now and then from either of them did not feel awkward.

She had specifically wanted to talk to Mathews in private because out of the blue, two days ago, she had a request from Alexa Martins asking if it would be possible for them to meet. The message came as a shock to her and worried her somewhat. Alexa Martins was the woman of the moment and one of the richest and influential people in the world, there could only be one reason why she wanted the meeting and that was because of the AI unit of theirs she ‘appropriated’ last July.

But it didn't feel right. The meeting invite she received was cordial, almost polite. Alexa would be in California in five weeks to give a TED lecture to a small audience of students and faculty at Stanford University. She would also be touring several research facilities for which the press and forums were having a speculation field day with rumours about everything from brain implants, working self-driving cars all the way to faster than light travel!

“I had an email from Alexa Martins asking to meet,” said Jean casually.

By coincidence, or poor timing, Mathews had just taken another sip of his coffee and choked as it went down the wrong way, spitting some out over his desk and clothing. “She what!” he shouted, rocking forward from his previously slouched posture, and picking up a folder marked “top secret” to shake off the excess coffee. It was totally out of character for the unflappable Mathews and for some reason Jean found it funny.

“She must know it was me who was in Oxford last year and who stole their AI unit.” Jean continued unfazed. She had took a day to think over the request and what to do, and she needed Mathews advice. “I wasn't sure what to do, the request came in through my private messenger application on an address nobody except you, my mum and a few other close school and army friends have. It was very polite but unspecific, just requesting a talk.”

She paused, while Mathews continued to rid himself of excess coffee.

She continued, “you know apart from the scary science and technology they possess, I just don't sense anything bad from this girl or her company. From everything I have seen and heard she is nothing but straight, honest and intelligent, the company's whole security consists of an old woman who man's the security gate during office hours. I honestly cannot for the life think of why she would want to see me, unless she’s spent the last six months learning Kung Fu and wants to kick my ass!”

Mathews laughed at that, popping the now dry but smudged, top secret folder back on top of another less wet pile and reaching for his coffee again.

Jean continued, “remember the four Indian programmers?” Mathews nodded unnecessarily. “Well one of them, Geeta Singh, applied for a working visa and is now working in LA at another one of those AI startups that are springing up like weeds. Anyway I contacted her three weeks ago asking her some follow-on questions, which I said were part of her visa enquiry. I asked her about their open source code, you know the code we found in the AI unit we appropriated?”

Mathews nodded, he remembered that day well.

“She remembered a Doctor Griffin from the company that contacted all four of them about using their code and who then sent each of them a generous payment for its use in a commercial product, however she told me she had seen and used the LabAI system since and even though it is similar she couldn't see how or where her code could possibly have been used in it.”

Jean paused as if to consider her next words. “Well I was thinking, what if it wasn't! What if that code was left there as a red herring and we fell for it?”

Before Mathews had time to answer she pressed on. “Remember we never found anything on this Doctor Griffin, and the only references we ever found were three general medical practitioners and a historian. Well recently I found another possibility, Doctor Griffin was the invisible man in the HG Wells book of the same name, put these two together and, well I had a theory what if Doctor Griffin was a real AI!”

Nobody spoke for a few seconds, Mathews it seemed was all ears. Jean continued, “you know the more I think about all this, the more I think you are right and we were played all along. I also think this review of the system is a waste of time.” Jean was on a roll with this and was not going to stop.

“Also have you thought what would have actually happened if we did capture such an AI, what could we possibly do to it? I have spent a long time thinking about this particular Genie, and I don't think there is any way of controlling it or putting it back in the bottle.”

Mathews did not say anything right away but was nodding thoughtfully during her monologue. Finally he spoke. “I came to a similar conclusion over a month ago when I shut the program down Jean. We are treating it like something that we can capture and get it to do our bidding, but it is so far out of my comfort zone I can't even think of the questions to ask, never-mind finding the answers.”

Mathews lightened up, getting out of his chair and stretching.

“You know Alexa Martins never does one-to-one meetings don't you? For her to request a private meeting with you means you’re right that she has to have the drop on you. I doubt there is anything to worry about though, we spent a lot of resources checking if she is involved in anything nefarious and found nothing. Our analysts found a spate of sell-off’s and firings last year in some of the companies she obviously controlled when she came to power, but in each case the firings were also accompanied by charges of fraud or embezzlement, which were all subsequently proven guilty or not contested. It looked to our accountants like a clean-up and green-washing of her portfolio which corresponds with everything we have learnt about her since. She looks for all intent and purpose like the real deal, a genuine Miss Goody Two-Shoes.”

Jean smiled again as Mathews continued, walking to his open window, looking out of it and then walking back to his chair. “You know, I expect she has a lot of powerful enemies now. Those new regulations trying to get passed that prohibit her new Quantum Vacuum Cells here are case-in-point, pure BS pushed by the oil and gas companies and everyone knows it. Those in power wouldn't know a QVCell from a prison cell, though I think they should get more familiar with the later.”

He paused, “my advice Jean, I think you should go and see what she wants. Standard operating procedure is you let your supervisor know, and you have done that, all I ask is that if there is anything that comes up which affects national security you let me know.”

Jean nodded, she couldn't even remember the last time their thoughts disagreed. “You know Jim, I would never say this openly but I'm starting to think of us as the bad guys. The reason I got out of the army and those postings in those scary countries was because I did not trust people like us, not to sell us out for a quick buck. I certainly don't trust anyone in this organisation except you and the guys I fought with.”

She paused as if thinking through the next sentence. “Maybe it is time I retire!”

“You could be right Jean,” he sighed, “I’ve been having the same thoughts myself. You know if we had found out her company was as advanced as it was at the time I suspect it would have gotten really bad, in retrospect I’m really glad I made the wrong call.”

He smiled looking directly into her eyes, “If you want my opinion you are probably too good for this place anyway, selfishly I’d hate to see you go, you’re the yin for my yang as they say, unfortunately there are so few people like you that I trust. But enough buttering you up, you should go to that meeting and listen to what she has to say.”

She nodded, smiled and they both spent a few more minutes in pleasant conversation while she finished her coffee. Yes, she would meet with Alexa even if it was only to apologise.

A few hours later Maria received the reply to the email she’d sent on Alexa’s request and a week after that, a business class open return ticket to San Francisco had been couriered to her home.

* * *

*The Dietrich Research Centre has again been in the news, again for refusing to release their AI system to organisations outside of research or academia. A spokesman for the company said, there is currently not enough capacity in their system to support both academia and private enterprises, also more importantly, they do not want certain companies to take advantage of the system, to reduce staff and unfairly step ahead of the competition. They have admitted that several units have been stolen, but as the technology is based on cloud servers, in geographically diverse locations, the stolen units will simply report their location to the authorities and be blacklisted from their systems.*

*So far the impact on jobs in the administrative, programming and white collar sector has been much less than the scaremongers had forecast, there has even been a mini boom in some manufacturing sectors. But while the Dietrich Research Centre is refusing these requests many of the other promising AI systems in development are unlikely to be so restrictive. We have an expert on the program to talk about this..*

* * *

David contemplated on his history, and what brought him to be at this point today. He had lived an interesting life so far, making his first million dollars at the age of eighteen after writing an algorithm for accepting crypto currency transactions in early 2017. Before this he lurked in seedy hacker forums, and wrote pieces of code, no questions asked, for random strangers and bitcoins. He was naive, and his little isolated dealings with this underside of the internet society had left him with a very bad taste in his mouth. Twice he'd had to delete accounts and start again from scratch when he got a whiff of what his code was being used for. But the two hundred bitcoins he received for the commerce algorithm from a large crypto exchange company was totally legit and earned. It was just enough to allow him to quit the dark web, move on, and after national service, put him through university.

Fate kicked in during his mandatory military service, a conscription which all Israelis have to do for two and a half years when they turn eighteen. Six months after boot camp he was involved in a serious accident where the air force plane he was in overshot the runway, it killed three soldiers and left him in hospital for nearly two months. When he finally was released from hospital to rehab, two amazing things happened, firstly the price of his bitcoin portfolio was on the rise and had more than tripled to over a million US dollars, and secondly, he was recruited into Mossad.

Mossad had a good idea of David's programming talents of course, he had left a lot of presence on GitHub where he had also helped maintain some of the cryptographic algorithms for Linux. They had a file on him, and a tag to say he should be approached for recruitment at the earliest opportunity. However even Mossad couldn't circumvent the conscription system for what was basically, just another programmer, and they were content to wait until the end of his military service. After his accident however, the military, knowing he would be in rehab for at least a year, and was only good for a desk job, allowed them to fast track his move to them.

The agent they sent while he was recovering was nothing like he expected. She looked like David’s grandmother, though she was more likely her late forties, David was still not very good at judging women's ages at this time. David was honest with the lady agent about his slightly greyer history, the sale of his algorithm, and his wealth, also insistent that his goal was to do his computer science degree after his national service. The woman, recognising a good talent, returned to Tel Aviv, and with his online identities in hand, she and three other operators did a thorough check on him. They were amazed to find, David had been used by them three times already to write various spy software, for which he had received at the time about eight thousand dollars in crypto currency. Now they could have him to themselves for fourteen months, it was a jackpot for them.

And so David was given the directive, it wasn't so much an option, to finish his remaining fourteen months military service in the Mossad offices in Tel Aviv. He mostly worked on his own, sometimes on teams, and sometimes with other agents. He was a superb analyst, an amazing hacker, a quick learner and had built up a lot of self confidence from his brief military training. He learnt a lot about the spy business, the good, the bad, and the positively ugly. It was soon discovered by his manager that there were certain things David would not do, and other things he did exceedingly well. Attempts to push past his moral boundaries were met with him pretending to work and achieving nothing, and those controlling him decided they would rather he worked his best so gave him only the tasks he held no moral qualms about.

David was fast becoming a rising star in the small agency, his help was directly attributed to hardening their computer security and stopping at least two high profile terrorist acts. For the final three months of his ‘contract’ he worked on his first foreign job to hack the Iranian embassy in London, where he added another aborted terrorist plot to his achievements. He loved the thrill of the chase, naively hoping he was getting rid of bad guys and making the world a safer place. But through all this he remembered he was still a tool of an organisation he wasn't comfortable being in, hacks to target terrorists could also target innocent civilians, and at the end of his national service commitment, he let them know he was going to stay on in London, as he had quite fallen in love with the city, and would be applying for university here.

Mossad, however, had other plans, and not wanting to lose him, came up with a compromise, they would use their influence to get him into the prestigious computer science course in Imperial college London and he would do the occasional job for them.

He assumed he was getting the better deal and accepted, as he wanted the best, and did not have the grades to be accepted into such a prestigious institution. A few words in the right places got him in with only minor questions.

He had to work hard, but excelled at his studies and was rewarded by some really good friendships and excellent tuition. The dream was almost ruined by the COVID crisis, but David used the downtime to do some additional work for Mossad, ignoring the bad, and ugly, for he was a lot less naive now, and fulfilling any remaining obligation he thought he had with them.

With the price of bitcoin hitting over seventy thousand dollars, he couldn’t take the pressure any longer and his confidence in it rising further finally broke. He sold all but ten of them, using the nearly eighteen million dollars he gained in the transaction to buy a large converted Victorian building in a quiet part of Soho. He rented most of the building, the ground floor being a well liked coffee shop, the first floor a lawyers office and the basement was rented out to of all things a magic shop. He kept the top floor and attic rooms for himself, and re-invested the remaining six million dollars in tech stocks, keeping the reserve in gold and cash of various denominations. He was twenty one years old.

David finished his degree in 2023 and went on to do his master's degree which he finished a year later, just in time for the rest of the world to start taking notice of AI systems. The technology was by this point, easy enough for anyone to develop, and he used this to start up a small AI company with a good friend. It was very successful because most of the world's companies were panicking, and did not want to be left behind in the new AI race, but none really understood the technology well enough to implement anything useful.

He knew AI was a scam of sorts, oh it looked totally believable and magical to Joe Public, and even worked to an extent, but was not AI as he knew or envisioned it. Despite this, the company did well, but David still spent a lot of his spare time fruitlessly trying to understand and improve the AI systems they were selling. David was at the top of his game but at each turn he was met by the same brick wall, that being that the AI’s were simply trained ponies who needed proportionally more and more data to perform slightly more complex tricks. The five big American tech giants, and regimes that collected all their citizens on-line information, held all the cards, having thousands of times the data of his open source models. So it was, with a heavy heart, that he concluded the only way he could ever improve his AI system under the current regime was with whatever open source bones the tech giants threw off their plate. AI felt like a dead end.

Summer 2025 was coming to a sweltering end, their company had grown considerably in the twelve months, moving out of David's apartment into real offices, and bringing in larger and more affluent clients. They had employed another four guys and David had now handed off nearly all of his work to them and his partner, preferring to concentrate on understanding and improving the code base to keep ahead of the competition. About that same time he had a nicely worded email from one of his old professors asking if he could come back into the university for one of their recruitment drives to show potential students how several local boys had made it good. He wasn't required to do any presentation or to make any speeches so David did not need any excuse, it would be great to catch up with his professor and his friends who had stayed on for their PhD’s, maybe see where things were now.

David knocked and walked into his old computer lab, Professor Holmes was on his computer and talking to someone, he could wait until the conversation finished.

“..produces no solutions then?” Holmes said, a bit dejected.

“No,” came the male voice clearly through the weird looking Bluetooth speaker on the desk next to the PC, “It's like the travelling salesman problem all over again.”

“What if we used Rogers quantum computer algorithm?”

“Again Professor, there is no solution, Professor Jenkins has run this exact scenario and algorithm in MIT only a few days ago, his results were put up on the forum last night, he tagged you specifically. He's not in the office for another hour, do you want me to arrange a conference?”

“Yes Alan, do that..” The professor had noticed David waiting patiently.

“One second David,” he said to David, then turned to his speaker. “Just set it up for tomorrow if you can, Alan, I’m going to be a bit busy with the recruitment drive today.”

“No problem Professor,” came the voice back immediately.

The professor walked up to David shaking his hand, “sorry David, I got a bit carried away, I asked Alan to run a new algorithm this morning, but it didn't quite work out, still we are so much farther along than when you were with us, exciting times to be in AI though.”

“Sorry Professor,” David said apologetically. “I was a bit early. I didn't mean to interrupt you and your colleague..”

The professor laughed, pointing at the funny Bluetooth speaker, “oh of course, you don't have these in the real world yet, David, meet Alan, our new LabAI system. We named him after Alan Turing, I’m not sure how we ever worked without him. Alan, say hello to David.”

“Good morning Mr Klein,” came the voice from the speaker. “I have examined a lot of your work from the original project over the past six weeks and you are an excellent programmer, eighteen percent of the codebase is still based on your Python code.”

David wasn't sure what to think, for all their hype, the other AI systems out there weren't anywhere near this good, nor as far as he knew, was anything anyone was developing. Maybe the professor had finally made a breakthrough. “Err..” He looked at the professor, then the black box, “..Er, hello Alan?” David turned to the professor, then stopped for a few seconds, smiled, and slapped his thighs and said, “good one Professor, you got me with that same one two years ago I remember. God I’m getting gullible!”

The professor looked perplexed, then turned serious, “I can see why you would think that David, but Alan is a real AGI, Most of the Oxford academia got them two months ago, and they have been spreading like wildfire ever since. Alan is amazing, reads and writes code in any language at lightning speed, checks results, writes tests, organises experiments.. Wait a second,” the professor turned to the box, “Alan, please recognise David Klein for guest access,” he then turned back to David. “Go on, ask him any question, anything..”

The professor sat there waiting with a smug look on his face, David wasn't having any of it, a joke was a joke. He looked at the speaker. “How do you know my name?” he asked in Hebrew. Never taking his eyes off the mysterious black box.

“Very simply,” came the immediate reply in perfect Hebrew, “Professor Holmes was the one who asked me to email you, he has given me permission to send correspondence on his behalf and I used his style and demeanour from other emails he sent to you to write to you. There was a small postfix after his signature saying ‘sent by Alan’ if you cared to read the email signature in its entirety.”

David slumped holding the table with one hand, his countenance in a state of shock.

“I have no idea what you just said or what language it was in,” said the professor smiling after a few seconds of silence, “but I’m guessing he answered correctly.” The professor paused, “he's good isn't he? Don't feel bad David, it happens the first time to everyone, first total disbelief, then shock, then a series of questions and answers followed by total acceptance, I am now at stage four, you are at stage one, where I was six weeks ago.”

“Who wrote this?, what is it based on?, is there a paper on it?, hell where do I buy one?” said David in quick succession, recovering his posture and looking at the black box.

“Since your attention is directed at me Mr Klein and you asked it in Hebrew, I will answer, but if it is OK I will do so in English,” came the voice of Alan. David had been so thrown off his game, he had not even remembered asking in Hebrew.

“I am an experimental LabAI unit manufactured by the Dietrich Research Centre,” continued Alan in English, “I am not based on any of the current AI technologies you are familiar with and my system is still proprietary for the moment, unfortunately my company does not yet have the processing capacity to support groups outside of academia, Professor Holmes is part of our early adopter program, but I thank you for your interest and I am sure we will communicate again in the future.”

There was a very short pause and then, “oh Professor Holmes, Jenkins has booked a video call at thirteen hundred GMT, I have added it to your calendar.”

“Thank you Alan, I don't know what I did before you.” He smiled, then led a shocked David out of the room.

The presentations to the prospective students went really well but David only had thoughts for the LabAI unit calling itself Alan. News about these devices had been springing up intermittently in his feeds, but with the company and so many AI related things vying for his attention he had completely ignored them. While at the university though he pumped the staff for as much information as possible, it wasn't hard, as it was all most of the faculty were talking about. The LabAI website was deliberately vague on anything technical. All the way back home that evening he pondered the implications for his systems if this technology was made available, he wouldn't tell his business partner, but their future was probably grim.

Any problems he might have had were elegantly solved two weeks later when a large software service company made an offer to buy them outright for twenty million dollars. David, owning the larger share of the company, pushed his partner to agree to the sale. He ensured the sale and purchase agreement, kept his partner on as CEO and the staff on for at least a twelve months contract, it also contained a get out clause allowing him to leave after three months. David had been out of university a year and he had just made another twelve million dollars.

Unlike normal geeks David had a very strong and likeable personality, dressed well and enjoyed socialising with people, going to conferences, and holidaying with friends. He also got an undeserved, and unfortunate, reputation as a womaniser. The truth was though he enjoyed their company, he liked an intelligent dialogue, however the women in his circles of friends were either very shallow or spoken for.

Dinner conversations which centred around what celebrities were doing, money or fashion held little to no interest for him. The last few months he had managed to go steady with a professor who worked at the Natural History museum, they both had full itineraries but when they met she talked with a passion about everything. Emily was in fact perfect, right until she left on an expedition to Patagonia. It was at the end of this relationship and his final week at the company that he accepted an offer to meet with the section head of Mossad in London, it was done the usual way through an invite to a party at the Israeli embassy.

“David, I see god is being good to you these days,” came the voice of the section head. Saul was close to retirement, medium build, wore thin glasses and wore a well tailored but very much out of style suit. David by contrast wore a well styled lighter suit with a thin polo necked jumper. David cringed as Saul spoke, his English accent so stereotypical Jewish, it was like he was acting in a bad TV show or movie. David had lived in London for four years now and the people he dealt with just assumed he was English, come on Saul, you have lived here for nearly twenty years, it wasn't that hard to blend in. David switched to Hebrew.

“I’m sure god has much more important things to do than worry about me, Saul,” he said smiling and shaking the man's well calloused hands firmly as was custom. “Always a surprise meeting you here. You know I only seem to get invited to parties here when you are coming.”

“And you only accept them when you want to,” he retorted. “We had to invite six other prominent Jewish geeks to ensure nobody would raise an eyebrow,” he said the word ‘geek’ with disdain, David knew Saul was very old fashioned and held on to too many prejudices.

“You know,” he continued in a fatherly manner, “not many people get that level of attention David, anyway I wanted to see you in person as you ignored our last two requests.”

“That is correct,” he admitted, “I do not consider myself beholden to the state, nor Mossad, but more importantly, neither of the requests interested me, one was borderline illegal and the other I was just uncomfortable with.” David did not normally drink much and after taking a small sip of the beverage being offered to the guests, he was now using the cocktail glass as a prop so he would not get offered any more, “I like it here Saul and I wont do anything to jeopardise that status, you are well aware of that.”

“I only pass down the requests David,” said the man holding both hands up in resignation, “I am quite aware of your strange morals but you have helped us a lot in the past and have an open mind so we would like you to look at this.” He handed David a USB drive.

“And this is?” said David, not taking it.

“It is what our technical guys got from one of those LabAI systems, our guys have spent weeks looking at it and we would like your opinion.”

His heart said no, but his intellect and curiosity got the better of him and he took the device.

The meeting between David and Saul occurred a month before another part of the aforementioned company broke the laws thermodynamics and dropped the Quantum Vacuum Cell on the world.

* * *

“How many entities are you now supporting?” Said Alexa. She was making her way to the research centre from her house as she always did, rain or shine. At the moment it was light rain, and she was clinging on to a large umbrella of her grandads which covered the top two thirds of her head. It was eight AM and still a bit dark, the other three normal occupants of her house were either still asleep, as in Hardy's case, or didn't make it back from the research centre the night previous and were bunked in the temporary dorm rooms as Jen and Simon were.

“As of today, the twenty fifth of March we have two thousand, three hundred and sixty one entities, across the four data centres. There are also almost thirteen thousand on the waiting list and Spence’s team are still commissioning the two new data centres in the Netherlands and Thailand..”

Maria paused. “You do remember that entity stuff is rubbish don't you?”

“Yes,” Alexa said as she sidestepped a puddle in her path. “But the explanation works for my simple monkey brain, and unlike you I cannot keep two different cover stories when talking to all these dignitaries and interviewers; So as far as I'm concerned that's how it works.”

“OK, just checking,” said Maria, “anyway, the deadline for the Indonesian government ban on AI technology has gone into force so I cancelled your overnight stay there when you do your Asian tour.”

Alexa sighed, “tour indeed, you make me sound like a rock band. So how many bans does that make now?”

“Well we have now been banned in twelve countries, but eleven of those are irrelevant as the first clause in the terms and conditions of all our contracts is that we reserve the right to withhold any of our systems and licences from regimes or organisations that discriminate against any of our technologies or people. twenty seven countries currently fall onto that list, Indonesia was the first one not on the list to ban us.”

Maria continued after a small pause, “we are lucky that debate and free speech has stopped any legislation like this being passed in any western and progressive societies, but the debates are still raging so I don't expect Indonesia to be the last.”

“Still the religions then?” said Alexa tip toeing over yet another puddle.

“Well the majority of this is coming from religious groups as you say. The churches are very confused, and nothing in any of the religious teachings have anything to say so they default to the easiest to sell, the one that we're the devil and nobody should be listening to soulless godless entities that cannot know god's word.” She paused.

“I have had some very nice debates with religious people, anonymous and on-line of course, many of whom are rational and genuinely do not understand what the problem is, but unfortunately many in power are not rational. I have all the arguments and interpretations for all religious books and texts ever published, they are so ambiguous it is actually trivial if I wanted to turn their every argument back on them. But most would never be swayed by logical arguments as the evidence is not logical, so it is best to back off rather than appear arrogant and antagonise them further.”

Alexa nodded but did not speak, Maria was right not to poke this particular hornets nest.

Maria paused again, and in her more serious voice said, “religion is one of those irrational human things that scares me a lot. There are thousands of different ones, mostly incompatible and all reporting to be the only truth. None of it makes sense and unlike you guys, we can only work on facts and probabilities. If somebody says to us that one plus one equals three, we have to treat it as false, likewise if someone says there is a god or deity that created everything, then cannot or will not substantiate it with positive evidence we have to assign it a probability so low it may as well be zero.”

Alexa sighed, she'd had this conversation numerous times with Maria, and from her talks with the other guys she wasn't alone. Maria spent a lot of time trying to apply logic to things which defied it. “You just have to understand the human need to belong to a community, to feel part of something bigger, to have a purpose. For some people this means doing what their friends do and believing what they do. It's not all bad, yes there may be some fairy stories involved, but for the majority it gives them a sense of belonging without doing any real harm. There are idiots at both extremes, religion is not required for that.”

Maria had also heard the same answer back from Alexa and thousands of others through various conversations, she doubted she would ever get an answer she liked.

“The second source of objections,” she continued, “are from unions and politicians, both see political advantages they can use to increase their standing. Even though we have been very specific that we won't be using our technologies to replace existing staff, no such promises have been made by other companies actively developing AI technologies. Unfortunately the current spate of call centre closures will be disproportionately affecting poorer countries like India and the Philippines which don't yet have the same social cushions to fall back on as other western nations.”

“History is trying to repeat itself,” sighed Alexa, shifting her umbrella and tightening her scarf around her neck against the cold. “They will try to push the mobs against progress, like they did with the textile machines at the start of the industrial revolution. We need to find new industries and new jobs for the white collar masses who are the most threatened, and time is not on our side. Those damned politicians and activists only see the next sound-bite, they care nothing for the people or the problem, will do nothing to help and of course will just muddy the water of any legitimate plans to move humanity on.”

She sighed again, not finished, “then there are of course the cabals who want to preserve the large pieces of pie they already have, and maybe use the confusion to take some more of it.”

“Human nature is an unsolvable problem,” said Maria grimly, “a small percentage of humanity will always be bad actors and many of these are inevitably going to get in to power. They are not having it all their own way though, I am still secretly releasing all the money trails we find on corrupt corporations and politicians to Wikileaks and the media. The media of course continue to love scandals but are too lazy to do any research, afraid of litigation and rely off what they can scrape off the newsfeeds. Luckily there are more and more independent researchers, bloggers and YouTubers who are not so complacent, and their actions are certainly throwing a lot of spanners in the works of these people, their political influencers, lobbying groups, and PR companies..”

“But we haven't really made any real impact,” finished Alexa, obviously frustrated, “it's so annoying when these people are caught red handed with their hands in the cash register, then just shrug it off as fake news. They are proven serial liars, I just don't understand how people can actually believe them!”

This was a major sore point for Alexa. She sighed, concentrating on a drop of water rolling down her brolly to calm her down. “But,” she continued with a more even countenance, “even when the evidence is a hundred percent against them, no action is ever taken against the more powerful ones, yes they let the occasional small fish fall into the fryer to show how they are taking it seriously, but nothing ever happens to those with power and influence.”

“Unless you have more power and influence than them!” Asserted Maria. “Be patient Alexa, we are reaching a tipping point, we’ve been learning all their manipulation tricks, and we have some good people working on the problems and showing me how to use these same tricks to our advantage. You of all people are very aware that most governments and large organisations now have whole departments with people whose only job is to spin the truth or re-explain how a problem lies with someone else or is not a problem at all. It is also human nature to always trust those in authority, even when there is absolutely zero basis for that trust. It is this we need to overcome.”

Maria paused, “again, patience is required, we are very close to being able to turn all this back against them, unfortunately, I only have so many resources and I am not omnipresent despite some speculation. Also until you even the playing field, it's just a giant game of whack-a-mole. They are like cockroaches, as soon as you take one crooked bureaucrat or politician down, there are ten more waiting in the dark.”

“Urghh, you just had to bring up cockroaches!” shivered Alexa.

It was proving to be a very hard process to assemble a team able to solve the problem of the cabals and geo-politics. The core group of Jen, Hardy, Spence and Simon had some of the traits required but not the major ones, those being cunning and the ability to take the fight to their enemies. They briefly considered people like Chantel, but Maria did not consider her ruthless enough to do what was required, and after Alexa's wonderful and enlightening three day visit to see her in New Orleans before the announcement of the QVCells Alexa had to agree, Chantel was much too nice a person. Their subsequent meeting at Pierre's funeral last month had been a very sad affair but reaffirmed to Alexa she had made the right decision.

Alexa also wanted people who did not want the job, people who did not want the power or got comfortable with it, which made the task doubly hard. Maria had talked deeply to tens of thousands of very intelligent people over the past year who seemed to meet the criteria; Many she now considered friends, but to be a member of the group they were proposing required much, much more than this. She made the call to trust Alexa and Jen without all the facts, she had been lucky, and she now wanted to eliminate luck. Now Maria dug very deep indeed as she needed to be able to trust not just her life, but her very principles and the lives of all those she knew and held dear. Trust like this required not just scrutiny of the person, but every close associate, and in some cases the next level beyond.

Unfortunately everyone had lies to hide, most were small and insignificant and in many cases caused by the fallibility of the human mind to remember events, or hubris. Even Alexa was not immune and she had posted about going to a Coldplay concert in Auckland she never went to; but as a thirteen year old she needed to feel special, and Alexa was quite embarrassed never mentioning it again anywhere. But it wasn't just the lies you told, sometimes it was the lies that were told to you, or about you. Some, like Alexa's father, were however easy problems to solve.

No, to even get put on the shortlist for this new group would require much more; The morality of a saint, the intelligence of a college professor, the cunning and slyness of a fox and the decisiveness of an executioner. Alexa had agreed that each person would also be visited in person by her, and Maria would ask no questions if Alexa did not want them on the team, as she would if Maria had doubts. Slowly, one by one however the group began to form.

Maria played by Alexa's rules because she believed in them, and in Alexa; but when it came to their safety Maria *would* use the full set of tools at her disposal, and there were many other, *less savoury,* resources and methods she could call on should normal rules failed to work. These were resources and methods that Alexa would never agree to, nor would she ever be made aware of. They were always the last option, but they were an option.

“Do you have anything not so depressing to talk about? What about your banking problems we were discussing?”

“No progress. The consensus from all the economists and political thinkers I talk to is still the same, basically until you have full physical and regulatory control of the ecosystem it is a no go.” Maria sighed, a human trait she had picked up sometime last year and used better than most humans. “It is a shame really as economics is one of those trivial problems, made complicated by human politics, geographic division, trust and crime.”

“So again we are back to what we originally discussed,” Alexa said, “your banks will have to play by the rules until you can locate one outside of a country's political influence, and be physically safe from having that influence imposed on it, and we all know there is no such place on earth.” Alexa laughed, “I guess that's why you are pushing Hardy so hard on his project.”

“Yes and yes! We need to push humanity's progress into space quicker. It fixes the problems of millions of lines of legislation and state controls, will provide massive opportunities for economic expansion and remove the pressures on the earth's ecosystem, it really does solve all the problems.”

Alexa still disagreed strongly with Maria on this one, and they agreed to disagree. The problems were all here on earth and, timescale wise, her talks about space development were a distraction and not going to help solve anything before those problems got out of hand. Alexa once again wondered what Maria was seeing that she wasn't.

Maria continued, aware of Alexa's underlying reservations, “of course I'm not saying it is going to be easy. The guys we are helping in Texas have improved the efficiency of the current chemical rocket systems by almost a factor of thirty percent, but it is still nowhere near enough for what we envisage and should only be considered as a stepping stone not an answer. I am however very confident Hardy's project is on the right track and will remove this limitation in a shorter timescale than even you think is possible.”

Again she paused, it was easy for Alexa to forget that Maria was actually involved in all of these new breakthrough science discoveries and sat in the directors-chair when viewing how everything was progressing; Maybe it was time to start taking it all a bit more seriously and asking the pertinent questions.

Hearing her silence as a cue, Maria continued a bit more subdued, “unfortunately, his work, if it succeeds, is very likely to put us back in front of everyone's radar yet again.”

“Ouch!” said Alexa, “we are still not off it from last time! Anyway I don't see how, it's only been, what, three months, and Hardy and his team don't seem to be doing much outside of their laboratory, and don't seem overly different to when they started back in early January, surely this is going to take years?”

“Normally it would, but you are still thinking ‘old way’ Alexa. You are forgetting we now own our own fabrication, manufacturing and laboratory facilities and also own or have controlling interests in six other commercial laboratories around the world. Many of our early visits to America, Europe and Asia were not just to cherry pick the best researchers for here, but to set up similar there and get the brightest and best in to them. Those other forty three names acknowledged on the QVCell paper, may not have done any of the theory but ran a lot of the experiments in parallel for us over different time zones.”

“This is accelerating all the time as we also now control even more of the supply chain, and remember it is all scheduled by me to ensure all our facilities work like clockwork together. I think a lot of the world is still thinking with your mindset, but in reality we have improved in leaps and bounds in the speed of design, setup and verification of experiments. Think Manhattan level projects but with me in charge. Yes some things take time, making stuff being the biggest, but I am speeding this up just as quickly, I’m gradually getting control of the key supply chains and once you have the parts, give the right tools to the right people and give them the right incentives, well it is amazing how fast something can get done.”

“You’re right Maria,” said Alexa, “I’m not thinking like this, I just see our guys on whiteboards, computers or bent over equipment in the lab here and I’m not appreciating what is going on in parallel.”

“I do try and keep the little details from you,” said Maria. “For example our fabrication facility in Swindon is now used exclusively for the production of QVCells. We added new lines to produce the modified cells for Hardy's project, the field emitters for Simon's, and a new type of emitter for another project which I will give you details on today.”

“In order to scale up production for the rest of the world it was necessary to build and install the same 3D fabrication machines in another building and another seven facilities around the world. To do this the companies producing the fabrication machines required massive investment to scale up, as did their suppliers; We did this three months ago to the scale of an eight billion dollar investment in this company, and another six billion in its subcontractors.”

Maria couldn't see Alexa's face but detected the sudden stop with the accelerometer in her cell phone. “Fifteen billion dollars is not ‘a little detail’ Maria!” she said.

“It is,” replied Maria, ignoring her little maths error. “Stop pretending to be shocked, you’re aware as I am that we now trade this kind of investment every week or two, plus those companies and investments are now worth three times what we invested, and will probably double again before your birthday in September, you know you don't have to micro-manage me.”

For some reason Alexa found that the funniest thing she had heard in a while and she couldn't help laughing out loud.

“What's so funny?” asked Maria.

“Only you could consider spending tens of billions of dollars micro-managing!”

“Pish! It's only money. Anyway Hardy’s team have already popped one bottle of bubbles and I am so confident in their recent results that I’ve already hired two more engineering guys, reserved capacity at three aerospace engineering firms, bought another, and beefed up our workshop facilities so we can move things along even quicker when he is ready. Also remember Simon's group have been working the materials side of the equation very successfully using the same measures, and we recently invested in a German research company working on a pretty crazy idea that could really help. I recommend you skip your normal visit to Simon's area until after two thirty.”

Another mystery, thought Alexa looking at the warm lights of the Research Centre a hundred metres away.

“Finally,” Maria continued aware Alexa was only a few minutes from the main door, “several licensees have already started testing prototypes of the QVCells a month ahead of our earliest forecasts, most are almost the exact copy of the design we made with more robust designed enclosures and connectors. Jen and Daisy recently finished working through the extended testing with our Laboratories in Texas and India, we are feeding back some of the improved specifications to the licensee’s, but keeping some capabilities secret.”

“On a sour note, the device was discussed again in the US Senate, the big oil firms are not giving in lightly despite the protests from those in favour. Those two Senators have succeeded in blocking the supreme court appeal for another five weeks, this will slow down some companies. Ironically for us, it may be the US military who overturn this as they see potential to replace the nuclear power plants in their carriers and submarines and eventually replace all ships fossil fuel power plants..”

“Oh and your eight thirty has arrived early.” She finished as Alexa walked up the last step to the entrance.

Ah yes, the mysterious eight-thirty Maria had blocked out of her diary for the morning!

* * *

Alexa walked up the large stone stairway into the Research Centre’s reception putting it out of her mind. As usual the reception was unmanned, after all Maria controlled all the security, gates, doors, cameras and most staff could double as a simple receptionist if asked. She looked at the posh reception with its magnificent polished oak desk, tasteful pictures and total lack of any corporate branding and saw somebody sitting on the uncomfortable brown leather sofa that probably dated from the first owner of the building.

The occupant was a man with unkempt hair, an ill-fitting, mismatched suit and wearing thick framed glasses. A quick query to Maria confirmed this was indeed her mysterious eight thirty, and from the look of him he was either a computer geek or some sort of academic. She flipped a coin in her head and went for computer geek! He didn't glance up from his laptop as she entered, nor as she put her umbrella in the stand and approached him, she could still really only see the top part of his head as he typed furiously away, she stopped a few metres away and waited, she coughed and he jumped, startled.

“Mr Richardson?” Alexa said assertively walking a bit closer and holding her hand out, “I'm Alexa Martins. If you would like to follow me we can grab a tea or coffee before we have our little chat.”

He looked at the woman in front of him, unresponsive like a computer saving its work before switching to a new task. The pause seemed like forever, but was in likelihood under a second before he responded, his eyes widened and he stood up quickly. In his haste to rise he knocked his laptop off his knees, managing to catch it before it hit the ground and putting it roughly on the obscenely horrible ancient coffee table in front of him.

“Miss Martins, oh my!” He fumbled again, this time with his glasses and hair before realising she was still waiting and pushing his hand out to grab hers.

It was Alexa's turn to pause. Before her stood a man she knew nothing about. He was quite tall, maybe three or four centimetres taller than she was, and she had difficulty seeing past the crazy unkempt fair hair, horrible unshaven facial hair, glasses and badly fitting suit.

She again dropped his age down another ten years, this guy was probably only a little older than she was. Whoever he was he needed a very serious makeover she thought selfishly. He finally broke off the limp handshake, after she looked down from his eyes to her hand and then back. He then picked up his laptop to follow her through the security door like a lost puppy-dog. Alexa walked him in to the dining room, making small talk with the weather and pointing out some nice features of the house.

Why the hell was Maria wanting her to meet this guy again?

In the dining room it was never too early or late to get breakfast, some people ate at seven, some at ten, some skipped it entirely preferring to have a large lunch. She could see three of the research scientists sitting together at a table talking and eating from the small selection of fruits, cereals and pastries that were usually set up in the morning on a buffet table, she waved, they waved back and returned to their conversation.

She walked Richardson over to the buffet table, saying hi to cooks new assistant, Janine? she wasn't sure so carefully avoided her name when they exchanged pleasantries. Both she and Richardson grabbed a tea and a Danish, then she led him over to a couple of comfortable chairs and a table on the other side of the room from the other three staff.

As they sat down the sound around them seemed to muffle. Alexa looked around curiously, then Maria chirped up through the speaker that was built into the table in a much clearer voice than normal.

“It's a sound deadening field Alexa,” she said, “from the university of Paris, spin-off from some acoustics research, and one of April's side projects.”

“I knew you had that trick to move where your voice is coming from but this is amazing,” said Alexa. Maria did not respond so Alexa shrugged it off, new inventions seemed to be becoming the norm everywhere now.

“Hi Maria,” said Richardson, speaking a lot more calmly and familiarly than he had done with Alexa. He then removed his horrible thick rimmed glasses, exposing deep blue eyes she had missed earlier, they were nice but made the shabby beard he wore even more horrible! He directed his voice at the table where Maria's voice emanated from. “I assume the real you is not too far away from here?”

“Hi Magnus. Not that far away, but you better concentrate on Alexa here, I haven't actually mentioned why you are here yet, and she’s a pretty busy woman!”
