“Nicely done,” said Hardy thirty minutes later, “I’m impressed not only did you guys just about dismantle the four cabals, but you actually turned a massive profit off it.”

“Still getting over the alien bit and will need a bit of time to process,” said Jen, “but I agree, very nicely done.”

Alexa grinned, “there were a lot of pieces that had to be played together perfectly, and the group did that very well, but there was some luck involved too, especially in judging the human nature part which is not an exact science you guys would be used to. Also being able to access and real-time modify their communications was something we could never have achieved even a few months earlier.”

“Spence also really came through for us on this one.” Alexa said nodding to Spence. “When he finally met the Field Marshal and the Prime Minister two weeks ago and offered to create them an isolated AI to re-screen all the security cleared personnel, I think they were actually relieved. Let's face it, it must have been a hard pill for them to swallow, but they both agreed they couldn't have the system compromised again as bad as it was. Poor Spence had every possible security check done on him and Maria tells me it was for once very intensive.”

“I come from an army family so I have pretty solid ties to them, also the Field Marshal was actually an OK guy,” said Spence. “Alexa met him back in January when my father and brother came down and I introduced you, and as she said back then, it is hard for people like us to relate to military people. After the conversation she saw a human side to him, people like him have seen too much death and are well aware of the problems those who repeat history's mistakes, tend to cause.”

“Parliament passed an emergency law to improve the official secrets act, and have every single person who previously signed it, and were employed in positions that required it, to re-sign it. He put the whole of the Joint Intelligence committee and their advisors on administrative leave. Within three days most had been restored to their previous positions, one member and two advisors were arrested pending further investigation. The ones who passed are using the same techniques to interview others down the chain, another four were arrested. I doubt I will be needed in more than an administrative capacity before the end of the week.”

“So that's where you were these last weeks,” said Jen, “I guess we didn't want to pry as I assumed it was family related when they said you went home, but it makes some sort of sense now.”

“I can't believe the Field Marshal and Prime Minister requested or even allowed one of our AI systems inside their circle,” said Simon, “it was a brilliant idea to let them know about the experimental isolated AI system, I am not sure I hundred percent believe there is such a thing anymore though.”

“We did not actually lie though,” said Alexa, “we were just conservative with the answers we gave to their specific questions. Technically the AI will be totally stand-alone with no connections, and it will be storing its data on a government secure server. We re-purposed one of Spence's latest MOTHER systems, added the latest seed code and it was trained by the girls for a week on what its primary task would be.”

Spence continued for her, “I stepped back once we installed it, and while the initial audit takes place, all network traffic routing will be monitored by cleared operators from GCHQ. Churchill, that's the name they gave it, will use their secure servers for information storage, though we specified all data stored will be encrypted, and only three people have been given the management codes. All this was arranged by a special closed door cabinet meeting, even the Prime Minister agreed, reluctantly to be checked. I quietly suspect a lot of the security community will welcome this.”

“As to the lie bit,” said Alexa, “the girls are happy for the government to wash its own dirty laundry. Of course their new abilities to monitor traffic are still there but they do have the highest moral standards.”

“Yes, the wormhole dipole is both amazing and truly scary both at the same time,” said Hardy.

“And we don't think the aliens have it.” Added April.

“You know I have been working through Magnus's theories for over a year now,” said Maria. “Even at our accelerated rate I really don't think we would be able to develop the same thing using the technology and science so far described in the message. Magnus's work is deceptively simple, the maths is elegant if totally non-conventional, and somehow bypasses several parts of our current quantum theory, which need throwing away anyway.”

“Yeah,” said Jen, “I can't believe we thought quantum entanglement was a real phenomena, even worse, thinking we were going to achieve superluminal communications with it. It does beg the question why you are calling the new devices QVModem's though.”

Alexa laughed, “quite simple really Jen, We already have QVThrusters, and QVCells, so QVModem's is kind-of on brand. Plus science fiction has used the idea of entangled quantum states as the basis for every instantaneous communications technology since they were discovered, even I know that, and the toaster operating manual is the closest I get to science. Anyway it's not trademarked and I think it's kind of catchy!”

“We couldn't change Alexa's mind,” said a resigned Maria, “and it kind of stuck, plus it nicely obfuscates the technology. The latest QVModem's are pretty amazing, though unfortunately maths is still the only way to think about them. I tried to describe it to Alexa without it, but everything becomes an enigma or magic when you move higher dimensional objects, and then try to translate them back into your three-dimensional realm. You are assuming we, being a bit more advanced than you, understand it all, but even in the Magnus's new maths there are probability axioms you need to assign. What came first, the chicken or the egg as you humans say.”

“The chicken,” said Alexa, “pretty obvious really!”

Everybody in the room gave her a funny look, sensibly they all ignored it.

## Magnus Opus

MOTHER [DRONE443 monitoring asset 226556 escalating possible contact for investigation local QV spacial grid 13922457-59427006-43321024]

April [Hi Mum. I need a consensus on this one. I have one of our newer reaction-less drones showing another what looks to be military-grade drone following Ian and Matilda's car. I targeted a QVModem onto it and the communications analysis show it is Chinese military stealth drone, running through one of their low earth orbit satellite connections]

Maria [This is the third time, they don't seem to want to take a hint. Leave it with me April, there is an RAF airbase twenty miles away at Boscombe Down, let's send them a present]

* * *

They all re-convened a few weeks later at the beginning of November, having had a basic 101 on some of the new technology, and after Alexa finally went over a very brief, but well received summary of their space plans for the rest of the staff.

“To tell the truth,” said Hardy, looking back from Alexa to the group, “I was super excited to try and go through the aliens unified gravity equations, but every time I kept getting bogged down as the maths is incomplete. It keeps referring to this 'letter after Z' which is not yet described properly, almost like the pages in their book are out of order, or it was put together by a high-school math teacher instead of a PhD professor.”

“I was looking over Hardy's shoulder the whole time,” said April, “There are gaps, but the message has moved on from mathematics onto materials technology, describing algorithms that their replicator technology uses to make certain molecules. If there is an explanation, it must buried later on in the larger message blocks.”

“Same with their reaction-less drive,” said Hardy, without the complete maths behind it, you just have the alien's word that it does what it does. Our version is much simpler.”

“That is actually a good thing,” said April. “Your design scales more efficiently, and we can use the newer processors we are designing to manage them without an AI. You can't do anything with the aliens version unless they provide the control algorithms later, again presumably later on in the data. So yet another win for team humanity as far as I can see.”

“I vote we keep our carbon nanotube processor designs in-house,” said Spence, “there is a bit of a renaissance in computer technology going on out there and human designed processors are good enough for just about anything as they stand, and they are still improving so no point in rocking that boat for nothing.”

“While on the subject,” said Hardy, “Simon, how did your team get on looking at the molecular replicator technology?”

“I’m a little scared of some of the field manipulation stuff,” said Simon, “the valency stuff is OK, we already found the way to break that using the correct low energy field manipulator settings. But the message seems to imply these newer field emitters can also be used to disrupt the strong nuclear force, and that could be very dangerous if used in the wrong hands.”

“I do not think it is as dangerous as you think Simon,” said Helena, “the field head itself would also be destroyed in such a case. But I also think your team's original approach would be better than theirs, we just skip the planned iteration now we know what's possible, and do something similar, though with our version we would be stuck with four elements per build head.”

“That's plenty,” said Simon, “Our current design only works with one element, carbon, and this covers all the structures we planned to build. There are still gaps we need to work through, but we believe that almost all of an Icarus three class saucer can be structurally printed within this limitation. Worse case is we fill those gaps old school, and add some parts in after.”

“Leo is ecstatic though, he was almost dancing around the room with Matilda when Helena announced how they were going to fast track the development of a molecular replicator, carefully excluding the mention of the word aliens for the time being. We also decided we would only proceed development at the rate we could understand the technology, which means we are going to have to stop at this level of tech for quite a while. Though me, Helena and Matilda have already seen one part of their system that can be improved.”

“I can also answer some of the timeline questions a little better now,” said Helena, “It is basically a big bootstrap process. We use our current fabricator machine, to make two arrays of modified field emitters similar to the QVThrusters, but with a completely different control geometry, these are mounted perpendicular forming a build edge. In conjunction we need to fabricate a base atomiser, our term for the new alien component, which sits above and below each build edge. Finally we need to fabricate a compute platform to control each array element, each plane, and each base atomiser, real-time. With these assembled and working properly, and perfectly coordinated, we can hold and position any atom within the 3D array. We need at least five thousand of these build edges per millimetre to enable it to fabricate our first, rough, molecular replicator assembly head.”

“To get to this start point is going to take us two months minimum, using every resource, and every spare second of processing capacity of all our systems. But with the molecular replicator assembly head built, we are now at the point where it gets scary and amazing at the same time.”

“How so?” said Alexa, who had been trying to follow this on a very abstract level.

“Well, basically because the molecular assembly head can now make an exact, or more importantly, a better copy of itself.” Said Simon. “This is another one of those scary and amazing moments, as each version is built with much more capable 3D processing elements, a denser array, and very importantly, each generation you also build it bigger!”

He used the palm of his hands starting with a small gap then doubled it each time, until it got very large. “I think you can see where this is going, theoretically, maybe only a few days after this, you have a molecular replicator head big enough for a one metre square replicator.”

“Now it's nowhere near as simple as Simon says it is,” added Helena. “The hardware needs very complex control layers, power, cooling, element condensers, processing, calibration, etcetera, and the build has to operate in a vacuum. Because of this we will have to stop at each doubling of the size, while we also scale up the surrounding infrastructure. The hardware basically scales linearly, but unfortunately the software scales logarithmically, so to control that one metre replicator we will need a million times the compute of its ten centimetre cousin.”

The people in the room, except maybe Simon, were being left speechless at what was being proposed, none of them up until this point had actually researched or understood the task. Simon and his team had of course, gone through the same jaw-dropping moment only days earlier. Even knowing the science it seemed impossible, but Helena had not finished.

“This only gives you your hammer. If you want to build something with it, you need a design. We have to reduce our design to a slice-by-slice blueprint at an almost atomic level. We will need to write algorithms to feed in the molecular models and manipulate the field emitters real time, this will take almost as much of our computing time, and be the limiting factor on the eventual size. Theoretically we could get to something kilometres in size, but practically, even with all our current compute ability we will hit a ceiling well before we get to even a metre.”

“This does not mean we cannot build bigger than this,” said Maria, “we can, and eventually we will exceed it. What we cannot do currently is coordinate every molecule when building more than this. To give you an example, for the saucer, it is not solid all the way through; take any cross section at its widest point and it is likely that seventy percent will be empty space for storage or for humans to walk around in. For that other thirty percent it is likely that most of that is structural solid graphyne, leaving maybe under three percent as stuff we have to really compute like power, electronics, QVCells, QVThrusters, screens, etcetera. So some complicated spots we have to go really slow, others we can go quite quickly.”

“Unfortunately there are trillions and trillions of things to go wrong even in a small build of a few centimetres, even having a single air molecule in the build area could cause the build to fail; The final machine therefore must work in a full vacuum and in an ultra-clean environment. That is why the clean rooms, vacuum chambers, and equipment are being built now, well ahead of there requirement.”

“If you have one takeaway from this, it is that building every square millimetre is a supercomputer level task in itself. Luckily using our method instead of the aliens method, we can have a layers of hard coded algorithms we can pre-load into the emitter substrate, so you stop the process for a nanosecond, load the algorithm for say graphyne, and it goes full speed on graphyne, and we don't have to think about it until we change to another pattern. The alien system has about a thousand such molecules it describes, we currently have five, all for carbon. This is why it will take so long, as in parallel we need to work out a way to design hundreds more molecule types, so we can have such things as semiconductors, soft materials, superconductors and lots of other things. We need a lot of trial and error to learn how to do all this.”

“OK I did ask I guess,” said Hardy, smiling at Alexa who was now totally ignoring the tech speak and playing with her nails. “So like a star trek transporter, but a billion times slower, you must be layering trillions of atoms a second.”

“Pretty much,” laughed Simon, “Hollywood does tend to make everything much more simple. I really wish we could conjure up atoms out of thin air, but we do have to physically have them first to manipulate. I haven't got my head around most of this yet, that's assuming I can. At least the disassembler, or recycling machine is relatively simple in comparison; No finesse required to destroy stuff.”

“And Helena forgot to mention,” he continued, “that with this we improve our whole tool-chain in every area, lab equipment, fabricators, extruders, recyclers, processing, the list goes on, you just have to be able to think of it.”

“Simon is right, but we have to start with processing and memory, this is where we are always constrained; Once this is perfected, and comes on-line, the bigger stuff will follow quickly,” said Maria.

She continued after a few nods. “For the proposed space habitat not everything needs to be molecular replicated. We still have our original graphyne extruder design, which we can enhance a little, and which can then do ninety nine percent of the station. We should have replicators near the end, but we should also be able to go really old-school, extruding metals, silicates and plastics by melting them with lasers or squishing them through a nozzle to 3D print if need be. I think even the most hardened masochist would think twice using a molecular replicator to make a space habitat.”

“So basically while Helena, Maria and April solve the hard problems getting the replicator working,” Simon finished with, “my team will work on the relatively easy task of converting a trillion tonnes of asteroid into a million tonnes of space habitat.”

“So that's about it!” said Helena. “Though Matilda did say she is going to understand this molecular replicator if it kills her.”

“Good on you sister!” said Alexa, her perfectly manicured nails now forgotten.

“While we are at it Helena,” said Alexa, “I was still processing the hard science bits and missed the part when you said you would have a replicator ready by.”

Hardy smiled.

“Well the science bits were a bit hard so I can see how you might have missed it, but about three or four months for the one metre square one.” Said Helena.

“Well I suppose the good news is it's all been done before by really clever aliens, so we know it is a solvable problem,” said Alexa.

“And the worst that can happen is we are delayed, or we go back to plan A but with a much better knowledge of how it's all done,” said Simon, also finally smiling.

“We are finding the most recent message blocks we have decoded are just recipes for new material molecules that can be produced by their replicator, most are common ones we already know, but there are some which seem to be similar to polyester which leaves us thinking that whoever created the message are likely organic and land based.”

“Do we have an image of the aliens yet?” said Alexa, perking up a bit.

“Sorry, not a thing on biology, plant, animal life or even molecular biology and DNA, I'm guessing all this comes in one of those later messages,” said Maria.

“So they could still be coming to steal our earth women,” laughed Hardy.

“Ha, ha!” smirked Jen.

“Have you girls thought of printing some real bodies with this new technology?” said Simon nonchalantly.

“Interesting idea,” said Maria, “I guess we could try when the machine is ready, but it doesn't appeal to me, the idea of being a flying saucer however definitely appeals at a weird level.”

“I’m with mum on this,” said Helena, “but currently we would be severely degraded by cosmic radiation, possibly fatally! that stuff scares the bejeezus out of me. Thankfully the active magnetic shielding we are trialling in Icarus two, and the new materials that will be available to us soon, should reduce most of that danger, possibly eliminate it completely. Personally I won't be happy unless it's less than or the same as here. Whatever happens however I want to be close to you guys, my mother and my sister, so I guess I’m staying right here until we are all ready to go.”

“Me too,” said Maria.

“And me,” said April, “but the second it's all proven good I’m up for a flying saucer body too.”

* * *

It was almost nine o'clock at night, Alexa was pacing the hall, waiting for the door to open, she would have waited outside but the mid-December temperatures had plummeted below zero.

The house was empty, Hardy was staying with his new boyfriend Jeremy in town, and Jen had finally mustered up the courage to ask Magnus out to a movie with Terry and his girlfriend Priscilla. It was a remake of Stargate, and she thought it fitting and appropriate to take him. Daisy was of course all excited too when she heard, but Maria got her out of the way with an “urgent phone call” and explained how Jen had been building up the courage for this for a month and Magnus had probably been waiting to say yes for the last nine. Terry had also booked an Indian restaurant for 9PM when the movie finished so Jen wouldn't be back until at least ten thirty.

“He's just saying goodbye to Albert,” said Maria, analysing Alexa's voice and face for the last hour, checking her pulse rate and stress levels and wondering seriously whether she was ill and she should get a second medical opinion.

The door opened and she grabbed David in a warm embrace as he stepped through it, “I'm so glad you're back, I’ve missed you so much David.”

David dropped the bag and returned the embrace. It was cold outside, below freezing, just walking from the car to the house was unpleasant. She was so warm, so beautiful and smelled just perfect.

“I have missed you too Alexa, more than you will ever know. the last three-weeks have been crazy, I of course knew about my mothers condition, but knowing about something, and then being told she has a month to live, are two very different things.”

He held on to Alexa for what seemed like an age, both arms wrapped around her not wanting to let her go, and her passion slowly winning over the sadness he still felt.

“Give me ten minutes to have a shower and get changed,” he said stroking a tear softly off her cheek, “and I will join you in the living room, I wouldn't say no to a small glass of wine if you are having one too,” he attempted a smile before walking up the stairs with his usual brown leather bag.

As she heard his door close, she too rushed to her room, checked her appearance, splashed some water on her face and made sure she was still presentable, she then rushed downstairs and into the wine cellar to get one of the Chilean Pinot’s Hardy had bought a case of last month.

“Oh god Maria, can you do something with the lights and maybe put some nice music on,” she said flustered as she tried to find a relaxed position on the sofa.

Maria guessed she was OK, this love thing was certainly getting infectious, first Spence and Jessica, then Simon and Allison, then Hardy and Jeremy, possibly Jen and Magnus and now Alexa and David, almost half her talks with the people she knew seemed to be about relationships, and it was strange how all logic and sensibility went out of the window where it was concerned. “Coming right up..”

Some lights dimmed and some went off. Spence had also wired Alexa's grandad's expensive stereo to a network controlled jukebox, as nobody could be bothered turning the record over to play the other side every twenty minutes. As she struggled to open the wine and get the table, and her position just perfect, the haunting tone of the music started to rise. It was weird David had very similar musical tastes as her grandad, another box ticked.

“Err Maria, any chance you could go and powder your nose for an hour or two.. Pretty please!”

“He's on his way, I will, as you say, go and powder my nose.” The speaker clicked off, something it never did, Alexa hoped she hadn't upset Maria, but she had to know it was nothing to do with her.

The door opened slowly and David peeked in wondering why it was so dark. Hearing music he walked in closing the door and looking around, the two sofas were sat next to the crackling open fire, it was quite dim but he could make out Alexa and the wines, and, oh his favourite album! He wanted to pinch himself as for a moment he thought he had died and gone to heaven.

He walked over to her, his eyes were gradually adjusting from the bright lights outside to the more demure ones here. By the warm glow of the firelight she looked stunning.

“I wanted to welcome you back and let you know how much I missed you these past weeks, then I realised you would be tired and probably sad and would just want to sit down and share a glass of wine.”

“You are tearing my heart apart Miss Martins,” he said playfully sitting right next to her on the sofa, he took her dainty hand and covered it in both his, “how can a man be sad, when all his senses agree he is sitting next to an angel. He let go of her hand slowly and picked up both wines, handing one to her.

He softly clinked his glass to hers. “To the two most beautiful women I have ever known. To my mother, who departed this world too early and I will remember in my heart forever, and to the beautiful, passionate and intelligent woman in front of me, who I don't think I ever want to let go of.”

God, this guy took romance to a new level, her eyes moistened again and a visage of pure happiness came over her face. They looked at each other through the wine glasses, then both took a slow sip. If a wine could have been harvested, fermented, bottled and presented for just this one moment, this was it.

His hand moved to hers, and he slowly took the glass from her hand, put both glasses on the table then, looking deep into her eyes drew Alexa into the longest and most passionate kiss of her life.

* * *

Maria, true to her word, did not intrude, but instead moved her attention to Magnus and Jen on their “Not a Date”. The atmosphere was certainly different from David and Alexa's, which was currently playing out like a million dollar BBC Jane Austin adaptation. In contrast Jen and Magnus were eating poppadoms, laughing with Terry and Pris, drinking lager from bottles, and arguing over which term in a finite sequence of the singularity equation would best to make the rippling water stargate effect.

[Humans!]

* * *

Christmas 2026 came to Benedict House with cold rains, misty mornings and not a hint of snow. Now mostly just referred to as the Research Centre, it had outdone itself this year thanks to Sharon. There was a beautifully decorated tree outside the main entrance, and smaller ones in the reception, the large dining room, and the other large room everyone had appropriated for their pub.

Normally the week before Christmas was busy, then, just after, it went quiet as people went home to family and friends. The centre never shut down completely however, there were always people who preferred to celebrate Christmas on their own, or just work through it as normal. Then there were the people who did not have an extended family, or who now found their family were the new friends they had made. For those people they both left the lights on, and arranged special meals and get together events to make them feel not left out.

Maria had explored millions of options for improving security. She had built hundreds of QVModem's at a cost of millions of pounds for the take-down operations, newer and better ones were added daily. All of these were in constant use scanning for new threats, known spy agencies, bloggers, journalists, or any known people of shady disposition.

Several of the modems were employed exclusively on scanning for bugs and other devices at their facilities, this was also done on visitors, deliveries, service personnel and packages arriving. It was all now coordinated through one of the non-sentient AI systems, which they kept up to date with any threat information.

It was in this light, that the staff rarely worried too much any more about security on the site. The last blogger who trespassed on site was discovered a few metres onto the property. As well as being arrested, and tied up in a hundred lawsuits, he had also somehow locked himself out of his social media accounts and was releasing cat videos daily.

The fact the world was generally aware through rumours and leaks that a lot of the take-downs of organised crimes and corrupt individuals was done using AI systems, nobody was a hundred percent sure whose systems. Also the world was also currently going through a boom phase because of it. All this and the fact that the Dietrich Research Centre had one of the highest approval ratings ever, helped keep security concerns to a background hum.

Because of the improved security, visits by family and close friends had now become quite a regular thing. Magnus had been home to visit his mother exactly once since moving to England, and as such he was now really looking forward to her coming over here to spend Christmas with him. He was a safe driver but still not very confident driving on the left hand side of the road, in winter, and so Jen had volunteered to drive him to the airport to pick her up. Jen was still one of the only drivers Maria trusted to drive better than her, Albert and, ironically, Magnus were the other two.

“Thank you for doing this Jen,” he said smiling warmly at her from the passenger seat, it still felt a little weird sitting in the left seat and not having a steering wheel in front of him, even though Maria had said he was better than most of the drivers she monitored. He believed her, he remembered getting driven by Alexa and she spent just about the whole drive looking and talking to the three other people in the car.

Maria confessed Alexa was a driver in name only, and with a QVModem now hard-wired into both the older Tesla's, she usually did everything once Alexa pointed the wheel in the approximate direction.

“..And thank you for the other night,” Magnus continued, “everything was perfect, you were perfect, and I had a really great time.”

“Oh thanks Magnus!” She briefly took her eyes off the road to meet his blue eyes, and giving him her nicest smile. She turned back to the quiet road. “Well the movie definitely wasn't perfect,” she laughed, and diverted the conversation back to the movie for the next twenty minutes, much to Maria's annoyance.

The car got to the airport and passed through two barriers which just opened as they neared, Jen following the very clear directions on the screen. They ended up in a small lane, directly in front of the arrivals, in front of a sign which said “No Parking Ever” and “Vehicles Parked Here Will Be Forcibly Removed”. It was only missing the sign for “Offenders Will Be Shot” to make the driver feel even more welcome.

“Just park it here Jen, I will park it and bring it back here when you are ready,” came Maria's voice from the car.

They left the car, watched by a row of bored taxi drivers much further away. A guy in a uniform was making his way quickly towards them, when he suddenly stopped, picked up his radio to talk to someone, looked at them, shook his head, and went back to being bored.

“Her flight from Reykjavik touched down thirty minutes ago, I don't see her name in the immigration system yet, so you have at least another thirty minutes if you want to grab a drink.”

“Thanks Maria,” said Magnus as he and Jen made their way into the airport building, and the car drove off silently, watched only by a very confused security guard.

“Why does airport tea taste so disgusting?” said Jen, looking at the paper cup in front of her, with its clear plastic top and piece of string dangling out of it. The wet label at the end of the string saying “Premium Quality Blend”, only added to the insult.

Magnus looked at Jen, then at his similarly ugly cup of peppermint tea, and they both laughed. “No wonder everyone drinks coffee these days!”

Her smile was infectious. Jen had been his rock since he came here, always smiling, always helping, and always so amazing. Without thinking he reached over and touched her hand. “Thanks again Jen, I really wanted my mother to meet the very special person I have been working with this past year, the one who helped me so much.”

Jen took her other hand, from around her hot tea, and placed it over his. He felt its warmth as she returned the affectionate look on his face. “It's me who should be thanking you Magnus, you have taught me so much and are so patient. I cannot believe you are the same man who walked into our lives nearly a year ago, I mean look at you, you’re charming, gracious, forgiving, I mean there are not enough adjectives in the English language to say how wonderful a man you are. I only wish..”

She blushed, looking around the busy airport cafe, this was not the place though, she wanted to cry, but held it in smiling.

Maria sensed something, she was listening to their conversation intently; Their date the other evening ended nothing like Alexa and David's, but with a fumbled goodbye from Magnus in the car, instead of the kiss Jen was probably expecting, her face that night impossible to read as she wondered what she had done wrong. Maria knew from observation and girl talk that Jen had no problems with relationships, but something was holding her back in this one, and it was an enigma to her. Magnus she could totally understand, Jen was his first love and he elevated her so high he thought her unobtainable.

Maria's thoughts lasted microseconds, the words barely out of Jen's mouth before having a million parameters analysed and compared to a thousand similar love stories.

“Hey guys.. Sorry to interrupt,” she chirped in a tone that said spontaneity, “but your mothers is in the customs queue and will be out in a few minutes if she doesn't get stopped, and I see no flags against her in their system.”

Thank You Maria, she thought.

“Come on Magnus, I’m dying to meet your mother.” Jen said, the about-turn in her tonal expression surprising Maria. She stood up, ignoring the tea and took his hand dragging him towards arrivals.

Jen's words pleased Magnus no end. He had never introduced a girl to his mother, they had never even discussed relationships, he had never known a father, it was always him and his mother. A smart, caring mother who spent every moment of her free time dotting over him, but as a college professor herself, she never seemed to have a lot of free time.

She obviously always wanted what was best for him, but being an only child herself and her mother dying before she could become a grandmother, she struggled to understand the magnitude of working full time and raising a son, and so reluctantly she had sent him to boarding school. School was nothing like being taught by his mother, there was no passion there, and the schools usually just regurgitated boring books day after day. The excitement of being taken to America and having to learn and talk to people in a whole different language had made it exciting for a while, but really it was just worse and in a different language.

He wished he could have made friends with the other boys, but he was always years younger than them and nobody wanted to be friends with a ‘child’ even in university, while his mother was so proud of his achievements, he was too young and too immature, his only female role-model being his mother. It also didn't help that he was bullied, by other kids at school and at university by college professors and other students. Moving out to a job in the real world turned out no better.

Seeing Jennifer on stage with Hardy and Simon that day a year ago, he had seen something of what he could have been with the right nurturing, everyone said Jen was not special, and unfairly, she had to do so much more to prove she was as equal a partner as the boys. Magnus had episodes of serious depression during those dark days, but he got through it with his mothers help, their constant video calls and her monthly visits to see him bringing him such joy. She had asked him if there were any girls in his life and he lied saying there were some and he was happy.

But Magnus's mother was not stupid and it only hit her what a horrible life he had probably had before on his last visit to California. Her sluggish, depressed, unpresentable caterpillar of a son had emerged from his chrysalis and been replaced by a happy, beautiful, well dressed and gracious man; One who now worked for one of the most prestigious companies in the world, it was everything she had hoped for. The night after his brief visit back at the end of spring she had cried with happiness, and their frequent calls since had always been warm.

Maria, who had a presence in his mothers university department, knew first hand how her whole demeanour had changed for the better that day, never a very popular professor, she was seen as clever but sullen and strict. The woman who now taught undergraduate mathematics, was now happy and easy going, and her popularity with everyone had increased as a result.

There was no nervousness in the woman who now wheeled her large blue suitcase in front of her, past a guard who let his small beagle sniff her case, then through two armed airport policemen, looking bored rather than attentive, and onward to a large set of double doors that had just started to open as she approached. Anja was just so happy to be able to see her boy again.

Going through the exit doors of an airport always gave her a weird feeling; You were now a stranger in a strange land, and the sea of strange faces, and drivers in suits holding cards or tablets, with strange names on, only emphasised that more. She scanned the crowd spotting him almost instantly, that new happy smiling face, her good looking well dressed boy was waving at her, and she wheeled her bag on a direct course for him.

“Momma!” he cried as he grabbed the small woman around her waist and spun her around.

“Magnus, oh Magnus,” she returned, her eyes closed but the smile and tears of joy on her face speaking words that could not be spoken.

Jen stood off a few metres away smiling, and looking at Magnus holding the small golden haired lady in the green pleated dress that was his mother. She thought how she looked surprisingly like her mother, but with glasses, and she remembered Magnus had worn glasses the first time she had seen him. Sharon or Maria, or Alexa, or all of them, had somehow persuaded him to get laser surgery in that first month, she remembered him asking her if he should have it done, and she said Daisy had it done a year in to university, as had her cousin, and both were very happy, and he did have beautiful eyes. A week later it was all done.

Magnus and his mothers embrace seemed to last for minutes, then there was a few minutes of, presumably Finish, that was spoken so fast you could have modulated a TV channel on it.

“Just lovey-dove stuff,” said Maria from the phone she was holding with enough volume to be heard just above the background. “I think he’s talking about you now..”

They were holding both hands facing each other, the woman looking lovingly and proudly at her son. She suddenly glanced her way, then quickly glanced back, just as Magnus looked toward her smiling and expectantly. He grabbed his mothers bag and walked it and his mother towards Jen.

“Jen, I’d like you to meet my mother, Anja. Mum, this is Jen.”

Anja looked at the dark haired girl a bit taller than her and quite pretty. She wrapped both arms around Jen and brought her into a deep hug.

“Jen, Jen, Jen, I am so happy to finally meet you, Magnus speaks of you all the time when we talk, he tells me about all these wonderful things, his wonderful friends but most of all he talks of you.” Anja's English was flawless with a tinge of what she presumed was a Finnish accent, Jen wasn't really sure what to say.

“You have a beautiful son Anja, everybody loves him around here and he makes everyday worth celebrating. I am so happy you can stay with us, it is so difficult to extract Magnus from his work, but I will do my best to ensure he gives you his full attention over the holidays.”

Magnus was already pushing her bag and moved next to his mum, holding her hand and guiding her toward the exit. As they walked out of the double doors, Jen’s car was pulling up into the same no parking zone, the rear boot already opening to accept the luggage. Magnus popped the bag in and opened the rear door for his mother, once she was in Magnus and Jen got in. Just as they set off the barrier started rising. It was certainly easier getting out of English airports than American ones were his mothers only thought.

Jen kept exactly to the speed limits, and showed no sign of her usual aggressive driving tendencies. The forty minute journey back from Bristol Airport was filled with observations of the flight, and the differences between their three countries. Jen was not as well travelled as others, wasn't particularly cultured, and spoke no other languages other than English. She had been once to Disneyland in Paris when she was ten, but remembered nothing of it outside the hundreds of pictures her mother took. She had also been around Europe before university for two months with a girlfriend, quite adventurous they thought at the time, even though it was just a few bed and breakfasts in France and Italy.

Of course, since the QVCell she had done a few talks, but, unfairly, she was usually only considered if Hardy or Simon were not available. Hardy freely confessed the people who ignored her were idiots, and didn't deserve to be in the position they were in, if they did not recognise the contribution she had made; The fact that Jen was the most popular with the students who attended attested to that. She didn't mind, she knew she'd had to work harder than the two guys, and always felt herself measuring up. Hardy laughed at her doubts, and said what she was feeling was called imposter syndrome, most smart people suffered from it one or more times during their lives.

But this last year had been different, things seemed to have been getting easier to understand, no longer was she struggling to understand the talks around complex maths and she found people taking her suggestions much more seriously. Hardy, Magnus and Jules surprised her one night a month ago with a bottle of wine and a cake, after Maria pronounced her the fourth person in the world to fully understand Magnus's Infinity Maths and the equations for their new QVThruster. They had another celebration a week later when Terry became the fifth.

His mother smiled again at Magnus as they pulled up to the Research Centre, she had been quiet the last few kilometres as they had travelled through the countryside, but as they pulled through the barrier and rounded the corner into Alexa's house, her eyes lit up.

Jen had asked Alexa a few weeks earlier if Magnus's mother could stay in the unused room above the garage, rather than getting a room in a hotel in town. The room had only been used a dozen times since its beautiful refit over a year earlier and Alexa agreed readily, saying it was as much Jen's house while she lived there and she didn't ever need to ask.

The boot popped open as the car came to a stop, it was still cold despite being early afternoon, and some of the northern aspects still had traces of frost from this morning where the sun had not found them.

“Oh my word Magnus,” said his mother, glancing around at the beautiful house and grounds, “this is not where you live is it?”

“No mother, I live about a kilometre away, but this is where Jen lives, and this is where you are staying for the next six days. The others are away for Christmas, though nobody has any idea where Alexa and David are, and Maria is not telling.”

“My lips are sealed,” said the car.

Anja looked back at the empty car confused, then Maria spoke again from the car in rapid Finnish and Anja smiled and said something back. It suddenly clicked who Jen was, and who Alexa was, who Maria was, and where she actually was. She looked at Jen, then at the house, then at her son.

“Oh you have so many secrets here,” she smiled giddily, “that was Tallos, our AI from the math department at the university, it seems the rumours are true that there is a lot more to those little black boxes than meets the eye,” she patted her nose smiling even more.

“That is Maria, mother,” said Magnus proudly, “she is a good friend too and she's everywhere here, you just have to say hi.”

“Hello Maria,” said his mother.

“Hello Mrs Richardson,” said the car, “we usually work on familiar names here so if it is OK I will call you Anja. Like Magnus said, the house is empty for at least three more days, but rather than move you around, we have the guest apartment you can use for your whole stay.”

The car boot closed itself, and one of the three double doors to the garage quietly started to open, a few seconds later the car moved slowly and quietly just the sound of the gravel crunching as it parked in the large area.

“Er Jen,” said the car before it got halfway in, “I’m not going to charge myself remember?”

The car continued into the garage and stopped in front of a wall charger, Jen followed it in and popped the lead into the socket then walked back. “Sorry about that, I hardly ever drive her these days, I’ve said Magnus can use my car any time he likes though, if he wants to take you anywhere, there are some nice restaurants in Bath which is about fifteen minutes drive from here.”

Magnus walked her suitcase to the right of the garage, and up some stairs, she followed, with Jen not far behind.

It was obvious Bella had been in earlier as there were fresh flowers on the table, the curtains were opened and there were fresh sheets and towels on the bed. It was also nice and warm, the temperature a balmy twenty five. Jen tutted and dialled it down to twenty two. The small kitchen on the right had a small plate with three fresh muffins in, and a note saying “Welcome to England”, “Bella”, and a little love heart written underneath. Jen smiled, the level of detailed planning Maria could put into something was unbelievable.

“Thanks Maria,” said Magnus as if reading Jen's mind.

“Bella, not me. She will be around soon to introduce herself, she and Albert live in the next house but she likes to help out around the house and they both come and go here as they please.”

“Oh Magnus, this room and this place is so beautiful,” said Anja, tearing up as she looked out over the back windows at the herb garden, the wall, the top of Bella and Albert's little house and the expansive countryside beyond.

Magnus dropped his mothers large suitcase by the bed. “Remember mother Maria is here too so if you need me or anything you just have to ask.”

“That's right Anja,” said Maria in a soft, all present voice. “All the main doors are unlocked, feel free to wander into the big house around the grounds or up to Benedict house where Magnus lives and we will visit later. The only place off limits for now is the little house in front of you, as that is where Bella and Albert live, but I am sure once you meet they won't mind you visiting. Most of the guys use the conservatory in the house as the default common room, that's where you will usually find Bella for a few hours in the morning clearing up and restocking the supplies. If you're lucky she will make you breakfast, if not just help yourself, though I expect Magnus or Jen will be around you most of the time.

Anja walked over to Jen and gave her a squeeze, “thank you for letting me stay in your house Jen, it is so beautiful.”

“Oh it's nothing really,” said Jen accepting the hug, “I’d love to introduce you to the other guys here but we have the place to ourselves, why don't we take you on a little tour then we can have dinner.”

They all walked back and into Alexa's house, as Maria had said, the door was unlocked. When they got in Jen hung her coat on the rack with a dozen others, and walked them through the living room, and then into the large kitchen dining conservatory area.

Jen put the kettle on and grabbed three mugs, putting a normal tea bag in one and two peppermint teas in the other two, Magnus really did take after his mother. She walked her around the rest of the house while the kettle was boiling, the door to Maria's area remaining closed and being fobbed off as a “utility room”. She briefly also showed Anja her room, which she thankfully had bribed Cathy from the big house to tidy up this morning.

She poured the three teas and took them to the large sofas everyone used in the underfloor heated conservatory.

“Help yourself to anything here, the place is always stocked with teas, coffees, food and some really nice wines in the cellar, I’m not much of a connoisseur myself but I’ll grab us a nice bottle for dinner. Magnus and I don't cook that well, so I have ordered it for six o'clock if that is OK?”

“Oh Jen, as long as I can sit and talk to Magnus and you, I would be happy with a park bench and a burger truck.”

“Mum,” laughed Magnus, “that is the first time I have ever heard you make a joke!”

Anja looked confused. “Did I?, oh I guess I did, didn't I!” she smiled too, “I guess I’m just happier now you have a real girlfriend..”

Jen choked on the tea she was sipping, as did Magnus.

Not seeing both their discomforts Anja continued, “and such a beautiful and talented one at that, oh Magnus I am so happy for you!”

Magnus looked at the floor, hoping the world would just open and swallow him. But then the most unexpected thing happened, Jen held his hand.

“My mum and dad are coming down tomorrow, Anja,” said Jen, “I’d love to introduce you to them,” she smiled at Anja, and when Magnus finally dared look at her she winked. He smiled in his best ‘I am so, so sorry Jen, I will make it up to you any way in the world even if it kills me’ smile.

Thank you god, thank you god, thank you god, thought Magnus, what the hell had he been thinking telling his mother that Jen was his girlfriend! He talked about her all the time and it just slipped out once when she was pestering him how he loved her. He had spent the last five video calls with his mum back peddling how they were just friends really. She obviously had not heard a single word. Thank you Jen, he squeezed her hand and silently saying, “sorry”.

Jen just did her little sweet pixie smile back to him returning the silent whisper, “it’s OK.”

Jen had arranged for her mum and dad to come down last week, Maria had booked them a nice room at the posh hotel in town where David used to work, and the one she didn't know she actually owned three point one four percent of. Maria thought the number radiated karma and trimmed the percentage in Jen’s monthly finance report spreadsheet accordingly. To her continued annoyance it was filed as always unread into a folder called “boring finance stuff”.

“They are coming early,” she said, not letting go of Magnus's hand. “I was planning on having brunch when they arrived, and we are booked in the restaurant in their hotel for tomorrow night, we would love for you to join us for both.”

“That would be wonderful Jen,” said Anja, taking her other hand. “I feel like you are part of our family already.”

Magnus could have died on the spot, but Jen kept smiling, though a lot less genuinely, and a bit more worried than before as she just realised the implications of what she had heard.

Maria realised the implications immediately, the next two days were going to be quite interesting, quite interesting indeed.
