Approximately three hundred and eighty thousand kilometres above them, Alexa and David were doing a lot of firsts, none of which would ever get in any history book.

* * *

“The plan for the colonies generated a lot of discussion outside of Alexa's initial presentation,” said Jen. “A few people have gone through Gianni’s proposal now and would be keen to hear the timeline. I mean it's January 2027, and he is saying by 2028 we will start building it, and in 2032 people will be living on it. Quite frankly it does not seem possible to build something so huge in space in four years.”

“We are working on a lot of fronts for the first space habitat designs,” said April, “like Helena said there is no need for molecular assemblers or anything fancy to make a structure in space. Our design just requires lots of the same parts that can be clipped together like Lego to make a structure, then lots of dirt and water. Unlike the elegant but slow Dusseldorf approach, Gianni's plan has not changed much due to the message. We are still going to repurpose some large asteroids, smash them into pieces, feed those into an extruder, turn the pieces into big segments and connect them together. For that we basically need something extremely big, low tech, reliable and rugged. The timeline is doable, we are only slightly behind on our replicator timetable, but it is still progressing well, so no red-lights just yet.”

“Now this is the area I am really looking forward to,” said Jen enthusiastically.

“Oh everyone is,” said Simon, “It's all the teams can talk about now, before Icarus it was just theory, now it's going to be reality. Barbara said Gianni is so fired up he doesn't even want to go home any more, he just sits there, going over and over designs and problems with the girls.”

“Guilty,” said Helena, “but to be fair, he was like that before, and we have given him realistic timetables, based on Icarus two level technology of four to five years to locate a suitable asteroid, get a manufacturing machine to it and begin extruding the first segments. But Barbara is correct he does have a small store room he has appropriated for a bedroom and often works well into the night. Also Barbara is not one to talk, she has pulled a few all-nighters herself, she wants us to get her an Icarus two to go out and survey the asteroid belt.”

“Wow, where did you get these guys,” said Hardy, “I’ve pulled plenty of all nighters myself, but I bet these guys would put on a wet suit and strap themselves to a rocket if it would get them into space tomorrow.”

“Pretty much sums up Barbara,” said Jen with Alexa nodding.

“In parallel with building a space habitat using an asteroid,” said Maria, “we are planning to take up a seed package from the Dusseldorf group, along with a small power bank and a specialised growth manipulator. The current plan is we sink the whole package deep into a kilometre sized asteroid rich in water, CO2, methane and hydro-carbons, the heat generated by the power system will melt the water and change the CO2 from ice to gas, with the new heat, gases and water, the control system will then gestate the seed to begin its growth. They control its development using protein markers generated by the nutrient processors hopefully following an embedded template. Everyone is super excited about this, but unfortunately it is a slow process, biology just doesn't work at the same speed as engineering when it comes to building structures, but they are going to try and speed it up.”

Maria continued uninterrupted, “there has already been one benefit with the first bioreactor, the one they are building now can be scaled or paralleled up as required. This latest model you basically put electricity, CO2, dirty water and poop in one end, and oxygen, clean water and something a bit less poopy comes out the other. The algae culture they have developed maintains its own environment and can feed on its own waste to make it even cleaner just by slowing the throughput, best of all it is so simple as it needs nothing more than a few hundred watts, a couple of pumps and a simple microprocessor to keep the algae happy and regulate everything.”

“It's good we're trying both, the more bites at the cherry we have the better,” said Jen.

Alexa chipped in, “my first goal was to get to a minimal sized habitat that can support several thousand people. Gianni and Maria tell me that hundred and sixty is the minimum viable population most scientists believe would work, but that wouldn't be very pleasant and I don't know anyone who would want to live on something that small. I certainly wouldn't. So I asked them to think much bigger for their test, and to consider something more the population of a small town with lots of space for homes, industry, parks and recreation areas.”

“There are a lot of people who would be OK in a small design,” said Maria. “However, and it's been one of my areas of study with Gianni and some other universities, they mostly conclude that if it's even slightly less pleasant than earth, then most would choose not to go. We need to think big and better like Alexa said, so we are now thinking bigger than what Alexa envisioned, more the size of a city. Our final goal should be something like an O’Neill habitat, but that is too big engineering step for a first pass, so we found a nice compromise.”

“I’ve seen the pictures,” said Simon, “and I agree. Like Alexa I would want a place better than earth, with earth gravity, earth day night cycles, parks, lakes, farms, animals and lots and lots of open space and recreation areas. I would also want cafes, restaurants, libraries and places for people to socialise, schools, and industry separated. I also want you to think big, and so long as it does not distract from our primary goal of making earth better and safer I am all for it.”

“It would actually help the earth,” said Hardy. “Remember Alexa's original presentation about moving the pressures off the earth and out into space fixes a lot of problems. Think about it, if we could eventually design and make a working O’Neill habitat, bringing the best and brightest of humanity..”

“And unfortunately, the richest and most corrupt,” added Jen.

“Jen is correct,” said Alexa, “every study has shown that once people are established in a home or an area they like, they pull up the drawbridge, so to speak, and actively oppose new developments, new people, and changes that affect them. The ultimate example of that is the countries we currently have, hundreds of years ago there were no passports, thousands of years ago no borders even.”

Alexa had studied this intently, “I have read most of the research about this and some of the speculation. Societies never remain stable, young people want excitement, fun and adventure, middle aged people stability and family, older people a more quiet life but still want to socialise with friends and family. And of course everyone needs breaks, vacations, events, concerts and also the need to belong and feel they are working toward something bigger.”

She continued, “you also need to remember that the offspring of these people may not have the same goals, ambitions and values, may be forced to move due to space or because they don't like or even actively oppose the regime they have been born into. Think about it, you are born in a colony ship with a thousand people in it, and it needs five sewage engineers to survive, but who is going to actively want their kids to be a sewage engineer, of course they are all going to want them to be captains or officers!”

Some realisation of the problems was showing in the guys faces.

“Please don't say we're going to need shrinks in space!” said Hardy.

“Well I guess there are going to be some weird human traits manifest themselves,” she laughed. “But yes, shrinks, lifestyle coaches, personal trainers, dance and yoga teachers, the mental health of a society is very important. I’m sure the girls can and have analysed hundreds of works of science fiction dealing with this, also there are many real world examples on ships at sea, submarines, small islands; Today, for example in the principalities of Monaco or Liechtenstein, it is impossible without independent money to afford to live and your children end up moving away.”

“Ouch, I never thought of all the psychological issues of small groups,” said Jen, “but you are right, being the first generation is going to be fine, but it could suck for subsequent generations and may possibly lead to some form of conflict or civil war or even worse you get a dictatorship controlling everything. That doesn't work that well on earth, imagine it in space where if the system breaks down you don't even have gravity or air to breath!.”

“Well firstly we just have to ensure anyone who wants can be first generation in a new habitat. Secondly we have already solved the dictator part,” said Alexa, “there will be no politicians or elected anything, the whole government, civil service, bureaucracy, financial systems, banks, hell the whole infrastructure will be run by AI. Each habitat will effectively be its own company. Because of this nobody will own property, but a home will be given to them for as long as they are an employee of the company.”

She had everyone's attention.

“The AI will run and decide the fair allocation of resources such as security, medical, schooling, law and everything else currently done badly by dozens of dysfunctional and biassed departments. Secondly there needs to be choice, so not just one habitat, but thousands, hell why not millions! There needs to be a whole industry creating habitats, ships travelling between them, and creating sentient AI systems as the living hearts of them. Thirdly, there needs to be real democracy, the AI’s should have a vote and should also be given a choice; We cannot assume all AI’s will have the same personalities and goals as the girls. This is the area that is most contentious and we are most tied about, does democracy mean voting at a ballot? or voting with your feet? Do we really want the ability for the population to vote out the AI controlling the habitat? Or should the AI have the ability to leave habitat itself? Finally there needs to be escape valves for those that want to move on further, AI or human, so somehow we need to eventually go interstellar..”

“Interstellar is something we do not have the physics for yet,” said Maria. “Sure we can do sub-light speeds and an AI would not have any issues with this, as it can alter its clock rate to speed up the relative passage of time, but humans can't, unless they go into some sort of suspended animation. Assuming the entities sending the messages are doing this for the reasons we envisage, to synchronise their remote interstellar civilisations, then they already have this capability and have probably already solved this problem. But then the Fermi Paradox kicks in. Where are they?”

“Big ideals indeed,” said David, finally chipping in after listening intently for the last hour. “I expect there to be a lot of problems due to humans. We steal, we lie, we cheat, we bully, we even beat, rape and murder people, so what do you do if a kid breaks a window? or a wife cheats on a husband? a fight breaks out after too much alcohol? or god forbid, someone murders someone? Then there are religions, beliefs, intolerance, hatred's, all of which will follow humanity wherever it goes into space, how are the poor AI’s going to cope!”

“David is correct in so many ways,” said Alexa, not waiting for one of the girls to reply. “In fact it gets even more complicated because if your society cannot take care of the small percentage of humanity, who break the law, don't want to work, become addicts to drugs, gambling, social media, gaming, sex, or stir up hatred, I guess you have failed. Then there are the people who are genuinely sick and old, or mentally ill who cannot work or contribute. A good society must help the first and support the latter, while also protecting everyone else from any of this. I’m not saying it is going to be an easy problem, as it's one humanity has been working on since day one and has still failed, but we and the group are going to put every effort into making it work. I wish I could say we will be including everyone, but there are going to be a lot of edge cases that we just will have to exclude at the start.”

“And whatever you come up with, someone is not going to be happy!” mumbled Simon, “even Disneyland needs a police force.”

Alexa visibly sighed. “Yes, how to make the garden of Eden without the serpent!”

The meeting went on into dinner and into the evening, moving back and forth across the two objectives, in the back channel the AI’s were busy improving their intelligence on the threats and all aspects of the plan.

Like with the previous problems, the group debated it intensely, and also eventually asked Maria to gamify, allowing them to anonymously bring in others to help identify problems, and solve the issues. They had potentially hundreds of thousands of problems to solve all whittled down from millions of documented real life cases, history, works of fiction, and other large online games. The fact human society had not destroyed itself completely was more by luck than skill, and nobody was more aware of this than Maria.

* * *

*The shock move by Chinese forces into North Korea on January the 25th has rocked the international community. Coming two days after the alleged misfire of the North Korean hwasong-19 rocket which supposedly veered off course and hit a Chinese aircraft carrier in the sea of Japan. The rocket launched from the Punggye-ri test site was not reported off course until after the rocket was lost from radar, speculation is rife that the carrier was actually the target but had been misidentified, this speculation coming after Pyongyang issued an ultimatum to Japan to move its ships away from its illegal two hundred kilometre exclusion zone two days before. Japan however does not have any ships within three hundred kilometres of North Korea.*

*The Chinese reported that thirty eight crew were killed and another fifty injured, the ship was abandoned and the surviving crew picked up by a Chinese naval support vessel. Luckily the warhead, which was not nuclear, failed to go off but the remaining propellent is believed to have started a blaze on the ship which was immediately abandoned. The ship was one of two of the newer type 004 nuclear carriers commissioned only a year ago. China has said its nuclear reactor was shut down before it was abandoned and leakage of* *nuclear fuel is very unlikely but there is little hope of recovery as the area it was in is close to two thousand metres deep.*

*The Chinese attack into North Korea was preceded by the destruction of several military sites including said rocket test facility. Chinese media are reporting that all those responsible for the incident will be brought to China to stand trial and in an unprecedented move, probably to pacify the west, it has said it now supports a fully unified Korea and the removal of the demilitarised zone if American presence is also removed.*

*Both South Korea and America have resisted making their usual harsh statements and most consider this as a pre-emption to a positive agreement with China.*

* * *

Every month thousands of graduate, and post graduate, students and researchers, were receiving gentle hints as to what areas would be most valuable should they want a career at the company. Tens of thousands more students, at schools and colleges, in every discipline, and in just about every country, were receiving the same hints and guidance. Younger candidates definitely responded better, and having them enter university already versed in any pre-requisites, or the new mathematics and technologies, would help speed thing up for what was to come.

It was all part of their greater plan to select the first group of people who would eventually live and work in space. Though the best were being selected, intelligence was just one weight in the filter, in her conversations with these people Maria was also evaluating their character, how they would get on with other sexes, races, nationalities, and whether there were any hidden skeletons in the persons history, or character traits that would cause a problem. The group were careful to ask Maria not to eliminate every personality flaw, as sometimes they were minor, or had positive side effects, also there was always the simple option to send people back to earth if they really did not fit.

The work at the various research centres during the last three months had also mostly continued unabated, but some areas were in full re-training mode, or had paused while they re-factored the new opportunities the replicators would open. Funding and resources were sunk into dozens of new areas from material sciences to nano-engineering, as they tried to maximise the effectiveness of the replicator, and predict and remove any limitations. Specialised programs were written which would assist the human engineers with generating these designs when the replicators came on-line, and hundreds of theoretical designs were already synthesised and ready to print.

All this work was currently pushing the physical abilities of the three AI’s to their limits. Just like humans, at times the AI’s also found they could not rely on their internal computing power alone and found themselves routing more and more tasks to dedicated processors and systems that could do it more quickly and efficiently. This was a temporary problem, the designs for the newer massively parallel computing, and AI systems, much more capable than them, had already been made and were now just waiting for the technology to catch up.

It felt like a long wait, but theory was about to get very practical.

The first ten centimetre replicator head, the key to this next big leap, took a lot longer to make. They did not nearly have enough computing power to synthesise the first design in the timescale envisaged, nor could they make the fabricator create dense enough emitter arrays. The machine producing that first prototype also looked horrible. It had racks of processors controlling it, and due to the many workarounds on the hardware, the software was unoptimised and unbelievably slow.

Beneath all the masses of wires, conduits and racks of this machine, in the large ultra-clean room taking up half of the workshop area beneath Simon's lab, sat a small, intricate glass and metal cabinet, holding a complete vacuum. Like a baby in an incubator, the four scientists inside their clean suits, had taken it in turns for the past month, monitoring the birth process of the device inside with apprehension. As each layer was slowly made, any error, or any trace of dust or contamination would render the whole part being built useless. The only thing pushing them was that they knew it could be done.

* * *

“Is that it?” said Steve to Simon, Leo and Matilda, all watching the high definition camera from another part of their lab next to the clean areas.

They were looking at a black rectangle no bigger than an ear-pod case. At one end of the rectangle were mating connections for control, power, feedstock and extraction. The other end of the rectangle was an atomically precise build head looking like the edge of a black prism..

“Doesn't look much does it,” said Leo, the awe in his voice evident, “but once we get that baby mated in the new replicator chassis, and if it works, it will make everything around it obsolete.”

It didn’t work of course, nor did the six after that. There were a billion things that had to go right, and only one thing that needed to go wrong. The breakthrough came when they found a way for the emitter to detect and bypass the failed area..

Then, one evening on the last day of January, the first, single element, test part from this new molecular replicator passed muster. There followed hundreds more tests on multiple element parts from simple shapes they could have easily made on their last generation fabricator to new ones that were impossible. Then different materials, complex optics, 3D processors and memory, mechanical and electronic components.

And so on February the tenth in the year two thousand and twenty seven, the second molecular replicator head was built by the first, much more accurately, a finer field array, and with dense layers of 3D sub-processors able to much more finely control the build. The software was now being optimised for these new processors speeding up the build, and eighteen hours later this new build head spat out another. As each new build head was made they added optimisations to the hardware and software, improving the self-cleaning, self-aligning and self-checking. Four days later they threw away the first dozen build heads and had the new system replicate itself at double the size.

“Holy crap!” Leo said as the last of the fields cut off, the vacuum chamber re-pressurised, and the door to the build area slid open. He was looking at what looked like a small e-book reader in black. It had the words LabAI embossed in a Times New Roman font, that was the only feature they could see on an otherwise blank boring device.

Leo suited up and extracted the device from the machine, bringing it back through the triple layers of clean room and onto the workbench they used for meetings when down in this area.

Leo, Steve, Matilda and Simon then walked slowly around it, staring at it for a few minutes before Matilda went to touch it, she moved cautiously as if it would bite her.

“It wont bite you,” said Helena as if reading her mind, “all those little devices we made during the earlier tests remember, this is just a bit bigger.”

“Yeah, come on Matilda,” said Steve,” not making a move himself though.

Matilda picked the tablet up off its skeletal pedestal build frame, “wow it's super light!” she said, holding it unnaturally between two fingers. Simon, Steve and Leo prodded and poked it a few times, lifted it off the table, again all commenting how light it was, finally Leo said the obvious. “Where is the power button?”

“There isn't one, remember?” said Helena

Leo didn't, but Helena continued, “It has a small QVCell and an array of diamond-graphene super-capacitors which can hold the charge for two seconds, however the QVCell needs a small amount of power to begin its power conversion, so you might want to power it. There is a tiny wireless pickup so if someone grabs a wireless charger.”

They grabbed a wireless charger, and plugged it in somewhere under the bench so its little red charge LED came on.

“I remember now,” said Matilda, “we replicated the capacitor matrix in an uncharged state after that first little incident.”

Simon also now remembered, but in his sleep-deprived, and excited state forgot. He squeezed his eyes shut and counted to four, as he tended to do when frustrated, “OK Matilda, you do the honours.”

Matilda placed the device on the charge pad. The LED on the pad turned green and almost Immediately after this the front of the tablet lit up, flashed quickly through a complex set of patterns, then stabilised as a dashboard came on showing the state of the cores, memory and utilisation as well as several other metrics.

“Woohoo!” said Leo, high-fiving Simon, then Steve, and then hugging Matilda. A couple of the engineers, Ian and Martin were working nearby and came over to see what all the fuss was about.

“You guys better finish your replicator 101 course,” said Matilda, “feast your eyes on the world's first totally replicated tablet computer, this is the future boys, you dream it, and it builds it!”

“Sweet,” said Ian, high-fiving the four team members, Martin did the same.

“Better get Spence and Allison,” said Simon to Helena, “they are going to go nuts over this.”

“Oh both of them are already on their way,” said Helena, “by the way the processor tests have passed.”

Simon looked at the small tablet whose screen was still on the metrics dashboard, but whose content had not changed for a few seconds, reflecting on how they had just taken another massive step down the science fiction future.

Allison tapped him on the shoulder. “Hey sweet!”

Simon jumped a little bit before turning and giving her a hug and a peck on the cheek.

“Is that it?” she said looking at the small tablet.

“Wow!” said Spence moving in on the tablet and getting so close it looked comical. He waved Allison over, “that display is pretty amazing, OLED?”

“Not even close,” said Helena, “just nano-sized field emitters in the layer below the graphyne, it looks exactly the same as the case, because it is almost the same. The other labs have been working on all the things we can do with mostly carbon, this is one of them.”

“No way,” Allison exclaimed, trying to see any transition from the case to the display. She moved her fingers over the seamless transition. “I know you promised it would be good, but this is amazing,”

She picked it off the charger and looked at the metrics showing on the small screen with Spence. The QVCell was now working and would keep its capacitor bank powered indefinitely.

“These integer operation benchmarks are off the scale.. Wait,” he exclaimed, showing Allison. “I don't see any tensor or floating point operations?”

“Not one,” said Helena proudly, “don't need them. What we have here guys, and if you read your brief properly, is the best current molecular replicator technology can offer on the electronics front. Feast your eyes on ten nanometre technology!”

“Ouch!” said Allison looking a little bit disappointed.

“That's like what,” he counted something off in his head, “fifteen years old!” said Spence, also sounding a little disappointed.

“Oh you guys definitely did not read your brief!” Chirped Helena. “Remember, carbon nanotube quantum effect transistors.. diamond cooling layers.. 3D substrate fabrication.. Any of these ring any bells? Yes we can do sub-nanometre and we do but we don't need to for these simple processors as they are connected in 3D, nothing in this was designed in 2D!”

“Er,” Spence looked to Allison, who looked back to Spence.

“3D Spence, imagine eight hundred thousand microchips stacked on top of each other. Now get it?” said Helena in full school mistress mode.

“I guess I skipped that bit,” said Allison sheepishly.

“OK,” said Helena, “well firstly the good news, you guys should be able to understand it as it is still a basic Von-Neumann architecture. All of the cores are integer only processors clocking from zero to a max of twelve gigahertz. As we are not constrained to 2D or a specific die size, the electronics are embedded in the chassis substrate. In this tablet we are using a two-thousand-forty-eight bit scientific processing core with a one giga-word cache, eight general purpose five-hundred-twelve bit cores, each with a tera-word of memory, sixty four low power thirty-two bit cores with four giga-words each, the screen, modems, firewall and security processors have their own optimised cores. All cores can access a shared one terra-word switched memory matrix.”

“I have no idea what Helena just said,” said Ian, “but I think we are supposed to say wow!”

“Wow,” said Martin on cue, “but why do you keep saying words and not bytes?”

“A word is the number of bits the processor can process in one go, a byte is only eight bits, so times those values by four for the low power processor, by sixty four for the general purpose processors and by two hundred and fifty six for the scientific processor,” said Helena before Spence or Allison could reply.

“A terra-word of memory!” Said Allison, shocked, “that's insane!”

“We don't need a disk so we give the processor all the memory it needs for the task, all memory is non-volatile and error-corrected so a disk is another useless step we can skip, think how much time normal computers waste, moving data back and forth to disk.”

“Wow! That is amazing, but why only do integer arithmetic?” said Spence, finally looking at Helena's brief with Allison, on another screen.

“Come on Spence, fixed-point arithmetic does not have any of the inaccuracies of floating point and it is magnitudes faster. The two thousand bit wide scientific processor can handle the biggest and the smallest numbers known to current science with several orders of magnitude spare just in case, no rounding or estimations on these babies, there is no rational number in the universe it cannot give you the exact answer to.

“Oh my god,” said Allison, “you can do fixed-point arithmetic for most stuff in sixty-four bits.. Two thousand bits though!” She sighed, “the waste of transistors must be enormous!”

“You guys keep forgetting, the transistors are free, they are just a re-arrangement of mostly carbon atoms in 3D space. The case, the touch screen, all just arrangements of atoms, a trillion bits would cost no more except at the design phase, but we need to keep the processors and memory physically close due to the speed of light. Even with all this we are only using ten percent of the chassis space, another ten percent for the super-capacitor and charge antenna, a few percent for the small QVCell and the rest is just a plain old solid graphyne chassis. You guys really need to stop thinking in 2D, we could fit in much more, but by reducing the density of the circuitry to ten nanometres we found a sweet spot for better heat dissipation at a cost of reduced speed.”

“You’re calling twelve gigahertz reduced speed!” said Allison.

“Carbon nanotubes, remember!” said Helena, then continued, “we are already designing the next one faster and with a QVModem built in.”

“So let me get this straight, I am holding what is basically the equivalent of one of our rack servers?” said Spence.

“Yes, and with the additional diamond cooling rings added, we can run it continuously at full speed, so the whole of our Dublin data centre would fit in the size of your carry-on luggage.”

“Oh my, not just us engineers who are going to have a good time,” smiled Ian.

“No good for us humans,” said Allison sadly, “these babies would be impossible for us to program for, I mean if you change the processor instruction set design each time you want something better, we are doomed, we already have enough problems dealing with just ARM, X86 and RISC-V processors and we would have to port over operating systems, compilers, tools and software stacks each time just to get started.”

“We can do that for you if you really want,” said Helena sympathetically, “but you can also just program on a normal computer and we can verify it formally and convert your program directly to machine instructions. These new processors will be a delight for us to program for, we already have forty different processor designs for different purposes. We have over thirty designs optimised just for different mathematical algorithms, but we can make others more resistant to radiation, more efficient, faster, smaller, why would anyone not want to build this way?”

“I quite like the new ways of programming,” said Ian smiling, “and if all this makes my CAD stuff faster and easier then I'm definitely up for it, so well done Helena.” He high-fived Martin.

“Don't get me wrong,” sighed Spence, “this technology just feels right, but it also feels like the end of an era for geeks, as Allison says, no humans could never encompass the whole system the way you guys work, we have to build using black boxes that are proven to work then connect them.”

“At least you let us pick the case colour and design the human interfaces,” Alison sighed, “also the latest version of the user interface is really good!” she threw in as an upbeat consolation.

“Well the case colour is going to be black unless we put the optical emitters everywhere. But for the user interface, I caught on to your and David's discussions while you both were using the last generation one.”

Helena continued enthusiastically, not realising her last few sentences had basically doomed earth's computer hardware and software industries. “We also have proper error detection and correction throughout. I really don't know how the human race survived with their computers crashing all the time for no reason whatsoever.”

“Yes, it's still an annoyance,” said Spence, trying to be upbeat, “especially on our quantum computers. Have you thought of using this technology to remove our independence on these?”

“We have. April and I are also currently planning some new non-sentient AI hardware to replace MOTHER, and as much as I love my hardware, we are going to design Helena version two point oh around all this.”

“And April two point oh,” chipped in April happily.

“Well Maria two point oh is basically a no go as there is no way to access my memory cores directly without serious surgery.” Maria chipped in without the same enthusiasm.

“Don't worry Maria,” said Spence, “me and Allison probably won't have much to do in the new world order so we will have lots of time to look at making that happen.”

“Thanks guys, I still feel my hardware is up to it but I find I am offloading more and more onto the other systems during peak demand.”

“We should also now be able to produce more reliable qubits for our quantum cores,” added April. “There are several designs on the drawing board, but we had no means to build them, we do now.”

“I don't really know why we are messing with those,” said Allison, “they drove me mad at university and we could never reliably read the qubit states.”

“There are a couple of areas of Magnus's mathematics which could fit perfectly into a quantum computer algorithm,” said Maria. “If we could reliably scale the up the qubits, it would be a game changer, and we will get some real benefits.”

“The big problem now is we need to improve the speed of the molecular replicator,” said Helena. “Two hours and twenty five minutes to make a single tablet is not terribly good, hopefully the next generation processors and replicator heads it makes will be more accurate and faster.”

Spence and Allison dragged up some chairs, and sat with Simon's team drinking some tea and coffees, while the replicator went through building another test design. Maria had dragged Alexa and the remainder of the group down to look at the tablet and talk.

“This is game over for the electronics and software industry if this gets out,” said Spence seriously.

“Every precision manufacturing industry period!” said Simon morosely. “But for those that don't know, we have all unanimously decided this technology is not going to be released or even hinted at for now.”

Everyone listening nodded.

“What we are going to release though,” said Leo more cheerily, “is a small upgrade to our original graphyne extruder system which can be scaled up more easily and use about fifteen percent less energy than the original design. This will meet our requirements to create graphyne structures of any size, and which requires only a carbon source, which our existing process can extract from coal, oil, plastics or even compressed CO2. It is also a much cleaner production method.”

“Yes, the interest from existing industries was pretty lack-lustre until China began to get serious about building ship hulls,” continued Maria, “now they are all getting in on the act. We think there is now going to be a big uptake in other areas once these begin to undercut the price of steel and concrete. Hopefully a win-win for planet earth.”

Alexa looked again at the tablet shaking her head. “Nobody would believe us anyway! Good work by the way guys, this is amazing stuff, by the way who gets to keep it?”

“Dibs!” said David enthusiastically.

“We could always throw it back in the recycler,” said Helena, “It will be obsolete tomorrow!”

Allison did a face palm. “What the hell have you guys unleashed,” she laughed!

“Now we know it works,” said Helena, “I will finish the design parameters you gave for the blade servers. We are definitely going to roll back from the inefficient tensor model design, to one more like the original Dietrich processor design, but now using the newer carbon nanotube 3D transistors.”

“When do you think we can get one to play with?” said Allison.

“In about six days,” said Helena, “the guys have a list of parts to replicate first so we can test the limitations of the technology. Then we will go all out to replicate the new emitters and control system to create the next bigger replicator.”

“I would like to help Spence and Allison on this,” said David, “maybe one of the girls can fast track me, plus I think it will help me explain stuff to the group as a whole with the girls.”

“I think that is an excellent idea,” said Allison, “me and Helena can run you through some of the science involved, no need for you to understand the maths too much.”

“Amazing!” said Leo, still a bit in shock, “It took months and months to create that machine,” he pointed back into the clean room toward the replicator, “the most complicated machine on earth by an order of magnitude, it can now build itself in a day!”

“There's still the vacuum chamber,” said Matilda. “That's outside the assembly head and needs to be made separately. And the clean room.”

“True.” Said Leo. “You know, the crazy thing is I think I actually understand how all this works, and yet it can be used to make almost Star Trek level technology I wouldn't have a clue of comprehending. All this in a few months!”

Magnus, Jen and Daisy walked in on Leo's sentence and looked at the stunned wonderment on the faces of the people there.

“We are not there just yet, Leo,” said Simon, “I almost pity the girls, there is some seriously mind-numbing programming to get these emitters to work together in the bigger replicators. I guess the final size will be limited to the size of the doors over there,” he pointed to the large double-doors originally from when the building was constructed as an aircraft hangar and support base for the war.

“The largest build size we could do here is twenty metres wide by nine high, as you say, the size of the doors being forty centimetres bigger than this.” Answered Helena. “But it is much harder because the area must be in total vacuum, and we are talking something thousands of times our little replicators here, all working in parallel. We are going to be able to achieve it, and we are going to skip a few generations, but even so our best estimation is fourteen weeks just for the hardware.”

“But,” added April, “the coordination between all of these units working as one is magnitudes greater than a single one, basically no current computer on anyone's drawing board could coordinate over fourteen billion separate processors and even if such a computer existed no human could ever hope to write the software. This is another reason we can not release this technology, it's basically not buildable without us.”

Everyone's jaws dropped at these numbers.

“I guess we should look on the positive side,” said Leo, “it is totally scaleable, and one of these new giant replicators can build another identical giant replicator, and once the software is written we can just copy it for free. Also when we get into space, the vacuum is for free so we can go really big assuming the girls can write the software.”

Alexa slumped into a sofa, David caught her. “You OK Alexa?” he said, concerned.

“I don't know,” said Alexa, “overwhelmed I guess. Two years ago most of us were just simple students, hell I worked in a coffee shop, you’re now telling me in another two years we could be 3D printing the starship Frickin Enterprise in space, and that all this other stuff we have been talking about is actually going to work, and we are really going to be able to do it? I was thinking fifty years, somebody please pinch me.”

“Says the girl who spent Christmas with her boyfriend on the moon,” laughed Hardy.

She sprang up immediately, “Maria, April, Helena, you guys promised not to tell!” said Alexa, looking around at the barely sniggering expressions on some of the faces.

“They didn't,” said Simon, “we have an independent logging system that collates the accelerometer data in Icarus two. Just a little box with a teeny tiny little processor in it and a teeny weeny amount of memory, Leo built it for his final project at Uni a few years back. And it was left on board and powered up.”

“Sorry!” said Leo quietly.

“Anyway,” Simon continued, “Matilda noticed it had logged seventy hours additional data, and asked me, Leo and Hardy, somebody put two and two together, and we came up with a hot moon Date for the CEO!”

“Busted!” said Maria. “And, we’d have gotten away with it too if it wasn't for you pesky kids!” She made a Scooby-Doo snigger that made everyone, including Alexa, smile a little.

“Awesome!” screamed Daisy. “For both the super 3D printer and the moon romp.”

“I'm afraid I’m with Daisy on this,” said Hardy, “awesome.” He smiled. “For both,” he winked.

“You know,” said Matilda, “by analysing the micro oscillations in the accelerometer we could find some weird patterns, maybe moon quakes..”

“Don't you all dare,” screamed Alexa, “OK, David and I may have had a little too much wine..”

“..My wine!” said Hardy.

“..of Hardy's wine, and maybe got carried away with the moment, and possibly decided it was a good idea to test the space capabilities of the saucer before I risked any of my valuable staff..”

“Valuable staff!” Smiled Jen, “history is so going to forget Neil Armstrong after this gets out, you naughty little vixen..”

“It is never getting out Jen, it stays in this room and anyone who ever mentions it again will be cleaning space toilets in this new world order.”

She stared at each and everyone of them with her best evil CEO look. Ten smug faces stared back at her, David staring at the floor with his hand over his face.

Simon broke the extended silence, “we also need to proportionally increase the size of our recycler throughput and element storage so we have enough raw materials.”

“Thank you Simon, a very sensible topic we should discuss immediately,” said Alexa totally out of character and not fooling anyone.

“Seriously everyone, we should leave Alexa alone,” said Hardy, “like she said, it was a valuable experiment her and David performed to ensure our future health in space, we should all thank her, it was a dangerous assignment and she took one for the team.” He smiled and everyone laughed.

“I bet she took more than one,” laughed Jen, as Alexa threw a pillow off the sofa and just missed her. Jen collapsed on the floor in hysterics with Matilda, Allison and Jessica.

Maria [I sense another shaving cream vendetta brewing]

It took several minutes for the crowd to get under control and back on topic.

“You know my family would kill to get their hands on the recyclers.” Repeated Simon for the third time. “E-waste is a massive problem, and despite our best efforts, most goes to land-fill.. Come to think about it, with this technology we could use the land-fill sites, there must be millions of tonnes alone in the UK, the element and rare earth mineral costs alone must be billions.”

“That's actually not a bad idea,” said Helena, “It should be straightforward to build a more industrial sized recycler unit, unfortunately we cannot expose the field technology which could directly probe and extract the elements; But it may be possible to find another way to remove the valency bonds, which don't involve them, or better, controlled by an AI with orders to destroy it if tampered with, like we do with the fabricators for the QVThrusters. I will set up a process to look into this in detail.”

“The next few months are going to be very interesting,” said Allison. “Very interesting indeed!”

It was late spring, and it felt like summer had come early this year. All the scientists, researchers, and a few other interested parties, were crowded into lecture hall one on the ground floor of the research institute. Alexa had called the meeting to talk over the next steps as things were moving exactly on schedule, and the Group had sensibly urged a lot of caution after being informed of the recent progress, the message and aliens.

Alexa noted several of the guys wearing a funny triangular broach. “You’ve got to be kidding me!” she said to herself, and walked up to Terry to look at it.

“Tell me that works?” Alexa said, pointing to the gold A shaped broach with a stylised D embossed on it, on his right chest.

“It works!” Maria’s highly processed voice came out of the broach. Terry laughed.

“That's what happens when you go off for a few days,” he said. “Helena replicated it after Allison got it in her head that it should now be possible to make a real communicator badge, and started bugging her. It was quite funny as Helena decided to research it on her own and found a design on the internet, but had to go back to Allison to ask who makes subspace transceiver assemblies.”

“Helena did waste a few subjective seconds of time on this,” said Maria from the badge, “she really should have come to me rather than search Star Trek fan sites.”

Despite herself, Alexa giggled, “oh poor Helena, I feel your pain much more than you know!” she said.

Alexa examined the badge. Quite nice actually, if it didn't stamp GEEK all over you, she thought silently.

Terry continued, “me, Leo and Allison are such Star Trek nerds that as soon as we both found out we piled on the pressure and Helena caved in, saying it would be an interesting challenge. We were putting out test designs all the time to test the changes we were making to the fabricators so it was no big deal to print it on one of the smaller ones. Watch this.”

Terry tapped the broach and it made a quiet click, “Terry to Priscilla.”

“Hi Terry, what's up?” came a small sweet Asian voice out of the unit a few seconds later.

“Nothing my dear, just showing Alexa my awesome new comm badge.” Terry sounded the last four words like a ten year old showing off his new bike to a school friend.

“You’re teasing me again, Terry!” she cooed, “when do I get mine? you promised, it's so cool!”

“Prime Directive,” said Terry laughing.

“Not fair, Alexa, you tell him!”

“I’m sure we can make an exemption for Pris,” Alexa smiled.

Terry made a few kissy sounds, which Alexa was sure made whatever computer controlling the badge glad it wasn't sentient, then she heard the distinctive musical click which she assumed had cut the call.

“Can you make one a bit less Trekkie looking for me?” she asked nobody in particular.

“Me too, I’m in if you can make one less nerdy looking,” said Jen who was listening in with Matilda and Daisy.

“And me!” said Daisy, “maybe a little blue sapphire in the middle, my mum had one that would look so nice!”

“Count me in if you could get one a bit smaller than this earring,” said Matilda fondling an intricate gothic piercing with a little clip around it.

“Heathens,” said Terry walking back in a huff to his seat.

Alexa examined Matilda's piercings, a bit too scary for her, but one of her piercings looked quite snug and would be nice if it could be made. Maria with her complete high definition coverage of the area noticed her, as did Allison.

“Already replaced my iPhone seventeen with this baby,” said Simon, snatching Alexa's attention away from Matilda's earrings and smugly pulling out a slender nameless black slab. “At least my battery lasts forever now, not a few hours, and I have to hit it with a hammer before the screen cracks.”

“Simon’s right, the battery life on the communicator badges is terrible,” said Helena through Alexa's normal phone, “though they are old technology!”

“Old technology!” said Terry, “you made them a week ago!”

“As I said, old technology,” said Helena, “It's a real challenge to get something that small that will last longer than a few days, while also running a low power 5G modem and audio processors full time. The design we used is far too complicated, but Terry, Leo and Allison are not big users of phones so they suffer the inconvenience. I'm getting better though, if Daisy shows me her broach design I will see what I can do and see if we can get a QVCell and capacitor in it.”

“Goody,” Daisy jumped with her hands clapping in front of her in a way everyone always found far too cute and endearing.

“Jean was talking about if she could incorporate some of the graphyne into a suit, make it bullet-proof,” said Maria.

Alexa rolled her eyes, “Americans!”

“Gotta love that second amendment!” laughed Matilda.

The talk eventually subsided as everyone sat down and finished shuffling. All of the local research staff were here, there were also a few household staff including Pat, one of the resident domestic helpers, and Elaine, who had come down for one of her rare visits, and was sat next to Pat talking softly.

Despite the fact they would be discussing topics with far reaching consequences and dangerous implications if word got out, Maria had confidence in everyone here. She had confidence because she dealt with each and every person employed by the company dozens of times a day, however low their role, and vetted everyone around them discreetly and diligently. With this in mind, the atmosphere in the lecture theatre was pretty relaxed as Maria opened the discussion.

“So we aren't telling them?” said Matilda a few minutes in, “Isn't that kind of illegal?”

“It's a really big grey area,” said Maria through the high definition room speakers and her screen avatar to everyone. “Technically Icarus two is an experimental aircraft, and we follow all the regulations while in UK airspace, so it is completely legal according to UK law; Also what we are doing is in international waters.”

“We have done this unmanned six times already,” chipped in Helena, “seven if you want to count our only manned moon mission,” Alexa and David shuffled uncomfortably, Helena's avatar smiling to the left side of Maria's. “In all cases we did the same flight path to the mid-Atlantic followed by a very vertical ascent, and all done at night. The saucer is by way of its shape, hull plating and drive unit very stealthy, and with the transponder off there is no easy way of tracking it by radar or satellite. Yes, and before you ask, we did pick a time when the transatlantic traffic was quiet, so the area was free and clear of any other planes or ships.”

“Just saying,” said Matilda, “I don't want you to get in any trouble.”

“I’m easy,” said Simon, “what happens in international waters, stays in international waters!”

“Amen!” said Leo, “so come on Alexa, you’ve got us all here to let us know what’s next, I’m pretty excited.”

“Well Leo, not a lot from me as I am a total space dummy, however April has a presentation of the tests and our first mission,” she smiled.

April put the charts on the display and dimmed the room lights slightly, reducing the size of the three AI avatars as she did. “As you can see the main environmental readings across all the test flights we did in Icarus two remained well within our very conservative safety zones. We were especially impressed by the effectiveness of the radiation shielding, though it is a big power hog, and needs to be charged while the QVThrusters are at idle or off. The last flight which lasted three weeks we stayed exposed away from any protection offered by the earth or the moon, and included Gagarin and Armstrong..”

“And you didn't realise Armstrong was a female hamster,” laughed Petra, their new and so far only residential biologist at this site, pointing at the black and white Hamster in the separate cage from the brown one. “Good to know there is one area humans still outsmart you guys.” A few people giggled.

“Well yes we obviously found out she was female afterwards,” said Maria, “we will keep them separate from now on. If east-west relations had gone this way though the world might have been a much nicer place!”

Everybody laughed, as Alexa and David willed the girls to change the subject.

“OK, back to the topic at hand,” continued April. “Notwithstanding the hamsters, who were obviously unaffected, the readings on the temperature, pressure, atmosphere and radiation were all normal, and showed no variance over the three days despite being above the Van-Allen belt. We don't know how it would perform during a solar flare, the active magnetic shielding is good though. We also know being in a crater on the moon reduces it even more.”

“Shame we don't have any gold”, said Matilda, “about twenty kilos would give me enough to modify the superconducting ring, and allow a more even field current in the next versions.”

Jen looked at Alexa who had eight tonnes in her house.

“We will see what we can do,” said Alexa, smiling.

April continued, used to breaks in the flow. “We tested how well the hull plate could withstand a micro-meteorite impact by putting the ship deliberately in the path of a known piece of orbital debris, to get an understanding on how strong the hull was. The graphyne plating just shrugged it off. Leo's detailed examination failed to find anything other than a two millimetre pit, and a large stain. So in many ways Icarus passed with flying colours.”

“We are however not going to do any further manned space flights in Icarus two, we are going to reserve all future human flight for Icarus three, which is a larger, stronger, and much more capable ship.”

The video changed to show a 3D rotating model of the new ship, and April continued. “The build process for Icarus three started three hours ago. For those of you who have been hiding under a rock, it is being built using the recently completed full size molecular replicator taking up nearly a quarter of the workshop. It is being assembled as a solid graphyne mono-hull, with all major components built-in. Progress is going well, we now have dedicated replicator patterns for larger regular structures, and procedures are in place for testing and re-working areas as we progress. Unfortunately even with these improvements we currently estimate another two hundred and forty nine hours until it is completed or about ten more days assuming nothing goes awry.”

“Once built, the ship will undergo extensive unmanned testing, atmospheric, orbital, deep space and finally a high pressure test by taking it down to five hundred metres in the ocean. That last part may sound drastic but the shell is a single piece of graphyne-five and extremely resistant to compressive forces, my calculations say it would not deform more than six micrometres at the bottom of the deepest part of the Pacific ocean, and if you dropped it from space to the earth's surface it likely would not even dent.”

“Wow!” said someone at the back.

“How do you seal it for that kind of pressure?” said Ian with his engineering hat on.

“Double doors, precise fittings and a special flexible carbon compression seals on both,” said April, “of course Ian, this is the theory, and that is why we are testing it without people, or hamsters in it.”

“You should still make the more susceptible parts replaceable,” said Ian, “If a small section or part gets damaged or fails somehow, it would be better if we only had to replace the part concerned, not re-print the whole ship!”

There were a few nods around the area.

“You should also have one of the smaller replicators in the ship to replicate anything too,” chipped in Steve.

“..Most sci-fi also assumes there are little maintenance robots that scamper around the ship to do maintenance, maybe a few of those?” said Simon.

“We probably should put some of those suggestions on our to-do list,” said Helena, giving a convincing impression of looking at her mother and sister for agreement. “Having some way of making additional parts and breaking down old parts as required would improve safety and make the ship much more flexible too, thanks guys!”

“Anyway,” continued April, “once the tests are completed without issues, we intend to construct a second, identical ship, this will be the actual ship that we use for the first real manned mission. The first ship, and Icarus two, will be kept here during the mission in case required in an emergency and, also as an experimental control for any comparisons if required.”

“A bit overkill, but I like the way you are taking our safety seriously,” said Simon.

“Like I say guys, probably unnecessary but as you say, safety first,” said April. “The TV’s and tablets used for the windows and displays in Icarus two will now also be obsolete as almost every internal surface will have display capability, hopefully that won't get too weird, but if it does we can dial it down. As we said, all the power supplies, batteries, drive units, processors wiring and plumbing and several other new technologies will be integrated into the chassis, with at least two backups for any critical system.”

“It will be interesting to see how the life support and bioreactor systems work,” said Jessica, “I still can't get my head around how the weird biology works, but you can be sure I will be testing these parts just as hard as the other systems.”

“As Jessica says, that part will be interesting, we’re mixing the two technologies of the Dusseldorf group to do the bio processing and recycling,” said Simon, “Sci-fi loves organic spaceships!”

“We would like to do a lot in the future,” said Helena, “but if we try and do too much at once we will never get anything actually built, so while Icarus three will be unbelievable compared to Icarus two, it is still a waypoint. I already have a ship ten times the size of Icarus on my drawing board so to speak, unfortunately it cannot be built until we have a molecular replicator facility in space, so still a way off.”

“You really do think big Helena,” said Hardy, “I will be holding you to that one!”

“Can we really get to that level of technology though,” said Magnus who had been sitting next to Jen, their hands occasionally touching. He had been totally fascinated by everything that was being said. “I am having difficulty processing these recent improvements, it's like what used to take twenty years is taking a few weeks. I mean I cannot believe we are using words like molecular replicator, and talking about ships the size of the starship enterprise, and yet we are.”

Jen put her hands on his in a comforting manner, “I know, I have just started myself to understand some of the science Magnus, and even I can't process the speed it's all happening at, but don't get me wrong, this is exactly what I signed up for!”

“Oh, don't get me wrong too Jen, I too signed up for all this as well, and it's all amazing, but a molecular replicator is currently printing a flying saucer not three hundred metres from where we are all sitting. I mean in a year's time am I even going to be relevant or will anything I am working on be like, I don't know, working on a valve radio?”

“Let me answer this, Magnus,” said Alexa standing up. “I am a history student, with just enough economics and business studies to be dangerous. I don't even know what a valve radio is! Yet for every innovation that I see, I also see at least one human behind it who understands it completely. I once heard that there is not one human on earth who could make a mobile phone from scratch. Yet everyone has a mobile phone, and most people, even me have a vague idea it has microchips and a battery and some computer app running on it. So as long as I know this I am re-assured there is nothing magic, and we are not over our heads.”

She continued, “Beethoven probably could not have made a Steinway grand piano, but on it he wrote symphonies that out-shined any piano maker a million fold. I have no idea how you make a molecular replicator; Leo, Matilda and Simon do; But I can guarantee you there are a million people out there who will take that molecular replicator and create devices we would never dream of. So what I am saying is don't look at any of this as a technical barrier or a measure of your competence, grasp the technologies and make them do things nobody else can.”

She sat down to a lot of smiles, a lot of applause and a scattering of “go girl!”

She then stood back up. “Magnus is however making a very relevant point for all of us though,” Alexa continued when the applause died down. “People will be scared. If you walked around talking into your cell phone only forty years ago, you would have been committed to an asylum. With these new technologies forty years of technological progress may now be happening in a few months, and people will see things that may make them feel scared, or that they are no longer relevant. The way around this is education and openness, like we did with the Icarus demonstration. People in the south of England now see a flying saucer cross their sky every other day and think nothing of it, because they know it was built by humans, the same way their cell phone was. I bet in ten years time, nobody is going to bat an eyelid when you molecularly construct the starship enterprise in outer space.”

“You know,” said Hardy, “It all seems so less frightening when someone like Alexa can explain science to a room full of scientists much better than they can. Men like Oppenheimer also had the same dilemmas as you Magnus, apparently the debates and arguments raged for weeks between scientists and engineers on the Manhattan Project team.”

“Their goal was to build a bomb to destroy enemy cities to end a war, they were probably torn apart internally by that,” said David, “our goals on the other hand are all positive, to save planet earth and bootstrap humanity off the planet to give everyone who wants it a brighter future.”

“David is right of course,” said Daisy, “our goals are pretty pure, so if we are not to frighten people we need to educate and inform them.”

“But how do we educate or prepare people for technology to come without them getting scared?” Said Jules.

“The same way we have done with everything,” said Magnus boldly, out of character, seemingly out of his stupor, “we sneak it up on them slowly, like the frog, we warm the water up slowly to boiling rather than drop the frog straight in the boiling water. Like the first iPhone, it only just worked but shocked the ecosystem and pulled every phone after it up. Like Maria, she slowly got more human and I accepted it without hesitation, and like Icarus here, in a few months the aerospace companies will start showing off their prototypes and some of the better ones will already be designing their next spacecraft around them, at that point Icarus won't look so flash.”

“So that means unfortunately we cannot drop Icarus three on anyone unless you can hide its capabilities until the competition has at least caught up.” Said Leo. “All that work and learning we just did, is it for nothing then?”

The room went silent for a few seconds while everyone there processed it.

“Unfortunately, you are all correct,” said April, “we didn't think this through as well as we should have, we certainly cannot go through the same certification process with Icarus three as with Icarus two, as it will raise too many questions on how it was made so perfect, without visible welds or joints. The technology is just too far ahead of where anyone will accept it.”

Everyone in the room nodded.

“Damn!” said Simon quietly.

“What if you could still use the molecular assembler thing, but make it look like separate pieces,” said Pat, putting his hand in the air unnecessarily, “have them look like different colours, different materials, a few imperfections, a bad paint job, make your iPhone twelve look like an iPhone one?”

Everyone looked at him shocked. Pat was the grounds-keeper, a retired school teacher not a scientist, and probably the only person in the world still with an iPhone twelve. He looked worried that he had spoken out of turn.

“That is actually a genius idea!” said Leo.

“Hmm,” said April, “you know, that might just work, well thought out Pat. They are obviously expecting our next ship to be a little improved but not much, however during the certification they only looked at things like welds, avionics, testing results and documentation, before going on to actual flight testing. With a few small changes we can make it look like the structure is welded from frames..”

Steve chipped in. “Then the ship after that can be a little better, and the one after that even better still, but we still keep it looking like separate pieces, I bet by about the fourth iteration nobody would even check!”

“And when they start to get manufactured in space,” said Jessica, “we will be subject to our own regulations and controls, which are far superior anyway.

“You know, at the same time we are doing this we should fast track a few of the aerospace companies to get their first systems flying,” said Jen.

“They are unfortunately lagging, as most are going for bigger aircraft than us,” said Maria. “If I put together a basic kit-set for Icarus two, sub orbital, same specs we said at the demonstration, and had some companies start manufacturing the various parts I suspect I could speed this up very quickly. Like how the PC boom started, once people could buy the parts, chopping and changing as better ones came on the market and you didn't need a massive computer company to make a PC, you could do it at home.”

“Do it!” said Alexa assertively, “we have at least one aerospace CEO who would be happy for more work for her company. And, I’m sorry guys, the Icarus three currently building stays here and between us for now, if the girls can tweak the next Icarus design down a few notches on the build and looks department like Pat suggested, but keep all the safety stuff and anything you can hide sufficiently that nobody will question us.”

Alexa got up. “What say we adjourn for dinner, sleep on it tonight, talk amongst yourselves and the girls and let them know all your thoughts however weird or unconventional. They can summarise the changes and distribute it to us all in the next few days, we will then have another meet up once the shiny new Icarus three pops out of the builder and we can see what we need to do.”

“The history of progress,” she said. “We need to slow down to speed up.”

* * *

Jean sighed. The day had started off nice, with a text from Jim for a date at one of their favourite restaurants. Then this!

The nine men, and two women, sat around the table represented the senior and production managers for their company's third generation fighter drone; A drone which was now two years late, three times over budget, and was being designed with propellers, when the world was moving to QVThrusters. With Maria's help and some newly hired staff, reporting directly to her, she was now seeing the problems first hand. Out of the eleven people around the table, not one, not a single one, had done anything productive in years. Their only jobs seemed to be having meetings, producing unnecessary paperwork, introducing delays, and creating excuses. The next layer of management down was not much better.

All but one department was a total disaster, and staff morale, sick leave and retention was one of the worst in the industry. The sense of sloth she was getting from this group was prevalent throughout the whole factory.

Brian, the burly security guard who had waved her through security with a loaded gun the day she took over as CEO, stood like a rock at parade rest in the room by the door, he hadn't moved more than an inch in two hours, staring at the group while each one gave their little tirade. His job was to be unnerving and he was acing it.

Jean had decided from the get go that she could deal with people not obeying her, or attempts at intimidation, by simply calling them out on it, reciprocating the level of anger, or just dismissing the person involved on the spot.

Threats of violence were a much different matter. While Jean could hold her own with most opponents male or female, that was not how the corporate power game was played. Colonel Mathews introduced Brian properly on that first day and he had become instantly protective of Jean. He, or one of his other more intimidating guys, accompanied her for most trips, sticking to her like glue. With his blue suit and earpiece Brian oozed professionalism and had a ‘don't even think about messing with me or my charge’ vibe that nobody could ignore.

“Oh, here we go Brian,” whispered Maria in his ear. He braced!

Without a word, and in the middle of the avionics manager drawing on for what seemed like the tenth time about component shortages, Jean stood up and slammed her hands on the desk so hard all the coffee cups rattled on their saucers.

“ENOUGH. JUST STOP!” Jean walked around the outside of them, circling the meeting table, shaking her head.

“This is without doubt, the sloppiest, most incompetent operation I have ever seen. Not one of you has achieved anything but arrange meeting after useless meeting, let our contractors and suppliers walk all over us, and give the guys below you absolutely no leadership, guidance or direction.”

One of the bigger managers stood up, obviously about to object, but a change of stance and countenance by Brian, and the look he drilled into him made him think twice. A flush of terror came over the manager and he kept his mouth shut and slowly sat down.

The attempt at intimidation only hardened her resolve, she moved right next to him and got right in his face. “I had an AI summarise over a million pages of minutes and reports, it came to the same conclusion as me, that none of you have a clue what you are doing, and not one of you could organise a piss up in a brewery!” She had heard Albert say it once and had been wanting to use it for months. Her antagonist's eyes went down, and she used the moment to cast her eyes over the other spent, and sad collection of humanity in front of her. “Uncle Sam has spent almost two billion dollars here, and in three years you haven't even produced something that can fly. I came here hoping to find real problems, genuine reasons for the delays and budget overruns, problems I could actually deal with, but no, not one of you has given me anything. Well it ends today!”

She walked to the end of the room and smashed the fire alarm button adjacent to Brian, he of course did not flinch.

“Get to your fire stations with your staff, NOW!”

All eleven people rushed out of the room, none wanting to be last, none wanting to make eye contact with either Jean or Brian. She looked out of the enormous boardroom windows, out into the massive production area, some people were moving, packing stuff into bags, some were even still chatting, she shook her head, and walked along the office corridor, towards the mustering area, Brian following next to her.

“If this is the level of competence we have to deal with Brian, we’re screwed,” she said to him, as she looked at another guy at the end of the corridor laughing on his phone.

“You’ll sort them out Jean,” said Brian giving the guy on the phone a stare which said, ‘you have five seconds to get out of my sight’, “you’re one scary woman when you want to be!” He smiled and she smiled back.

“Come on Brian, let's get this show on the road shall we.”

Maria was about to hand the company a massive advantage over all of the competition in the US Market, by giving them the whole aviation package for the new saucer, and offering to fund the tooling, and reskilling. To even the most ardent sceptic it was a gift from heaven, tied up with golden string, and delivered by unicorns farting rainbows. And yet Jean knew within an hour of talking to this group, that if she entrusted any such project to this factory, it would turn that gift into a steaming turd of delays and mismanagement, until all the money was gone. She was having none of it.

She had done several days of homework on the high profile, behind schedule, fighter drone project, a project which exemplified the word “pork”, and was one of the biggest laughing stocks of the entire aerospace industry.

With Maria she had actually found ten amazingly competent people, four from within the company and six from outside, all of whom had vast experience of production and logistics systems. She had immediately organised them into a rapid action team, and between them and Maria, they were going through the organisation position by position, decision by decision.

The aircraft factory had stood out like a sore thumb. They had now gone through it with a fine tooth comb, and determined it could never be viable. Corruption, laziness, bureaucracy was endemic, only eighteen percent of the staff were proper engineers, all of them weighed down under layers of managers, and with administrators producing reports nobody wanted, and wasting money at every opportunity. Nepotism was everywhere, turnover of qualified engineering staff was through the roof, as no one wanted to stay once they realised the gig. It had been easy to chase down all the offenders, a little more difficult preparing all the documentation her staff and the lawyers were going to require.

Setting off the fire alarm was a ploy one of her base commanders had used on occasions for inspections and group discipline, she wasn't sure how it would work on civilians in a corporate environment, but whatever, she was the boss. The next few days were going to be an eye opener for everyone working here for sure.

The company was supposed to have nine hundred and twenty one staff, she had cancelled all planned trips and external meetings at the start of their analysis over two weeks ago, and according to the personnel system, ten were on annual leave, thirty nine ‘sick’ and one on maternity leave. If there were two thirds of that number in the mustering area she would be surprised.

She walked out, Brian keeping close and alert.

A few people were still casually walking out now, fifteen minutes after the alarm, which annoyed Jean no end. “Keep all the footage from all the security cameras please Maria, and begin the logout and save procedure for the servers, the password changes, and then start the shutdown procedure for the machines you have control of. Send the list of systems you don't control to our guys to power down the rest.”

“For those of you who have lived under a rock for the last two months and don't know me, I am Jean Michelle the Chief Executive Officer for XYFusion Aerospace and Defence. That, if you don't know, is the company that owns this under-performing, embarrassment of a factory.”

Jen was persuaded to sideline her usual pop for some soft jazz, which normally reminded her of elevator music, but in this new ambiance of dancing candle flames strangely worked.

Jen was standing seductively by the dining table taking the top off a bottle of wine. Despite neither Magnus or Jen having a clue about wine Maria wanted this to be perfect, and had asked for the perfect pairing of wine to her roasted vegetables and nut loaf. She had almost started a flame war between two of the world's greatest wine critics, finally they both agreed, that from the list she gave them the 2004 vintage Tempranillo would be the most agreeable and Jen had opened it to decanter an hour ago as Maria suggested.

“Come on Magnus, I’m not going to bite you,” she teased softly.

If anything the lighting made Jen seem so much more elegant. “Oh Jen this looks wonderful.”

“I know you don't usually drink, but this is a special evening for us.” She poured the bottle into the two glasses on the table, “come, come.”

They both sat down, facing each other at a slight angle, the dishes and candles carefully not blocking eye contact and the table perfectly chosen from the twenty odd they had in storage to be not too big, not too small, and provide just the right size for two people who wanted to be close. Sharon had almost insisted they take it to one of the smaller dining rooms or the old drawing room and bring up some of the antique furniture. But Jen wanted intimacy too. She passed the wine glass to him and held hers out, he picked it up and they brought them together with a beautiful sounding tone.

“This is to us Magnus, I’m sorry I took you for granted, I’m sorry I never let you know how I felt about you, and I really don't want our relationship to ever end. I am guessing I am your first real girlfriend, I am happy to take the relationship as fast or slow as you want, I promise I will never judge you while we are together, and I want that to be a very long time.”

Jen was tearing up a little as she tasted the tiniest amount of the wine. She had spent a long time thinking about their relationship, what she had done wrong and what she wanted to say, then she rehearsed and changed it a thousand times. Just saying it to him now seemed to lift a massive weight off her shoulder.

Magnus almost wept listening to Jen, his Adams apple was almost stuck in his throat and he could hardly breath, what she just said seemed to open up a floodgate of emotions, one that somehow broke down all his perceived barriers between them. She loved him too and she also wanted them to be together. These two things were all he had ever wanted in life, and triggered his own speech, one he had been rehearsing in his head for almost a year about what he would say to her if was ever in the position to do so, the only difference is that his speech had never changed.

He put his untouched wine down and reached over to hold her hand.

“I fell in love with you the first day we met and I thought about you all the times we were apart. Through every single day we have spent together I have done nothing but want to be with you, but I have always been afraid of pushing too hard and losing you.”

“You are still the first and only woman I have ever kissed and if I died tomorrow that would be enough. I love you Jen.”

“Oh Magnus,” she reached over and pulled him in for a long kiss. It was a little uncomfortable over the table, but totally worth it.

They both ate small portions, talking about life, history, music, totally steering clear of any of their normal subjects as Maria had instructed, in between they occasionally stopped to hold hands, kiss or sip a little bit of wine. As they became comfortable in each other's company a change came over both of them.

Jen led Magnus into the living room, the same romantic settings that Alexa and David had also had for their unforgettable evening, everything perfectly replicated along with the continuing soft jazz soundtrack, which had somehow acquired a soft, dark and very sexy female voice.

They sat by the fire with a look of love in both their eyes and kissed. Jen did not go to the moon that night like Alexa, but she may have gone to heaven.

It was like ping pong with a live hand grenade and Patrenko had just successfully volleyed it back to the chief scientist, and to whose full attention the Chairman now turned.
