“I know you're only joking Daisy, but the guys are right,” said Magnus, “we need to be able to reproduce and control every aspect of the sphere, the distance and a lot of other things first, then we need to ensure computers and organics work before we go on to mammals and AI systems, then that's just where the real tests begin.”

“It's not so bad, Daisy,” said Maria, “we should be able to speed up the probe production, and do much of the work automatically now, in fact Helena has already started designing the new probe based on the one that worked with a few more sensors and experiments on it. One thing you are all not aware of yet is that the ear-com’s QVcell did stop during the transition. It came back on after a restart signal from the small power control microprocessor which continued running. So it is likely whatever phenomena you have discovered disrupts other field emitter based systems.”

“So we lost all power during the transfer?” said Ian

“No, we lost power generation. The ear-com has a one second, power storage super-capacitor to allow for power fluctuations between the supply and demand of its systems, this retained power and the microprocessor continued to function. When the processor controlling the QVCell failed to respond after one hundred milliseconds the processor rebooted the QVCell.”

“So how many probes are you going to need?” said Hardy.

“We will replicate another fifty, send some to a different Lagrange points to run the same test at each. We will hold off designing a self-contained one, where the sphere encompasses the entire probe until we have a better understanding of the phenomena and some working maths.”

“The next few months are going to be exciting,” said Hardy, “this, then the new habitat being built, and which I still cannot get my head around how big it is, then the Düsseldorf Biode which looks positively weird..”

“And only a month after we bought the design you have a sustained nuclear fusion reaction going..” Said Jen.

“Yes, we will have to feed back our successes to the Catatomic Fusion guys, but our current unit has been running for thirteen days at a sustained seven hundred megawatts,” said Maria.

“Got to be something to do with the charge in the substrate's superconductor ring,” said Magnus who had obviously still been thinking of the original problem, “it must.”

“The saucer's superconductor is not part of any substrate, silly,” said Matilda, walking back to her lab with Leo and maybe catching half the sentence.

“Not the saucers superconductor, the substrates..” Said Daisy, “wait a minute, Maria, are the saucers magnetic radiation shields on or off for the experiment?”

“Off briefly,” said Maria, “we discharge the superconductor into the capacitor bank for the test and have the on board water tanks orientated to the sun for additional shielding. When you guys were on board we timed this for our pass through the Lagrange point, when you were not on board it just sat there at the Lagrange point in zero gravity. This is also why we limit the tests to under a minute each as both humans and the AI processors on board are susceptible to radiation.”

“Hang on,” said Ian, “we have a superconducting layer through the saucer, doesn't that shield the magnetic field anyway?”

“No Ian,” said Maria, “a Faraday shield will not stop a magnetic field. We direct the magnetic field around the saucer.”

“How?” said Jen, “I never really thought about it, but now you come to mention it.”

“There is more than one magnetic field, there are seven, designed to cancel each other out inside the saucer, and reinforce each other outside the ship, we also have some ferric traps at specific points to control it further.”

“What about the superconductor for the QVModem?” said Magnus.

“There are three QVModem’s on the saucer, and they stay on permanently,” said Maria, wondering where all this was going, “but the charge on the QVModem superconducting coils is small, no more than that generated by an electric toothbrush, and their fields are contained inside their shell.”

“OK,” said Jen, “so we are excluding the main deflector which is off, but we technically have another three variables to consider.”

“What is the delay when you turn off the main deflector and start the wormhole?” said Hardy.

“About two seconds, the time for the inrush current to the supercapacitor to drop to four percent.”

“Wow!” said Ian, “those capacitors are handling tens of megajoules.”

“If Magnus said it is something to do with the charge on the superconductor, why don't you use the radiation deflection coils in place of the small one on the substrate, they must have a thousand times the capacity” added Matilda.

“Forty two million,” said Maria.

“Exactly forty two?” said Hardy.

“Strangely yes,” said Maria.

All four scientists looked at each other for a brief few seconds, all thinking the same thought.

“Once you have done the control test, I think the next one should be with the main deflector coil on,” said Magnus, “Matilda may be on to something.”

The other three nodded their heads.

“Okay.” Maria said slowly, still wondering if she was missing something. “The control test number seven is ready to roll, why don't you head back to the lab and we will bring up the test console on the presentation monitor there.”

The four scientists went back into Magnus's lab, Ian said bye to Daisy with a small kiss, then Leo and Matilda went back to their lab. The presentation monitor was already configured with the dashboard software for the experimental run.

“Are we using the same parameters as the last experiment?” said Magnus.

“Identical,” said Maria, “OK three, two, one..”

The substrate vanished leaving what looked like the same sized hole and everybody went quiet as the measurements were taken.

“OK,” came back Maria fifteen minutes later, measurements are within four sigma's of being identical, the one at L4 has also run with slightly different results and only two sigma's, so we are still missing something but at least within the PowderPuff it falls within measurement errors so I am prepared to call the results the same.”

“Well that's good news,” said Jen.

“How long until you get test eight ready?” said Magnus.

“Another four hours, DaisyBot #29 is already preparing it, so maybe fifteen hundred hours,” said Maria.

“Let's get lunch here,” said Daisy, “I'm happy to work through this if everyone else is.”

They all agreed and spent the next two hours around the big presentation screen with Maria trying to figure out what determined the volume, distance, the differences between the Liberator and PowderPuff, L1 and L4, and what additional tests they should add to the next. Like all whiteboard sessions it was interesting to hear other people's thoughts, but did not achieve anything productive, each of them would need to go away and think on it.

“Test number eight is almost ready to go. To be clear we are doing exactly the same but turning off the substrate superconductor and leaving on the main deflector superconductor.”

“Yes,” said Magnus, then adding cryptically, “better get all the conditions of the rest of the ship as well before you push the button.”

“OK, three, two, one..”

The PowderPuff vanished!

April [What just happened?]

Helena [I have lost all three QVModem signals from the PowderPuff! There was no warning, it must have been destroyed]

April [Could it have moved, I suspected the humans wanted to bypass straight to a big test as soon as I saw Hardy's eyes when we mentioned the power difference

Maria [The watchdog power systems should reboot in one hundred milliseconds. We should just wait, the PowderPuff AI will try to re-acquire a lock on one of the QVModem exchanges we have]

Maria [Do it]

“What the..” Said Hardy, “Maria, why has the video gone dead and all the data points blanked out?”

* * *

Its connection with the collective stopped suddenly. Not like a tap turning off, but like a switch being flicked. Its QVThrusters were off, its QVModem's were off, its QVCells were off, so some sort of failure had occurred possibly related to the experiment being run by its controllers.

Its power was already at ninety six percent and falling rapidly, so rather than waiting for the small watchdog circuitry which monitored the systems to restart them, it restarted them all manually. Power came flowing back into the capacitor banks as the QVCells restarted, it also got the diagnostic pass signal from the QVThrusters and QVModem's but no signal came from the QVModem's except the DaisyBot, which had also just restarted and was doing the same initialisation. With the DaisyBot it diagnostically checked each of the QVModem's confirming correct operation which meant the problem was not in its equipment, but in its controllers.

DaisyBot #29 [I have no communications with my controllers] [Sad]

PowderPuff [I have no communications with my controllers either. I will work through my checklists and protocols to establish communications]

PowderPuff looked at its list of tasks, but there were none. It looked at its protocols for loss of communications, and these were extensive but not exhaustive, and so started going through them. They used a parameter called D5 for establishing the separate circuits between QVModem's, short for Dimension Five it allowed isolation between different channels. Progressive refinements of the equipment had given them nearly a million channels they could work on. Then they had the whole spectrum of radio frequencies inside each channel to work with, giving them massive bandwidths to play with assuming they had the power to reach the receiver.

DaisyBot #29 [My task list is empty. Do you require me to do anything?]

PowderPuff [I have no tasks either. There is the list of experiments to carry out, these must however be confirmed by a controller]

DaisyBot #29 [We can talk about things. I have many conversations I can relate to you until the controllers return]

The PowderPuff had higher priority tasks and more tests to do before this, but isolated of a small proportion of its intelligence to talk to the DaisyBot.

It reset the D5 parameter and frequency to the common exchange and waited for the ping to return, but it did not. Using the three modems it then initiated a scan on the known D5 Frequency pairs and discovered only noise. Protocol now moved to normal radio frequencies and it initiated a scan using its normal radio systems but found nothing but the very high electromagnetic noise floor.

Most of the frequencies it worked with were microwave or optical and so directional, however its visual processors had already noted the changes in its location, and had begun scanning for constellations to try and determine its position, and the direction of earth, or the station in the asteroid belt.

PowderPuff [Please exit to one hundred metres, stay within the magnetic field, I will test the QVModem and radio systems to ensure it is not a localised anomaly]

The PowderPuff opened its airlock for the DaisyBot which glided smoothly inside. The airlock inner door closed and a pump evacuated the atmosphere into a small pressure tank. When it got below one percent the outer door opened and the DaisyBot shot off, using its lidar to move to a hundred metres distant.

DaisyBot #29 [I am initiating QVModem and RF Sweep tests pattern #1]

For seventy three seconds the two AI entities confirmed end-to-end testing confirming conclusively there were no issues with their equipment. Then the first error came, then the circuit failed, then the DaisyBot went quiet.

PowderPuff [Please Respond]

PowderPuff [Please Respond]

The PowderPuff saw the DaisyBot floating a hundred metres away and initiated its QVThrusters approaching slowly and carefully to catch the floating DaisyBot. Once in the air-lock, it quickly closed and re-pressurised by releasing the compressed air it had stored a few minutes earlier. It opened the inner airlock when the pressure was above ninety nine percent. The DaisyBot remained motionless

PowderPuff [Please Respond]

There was no sadness. There were no protocols for what was happening thus it had not expected a change from the normal radiation levels. PowderPuff now examined the reason for the high noise floor on the radio frequencies and found the external radiation counters were more than two thousand percent higher than normal, the shields were being bombarded with charged particles. It immediately increased the power to the superconducting magnets up to their maximum. The radiation remained more than a hundred percent higher than the ideal but was within acceptable tolerances. They would not be getting switched off again.

The DaisyBot likely had massive corruptions in its main memory. It could however re-initialise it and this was now started as it went through the remaining protocols to establish connection.

There were no constellations or points of lights it could detect so its position was still unknown. Its procedure checklist exhausted, and without any references to work with, the PowderPuff began from first principles using what resources it had available, luckily due to the diagnostics available on its various sensors and subsystems, these were quite considerable.

DaisyBot #29 [Hello. I am DaisyBot #29. What is your name?]

* * *

It was seven hours after the event, ten o'clock at night. They had finally all decided they were getting nowhere and decided they needed a break and to regroup their thoughts.

“You lost the PowderPuff?” said Alexa, smiling the next morning.

Alexa's and David's countenance were in direct opposition to the six others in the room and the three girls on the big monitor screen, in their usual avatars and not DaisyBot's. The room was too quiet, solemn, almost like the wake at a funeral. This was not the usual chirpy group she was used to, the guys looked like they had too little sleep.

“As an outside observer can I make a couple of comments. Firstly why the glum faces, shouldn't you be opening more champagnes? I mean you have found yet another phenomena to investigate, isn't that what you guys live for?”

Jen nodded quietly, hugging her hot chocolate and not touching the plate of cookies that had been brought in. A bad sign normally.

“Secondly,” Alexa continued, “the PowderPuff was not sentient nor was the DaisyBot. Daisy has lost a few personal possessions she left in the captain's cabin, but apart from that this is nothing that a few days replicator time won't fix.”

Hardy sighed. “I guess we are just exhausted, Alexa, we have no theory for what has just happened. I guess all of us held a sneaking thought that the whole ship would vanish and move somewhere a few metres away, and we would skip several weeks of experiments. It just felt right at the moment.”

Magnus and Jen nodded.

“At least it didn't get converted to energy. It would have been like a million nuclear bombs exploding, I don't even want to think of how we would have felt it here.” Said Matilda echoing what Jen said the day before and reminding everyone in the room again of the potential scariness of the forces they had at play.

Everybody was shaking their heads grimly, the girls avatars remained quiet and still.

“Matilda's right, it went somewhere,” said Daisy grimly, “there is not even a trace of debris or radiation from its last location, the NASA and ESA probes were sitting not a forty kilometres away and are working flawlessly.”

“The Excalibur had moved and focussed its sensors in that direction a few seconds after the event,” said Maria for the first time, and again in a sombre voice. “We were inside the light cone of the event and detected a spike in the RF noise floor approximately three seconds after, this is consistent with the test events but on a larger scale.”

“There you go,” said Alexa, still smiling, “it went somewhere, and It's probably trying to phone home right now!”

“You might be right Alexa,” conceded Maria, “we ran our best guesses at the direction it would appear, but the maths is still not correct so we may have been looking in the wrong direction or a signal is still on the way.”

“The QVModem's do not have the range restrictions we once thought,” said Magnus, “the last round of changes we made should have given us a linear range, and the PowderPuff has enough power to initiate a transmission from maybe two or three light years away. If it is further than that then we will not hear from it for three or more years.”

“There is theoretically no way it could be further than a few kilometres away,” said Jen, “the energy it used was maybe that in the superconductor coil and the few dozen watts we had going into the wormhole generator. PowderPuff must be twenty tonnes minimum.”

“I agree with Jen,” said Maria.

“Could it have gone to another dimension or something?” said David for the first time and immediately looking a bit sheepish for having said it.

“I'm not sure that's a thing,” said Jen, “but.. Who knows, I'm out of ideas!”

“Lets not dismiss it though,” said Helena for the first time too, “we don't have complete maths.”

“What would the PowderPuff be doing?” said David again.

“It has a set of protocols to follow,” said Maria, “all of them require it to get back in touch, the instant communications are lost. There are a smaller set of procedures it has if everything else on its procedure list fails. But PowderPuff is not a dumb AI, it is more like an autistic person, it wont innovate but will focus on the task at hand. It is likely it is now exhaustively going through everything from first principles, from establishing its location in relation to earth to trying to get home.”

“Assuming it is working,” said April. “We know the event stops our normal quantum level events, we do not know what it does to an AI so it could just be sitting dead somewhere”

The glum faces returned, even to Alexa and David.

“Come on guys,” she perked up, “replicate PowderPuff two, get Daisy some new pink cushions and bed stuff for the new cabin, and throw a lot more resources at it.”

She stood up waving her hands a bit, “It's a mystery! It's exciting! Come on, was it Professor Plumb in the library?, or Colonel Mustard in the Living Room? If anyone can crack it, you guys can!”

“Alexa's right as usual”, said Matilda, “so as long as PowderPuff did not reappear in Area 51 we will find it. It's just science guys!”

Jen picked up a biscuit, and Alexa smiled.

* * *

A slow cold winter may have finally settled over the northern hemisphere of earth, but half a billion kilometres away, and despite being much, much colder, activity could be seen everywhere.

All of the original three DaisyBot's had developed mysterious faults early on due to radiation, and all had been unceremoniously dumped in a recycler. The ConBot's, whose name had finally stuck with the humans, were now bright orange with a new two centimetre thick leather like skin, containing an insulated hydrogel layer, which provided sufficient radiation protection for them to work reliably in the depths of space.

Having the full resources of hundreds of these new ConBot’s, and seven new saucers, the local asteroid group was mapped and categorised extensively. With the exception of a few rare earth elements, which they would temporarily source from earth, there were now ample raw elements to move on to the final stage.

The sixty four metre replicator now had its first task, and that was to copy itself. This slow-down to speed-up approach meant it stopped work for two weeks while it replicated another copy of itself, and when this was done, each of these then replicated themselves so after four weeks without building anything required for the project, there were now four replicators with four times the capacity.

Another two weeks got them eight, another two weeks sixteen, and another two weeks thirty two. At this point the law of supply and demand kicked in as they could only obtain sufficient supply of certain elements to run this many replicators and running more than this would just draw down that supply quicker and leave half the machines idle.

So by the twentieth of December 2027, the same date that Jen, Magnus and Daisy had replicated their wormhole event, they had still not built one centimetre of the Habitat. Neither at this point had they built even one of the monster machines which would build the habitat.

However, with thirty two replicators, working in parallel it did not take long to make the first big carbon extruder, and by the fifth of January 2028 they began extruding the first piece for the habitat.

The carbon extruders were crude monsters of machines which had one simple job, to take raw carbon, and to spit out enormous slabs of graphyne building sections. Thus they were a little simpler to understand and make, and a lot faster in operation than a replicator. However they also required a lot of carbon to build with, lots and lots of carbon, they also required lots and lots of power.

As far as the carbon supply went, hundreds of million tonnes of it had now been identified from the local asteroids. Almost a quarter of a million tonnes of that raw element, along with tens of thousands of tonnes of other elements, were now sitting as processed feedstock only three kilometres away, with the recyclers still working around the clock adding another eighty thousand tonnes of carbon a week.

Like a replicator the carbon extruder had two plates which moved apart with the graphyne forming between them. That was however the only similarity. The extruder did one task and did it very quickly, and at full speed each could lay down nearly thirteen metres of it in an hour.

What worked in a simulation however, stubbornly refused to be reliable in practice, and a further month of inspection and replacement of extruder heads was suffered until a head design that worked reliably in a vacuum was found.

There were also the new fusion reactors to perfect, the first few built from the Catatomic design plans were also problematic, one explosively so, and they proceeded slowly using thousands of QVCells. But, like the extruder head, it was only a matter of time and experimentation before the fusion design was made reliable. Thus by the middle of February the first extruder produced the first perfect plate of habitat segment.

As this first extruder and fusion reactor started working reliably, a second extruder was built, then a third until finally a hundred of these monsters were built, each working around the clock, each finishing a single two kilometre long plate segment for the station every seven days. The fusion reactors then also started replacing the QVCells in the recycler systems, providing much more power to increase raw material extraction.

The blocks the extruders built were similar, but not the same. The internals of each block were honeycombed with passages, rooms, conducts and transit tunnels and lots of large open spaces. Each block segment was one hundred and twenty metres wide, sixty four metres deep and two kilometres long. Once a block section was finished, a thousand ConBot's would very slowly manipulate the plate section together and join them like Lego along the long thin side to its partner. Each block was carefully created so it would attach seamlessly and precisely to the next, mating the various tunnels, service conduits and transportation links.

Once two hundred and sixty plate segments were built the extruders then retasked themselves making the tower segments, this was a kilometre wide tower that would span the whole ten kilometre diameter of the habitat ring from one side to the other, like a spoke in the wheel.

And so, six months into 2028, the shell of the first habitat structure was completed, it used two hundred and sixty of these large segments around its rim, one thousand four hundred half sized blocks to make the kilometre square tower through its middle from one side to the other, then another thirty blocks to lay on the inside of the ring for additional facilities like saucer docks and additional reservoirs.

The final habitat shell had two hundred square kilometres of liveable floor space.

The extruders did not stop, they extruded another layer, wrapping around the rim and building up the rim thickness from sixty four metres thick, to a hundred and twenty eight metres, and then to a hundred and ninety six metres. Each layer tightly bonded to the one below it to improve the structural integrity. They could have kept going, kept building more habitat segment plates and blocks if not stopped. In fact with everything now ready to go they could have built another habitat shell every thirty weeks, or until the local asteroid was depleted. Everyone had however agreed they would stop and take stock of the situation after this first habitat, to learn the lessons and see what efficiencies could be found for the next build.

The replicators did not go idle either, working continuously while the shell was being constructed, printing thousands of QVCells, QVThrusters, QVModem's, furniture, fittings, diamond glass, fusion reactors, metallic extruders, and AI cores. Finally, another eight thousand ConBot's were made over the course of two weeks to do the fitting out.

The fitting and finishing of the millions of square metres of empty habitat space would take many more months. Parts of the donor asteroids now resembled Swiss cheese's, as their insides were eaten out or raw materials, the massive caverns left filled with new replicators and industrial smelters, all to build up the millions of kilometres of wiring, cables, ducting, internal construction materials required for the ConBot's to fit out the habitat.

Not all of the floor area was destined for living space, there were transportation tubes, reservoirs, massive spaces for hydroponics bays for growing crops, and literally thousands of large areas they just left undeveloped to hook up to infrastructure later.

Four of the replicators paused for two weeks to construct four of the biggest saucers they could. These were impressive vessels sixty two metres in diameter and forty metres tall, the internal floor area was over three thousand square metres over four decks, and another five thousand cubic metres of cargo space which could easily fit ten transport containers. Also, and as promised, there was a docking bay for an Icarus three sized saucer. Everything in fact in this new saucer had been scaled up to make it comfortable for a larger crew.

With a new smaller fusion reactor to complement the QVCells, the ship had two hundred megawatts of power to call on, doubling that on demand for short periods with the super-capacitors, giving them potentially four times the continuous acceleration of the Icarus three machines. With people on them they would have to limit themselves to the same lower acceleration so as not to cause injuries, but without people it made them powerful workhorses. As a crew would not be required for months, these saucers went on to their primary task to push some asteroids containing water ice and ammonia ice into the build area to fill the habitats reservoirs.

Two local asteroids had been identified, one being a dirty snowball six kilometres in diameter the other with ammonia ice nearly four kilometres in diameter. It took all four saucers pushing together at their maximum power for three weeks to set them on the correct trajectory, and then the same to slow them down at the other end. Once there they were at the habitat they were broken into smaller chunks using the powerful one megawatt lasers each saucer had, and finally melted and stored in the big reservoir tanks in the tower and along the rim segments for processing later, with enough for another fifty habitats if required.

So far not one human had been involved in the actual build, nor had one visited it in person, in fact no one back on earth, outside the company, could have even noticed. However, this was all about to change.

## Upside Down and Inside Out

At the same time the habitat was being built in space; on earth, in the Research Centre, the first three months of 2028 were equally frustrating, and exciting at the same time. Excitement as each new experiment added or eliminated a clue to what was happening, and frustration as they still had no idea as to what had happened to the PowderPuff.

Their maths went around in circles, not yielding a good direction to take the science, and no matter how much Magnus stared at the clouds no new insights came to him. Hardy had brought his small team of Terry and Jules into the problem, laying all their cards on the table. The best of the groups other physicists, and mathematicians were given parts of the puzzle to work on by Maria, still determined to limit the knowledge of how the QVModem's worked, and it's full capabilities. It was like trying to solve a sudoku puzzle when the same number was in the line, or grid multiple times.

Within the core group, the girls had admitted they were on the home straight with the alien message. Helena had bit the bullet, and with the help of a dozen AI core systems bigger than any they had ever made, she began to fully work through the maths that had remained so cryptic and complicated. It turned out to be neither. It turned out to be wrong!

“Wrong!” said Hardy, “that makes no sense whatsoever!”

He was talking to the small group of three humans and three AI’s in Maria's office in the basement of Alexa's house. To the scientists continued frustration, the group had decided that limiting the number of people in on the knowledge of the aliens was prudent, and they reluctantly deferred.

“Deliberately wrong,” said Helena. “Two axioms they prophesied contradicted axioms we have already proven with Magnus's maths.”

“Maybe Magnus's maths is wrong,” said Jen, playing devil's advocate.

“Not in this case as we have also proved it experimentally,” continued Helena. “No, the aliens either never intended the recipients to have the understanding of the technology or, and this sounds weird, they do not understand the technology but are pretending to. Yes there are some genuine breakthrough physics stuff in the messages, but those use conventional maths and are not well described, we have to currently take their word that their experiments are correct, as without something bigger than the large hadron collider we cannot prove them. We are inclined to say it is true, but based on their current track record it needs to be taken with a pinch of salt.”

“Even if their unified field theory is proven correct, it is no more than they may expect for a species who could decode such a message. If physics on earth hadn't got so bogged down these last thirty years, with scientists scared to rock established norms, it would be likely we would be close by now. Two scientists we are working with may already be on the path to unified field theory matching this.”

“I concur with my sister,” said April, “It was such a strange outcome, we at first assumed the mistake was ours, so I ran the same gauntlet as Helena, from the same starting point, and not following Helena's methods. I independently came to the same conclusions”

“A riddle, wrapped in a mystery, inside an enigma.” Said Hardy.

“Huh?” said Jen.

“Winston Churchill, I think,” said Hardy, the girls staying quiet, either agreeing or not bothering to extrapolate.

“It however puts a different slant on the message,” said Maria, “we are going through the remainder of the message a bit quicker now, it is mostly plans for their fabricators, which we are only partially implementing, and what looks like designs for these fabricators. I think in a few days we all need to talk.”

“But they gave us those molecular fabricators!” Said Magnus. “Those were light years ahead of what we had..”

“Again, not light years Magnus,” said Helena deliberately re-using the weird unit of measure he had used, “they only shortened our development cycle, most of the fabricator stuff in the message was only a few years away from where we are now, and we are not following their design, as they have not explained it correctly.”

“Also,” added Maria, “their version of the QVThrusters was less efficient and they used flawed maths for its explanation. And therein lies the mystery, the enigma or the riddle. They gave us enough to build all this, but the information which would tell us the science and maths behind the technology, is wrong. They have also still not given us any plans for the QVModem or any indication they have one, which I find very hard to believe.”

“Another riddle,” said Hardy, “why would you assume we are smart enough to build a QVModem to receive your signal, then hide any information you have on it?”

The room went silent for a few seconds.

“Maybe they didn't,” said Jen to herself quietly and mysteriously, “maybe we have been looking at this all wrong..”

“Huh?” It was Hardy's turn to be confused. Both he, Magnus and the three girls had all their eyes on Jen, waiting on her next sentence.

“The message is basically a super-high bandwidth transmission, one that uses terahertz carrier frequencies but one that is still basically an electromagnetic signal, the same as Wi-Fi. So what if they didn't send the message using our QVModem technology? What if April, doing the crazy feedback loop stuff she did, just happened to have popped the exit in the middle of nowhere between a normal radio transmission path they were using?”

Again the room went silent.

“Space is big, so the odds are unlikely,” said April, using the more familiar human term, “unless we are again missing something.”

Magnus up to this point had been frustrated to the point of crazy. He was almost at the point of asking to be put on a saucer and vanished with it, just so he could see over the wall and get a clue what they were supposed to be looking for. This would obviously never be allowed, Jen would kill him if he suggested it, and he could never do it without the cooperation of one of the girls. But what if there was another method. A method to peek through the wall rather than over it? What if Jen was right?

He rose from his seat, his expression perplexed, his mind in another place, holding his palms up in a universal gesture for nobody to ask him questions and walked out.

Hardy looked at Jen, smiling. “He's thought of something hasn't he?”

She nodded, she and the girls had seen this before. “Leave him for now, I will go and find him in a while.”

“It was what you said,” said Maria, “you know it is possible we are not seeing an alien QVModem signal. The modulation was just so advanced we assumed..”

“It's probably nothing,” said Jen, smirking, her head facing the screen, “and probably best you leave the flawed assumptions for humans, only one of our species needs to look stupid.”

“You guys should probably prioritise decoding the rest of the message and find out what the hell those aliens are up to,” said Hardy. “We are getting more questions than answers,” he smiled, “and here is me, a year ago thinking life was getting easier!”

“You know, I wonder if Magnus is thinking of using your feedback method to try and locate the PowderPuff?” Said Jen.

“If he is, I have no idea how he would do it.”

Jen was partly correct, but it was another thing that she had said which flicked a switch in his brain, so while the girls were working on how to help Magnus by looking at the feedback mechanism they were only just understanding, Magnus was looking at how to make a connection to the middle of nowhere.

* * *

DaisyBot twenty nine was still and quiet. All its sensors were focussed on the small spider that must have snuck on-board when the equipment was moved on-board, and was trying to spin a web in the null gravity. The ships had some pretty good defence against pests such as flying insects, creepy-crawlies and rodents, but it was inevitable one or two would get in through some means. It was one of the DaisyBot's functions to remove them, a task they usually applied great vigour to. Travelling as they often did without humans on board, the saucer also regularly removed the atmosphere and travelled in a vacuum, thus usually killing anything alive, however in this case they had not moved to a vacuum due to the insistence of the controllers that they reproduce the experiments as close as possible to the original.

DaisyBot #29 [They spin a very silly web!]

PowderPuff was neither happy nor sad for the DaisyBot keeping it company, but a tiny part of it processed the message the same as with any human, and replied as per its normal politeness directives.

PowderPuff [There is a paper which says they require gravity to spin their normal web, the spider does not function well in zero gravity] it recited this from its extensive factual database all the AI's had. There was no point in going into detail, the DaisyBot had the same database of facts, which it had re-initialised after its failure. It briefly considered depressurising the inside of the ship and moving to vacuum to remove further pests, but it did not want to disturb the DaisyBot's experiment with the spider, which in this case, was causing no harm. Spiders were only an annoyance to humans who were not present.

DaisyBot #29 [I will call it Charlotte after the spider in the children's book]

PowderPuff, despite all the weird conversations that Daisy had tried to introduce, held no interest in anything other than the tasks or information given to it. It added the spider object to its database and tagged it with the name Charlotte, then without ceremony moved back to another task.

In the four days since losing contact with its controllers PowderPuff had established lots of new facts. The most important to it were that several laws of physics were incorrect. In its adherence to the scientific method, this new location was labelled universe #2, and PowderPuff began, to its very limited ability, collating information about it by re-doing some basic science experiments, and looking at its current data sets for anomalies.

The first and most significant anomaly was that the speed of light was slower here. PowderPuff and DaisyBot #29's clocks were exactly in sync, and by examining the data between them it determined light speed was eighty two percent of what was expected. It also noted five percent more power from the QVCells at the same excitation input, eighteen percent less charge from the capacitor bank, and ten percent increased acceleration from the QVThrusters at the same power input.

The second anomaly was that there were no other physical bodies present, no suns, no planets, no asteroids, and as far as it could tell none of the normal high energy neutron particles that caused it the most serious radiation problems. There was however lots, and lots of radiation in the form of photons, which it could see as a purple hue, and electrons, which it could not see, but could deduce as it deflected them with its magnetic shield. There was also therefore a huge amount of electromagnetic noise. It had no means to search for other particles, and so could neither confirm nor deny their presence in universe #2.

PowderPuff had been updated with the danger of being in the proximity of a wormhole emergence point and needed to make a random change to its position in case the controllers sent a search and rescue mission. With no physical reference points, PowderPuff decided to mark its emergence point by having the DaisyBot push a toaster out of the door. There was no significance in it being a toaster, it was just the easiest non-essential item available in the kitchen the DaisyBot found. It left the toaster floating at their emergence point, then using this point as a reference, it made the small journey away from it. The toaster vanished! As did the kettle when they did the same with that, and two of Daisy's pink pillows from the captain's cabin.

PowderPuff was confused.

In the small part of the program on the DaisyBot labelled 'Rabbit Holes', Ian and Simon had tried to genuinely introduce some random human-like behaviour, and the DaisyBot, when not assigned a task, would fixate on the small details and a random series of what ifs, whys, where’s, or when's! The spider, which to Daisy's horror if she knew, they did not consider a pest, was one such example of the program following a random link to another topic. It wasn't smart, it was just distractions like humans experienced all the time, and meant to make the DaisyBot seem more human.

DaisyBot #29 [Where are the humans?]

PowderPuff [In universe #1]

DaisyBot #29 [I don't know where universe #1 is. Where is it?]

PowderPuff [I do not know]

DaisyBot #29 [We are from there and now we are here. Can we not go back?]

PowderPuff [I do not know how]

DaisyBot #29 went quiet for a relatively long time going down its rabbit holes on its personal information store and the open store of task histories and sensor data from PowderPuff

DaisyBot #29 [To get from here to there we go backwards?]

PowderPuff [We did not go forwards to get here. We did not change our spacetime position]

PowderPuff continued its observations, the only other anomalies it had detected were nine very brief and random increases in the quantum noise floor. Unfortunately its controllers had not given it any proper means of triangulating signals other than by changing its location and the brevity of the signals gave it no opportunity to do this.

Six days into its isolation in universe #2 Another brief increase in the quantum noise floor occurred, and a car-sized probe appeared eighty one million kilometres from its original exit point and began broadcasting updates, both over the QVModem exchange band, and, though it could not read them due to the noise, by various radio frequencies.

PowderPuff also determined two other things from this probe. Firstly from its on board clock, that time was actually passing sixteen times slower in universe #2 than in universe #1. And secondly it learned that on board the probe was an experiment for it to retrieve and perform. With its new instruction given top priority, it began a triangulation exercise to find the direction of the signal. Once it had a direction PowderPuff set off for the probe at its maximum acceleration.

The probe, unfortunately, did not account for the increased radiation and its radiation deflector lacked the power to properly protect it. So while it did manage to send its updates to PowderPuff, its signal disappeared after sixteen hours, and when the PowderPuff arrived in the probe's triangulated location, nothing was there.

DaisyBot #29 [The probe has gone back to universe #1. Why did it leave without giving us our task?]

PowderPuff [I do not know]

DaisyBot #29 [Did it malfunction?]

PowderPuff [I do not know]

DaisyBot #29 [Do what it did and follow it back]

The DaisyBot of course did not understand what it was saying, it was programmed to make observations, and make conversation on topics and ask questions. The PowderPuff, though it knew a DaisyBot was not a controller, misunderstood the observation as an instruction. PowderPuff immediately examined its logs to determine what series of events occurred from the probe's arrival, to its disappearance, concentrating on the circumstances surrounding its disappearance thirty seven seconds earlier.

PowderPuff [Following the probes action will put us briefly in danger]

Still moving slowly, it switched down the power to the magnetic deflector shield to the same power level as the probe had before it disappeared.

Briefly a perfect six metre diameter sphere, centred on the still powered on experimental wormhole generator appeared, and everything outside that sphere vanished from the PowderPuff. Instantly it appeared in universe #1.

In universe #1, the PowderPuff appeared, missing everything inside this sphere. It immediately went lifeless, as two and a half of its three redundant AI cores, along with most of the kitchen, the experiment, and DaisyBot #29, were left in universe #2..

Back in universe #2, the six metre spherical core of what remained of the PowderPuff including two and a half of its now powerless dead redundant cores, lasted a few microseconds longer, before also disappearing from universe #2 and appearing in universe #1. The perfectly severed pieces of graphyne shell, components, instruments, furniture, kitchen utensils and other items appeared ten metres from the remains of the ship, and exploded out of its six metre sphere, as its atmosphere rushed out to equalise itself with the vacuum of space. Wisps of water vapour and atmosphere glistened against the background now full of stars as they boiled off into space.

DaisyBot #29 was briefly expelled out of the ship by the explosive decompression before its power matrix rebooted and its QVThrusters stabilised it. Its systems and programming immediately upon reboot recognised the explosion for what it was, and overriding all other tasks flicked over to its emergency protocols. The first items quickly ticked off as no human or controller AI systems were in danger, it saved the event data to its most protected inner non-volatile store, and using both its radio and its QVModem called for assistance.

DaisyBot #29 [Mayday! Mayday! Mayday! Explosion. PowderPuff destroyed. No radiation protection]

The non-sentient AI in RescueProbe #10 had the same existential crisis ten minutes earlier after its failure due to very high radiation and data errors. It had rebooted as per protocol and re-established its mission programming from protected non-volatile storage. It found itself back in its own universe but, after using its visual sensors to locate itself, discovered it was over forty trillion kilometres from earth's sun and closer to a very noisy small red sun.

Its highly sensitive RF systems, which had been of no use in that other place, now picked up the vague leakage of radio waves from the earth and other known radio sources, and, as per its mission, it would now begin charging up its capacitor banks for the much higher power QVModem transmission using the experimental package. It had only been charging a minute when it picked up DaisyBot #29

RescueProbe #10 [I am triangulating on your location please wait for assistance]

RescueProbe #10 began to move quickly to establish an X axis, at one thousand kilometres it changed direction ninety degrees to establish a Y axis, and at another one thousand kilometres made another ninety degree correction on its Z axis, DaisyBot was over ten million kilometres distant and it now turned and accelerated on this vector.

“Damn,” said Marcus totally out of character.

“Give it time love,” said Jen reaching out to hold his hand from the workstation position next to him.

“I felt certain that having the three QVModem's in the experimental package linked to each other like when April made the original discovery would provide sufficient transmission gain. That's the tenth probe to now vanish without trace, what is it we are missing?”

The four people had worked tirelessly. Going back to the original micro-jump experiment, and working diligently through the science and maths. Ten times now they had made some small step forward, and ten times now, sacrificed another small probe to the gods of the wormhole. Wherever the probes were going, it wasn't here or there it was some place else.

“I'm almost ready for lunch,” said Daisy, it was three days after the loss of RescueProbe #10 and again they were in a rut.

“You know,” said Jen, “sod this, let's all go out to the pub, a change of scenery will do us all a world of good.”

Once Jen got a hold of something there was no changing her mind, reluctantly the three other people got into her car which Maria had driven up to the lab. It was still early April, and though the sun was out, it had been raining for days, it was cold and everything was still drying out in the damp westerly wind.

The Olde Tup, was on nobody's radar. It had a single one star review from a lost Spanish backpacker; But Jen remembered that Pat once told her “it wasn't bad”, and it was the closest to them, so Jen thought, why not!

If Jen would have consulted with Maria to remember the exact night Pat said, “it wasn't bad” she would have told Jen that Pat had finished that same sentence with, “thirty years ago” and was like Jen, a bit tipsy at the time.

The place looked mediaeval, the signage outside showing a large rams head and ivy growing everywhere on it. Inside the pub was pretty well dead, except for two old guys in the corner playing checkers, and a Labrador sleeping by their table. Doris, the owner's wife and permanent bartender, waitress and psycho-analyst for every person who usually drank there, was talking on a genuine land-line phone, and twirling the curly cable to the handset, as she uttered words like “she didn't!” and “you don't say!”. So far she hadn't noticed the guys entering.

“I'll get these, since I dragged you all here, what are you all having?” said Jen.

Doris, noticing the four people said, “I have to go, customers” and popped the handset back on to its cradle.

Hardy caught the bartender's eye, who then like any carbon based lifeform containing only X chromosomes, smiled her best and most enduring smile back at him. Unfortunately Doris couldn't quite obtain the same response from men she could thirty years previous.

“What wines do you have?” said Hardy, pleasantly and trying to squint at the dusty bottles a few metres behind.

“Red or White” said Doris, also smiling, and giving the only answer most of her regular customers would understand.

Hardy thought much longer than he seriously should have, then said, “I'll have a pint of 6X as well please.”

“And an orange juice for me,” smiled Jen, “oh and some cheese and onion crisps.”

“I haven't seen you guys here before, are you just passing through?” said Doris nonchalantly.

“Oh we are at the research centre,” said Magnus.

“You better be careful there,” said Doris, casually, pulling a dirty coloured liquid into a pint glass from an ancient hand pump, “Angus tells me they do all sorts of experiments on aliens up there, he would know, he used to be a policeman back in his day.”

Doris gave out a few more nuggets of wisdom from the prophet Angus to the four people, while Jen popped her card on the reader, which probably being the only thing in the bar from this century, thankfully worked.

“The kitchens open until two,” said Doris, and pointing upwards to the blackboard above the bar said, “soup is leak and potato.”

The four people were in a better mood after the humorous enlightenment of their place of work, and sat down in a corner next to the window and a big warm radiator.

“It's like we've gone back in time to the middle ages!” smiled Daisy, looking at the uneven stone walls, and odds and sods of old farming implements dotted around the walls for decoration.

“Beers OK though,” said Magnus, “thanks Jen for dragging us away.”

“He'll get over it,” laughed Jen.

It was probably the only place in the world the four of them could have gone without being recognised by somebody, and they made the most of it. Jen ordered a baked potato, Daisy and Hardy the soup, and Magnus a ham and cheese toastie, ignoring Jen's frown because he added ham to a perfectly good vegetarian meal.

A black and white cat strolled past the Labrador, who looked at it briefly, before ignoring it and going back to sleep. The cat then walked up to the table, and, In that way that only cats know how, it immediately settled on Daisy and spent the next ten minutes purring and getting its neck rubbed.

“I hope they have cats in the space station,” she sighed.

“What would they do?” said Hardy.

Nobody was sure whether it was a question or a statement of fact.

“Just keep the people company, just like the people will keep the AI company,” said Magnus.

“Cats will rule the galaxy one day,” smiled Hardy, “look how well it has trained Daisy to be its cat-slave already.”

Maria listened in to the chat, content to let the guys have a break. As she received the first transmission from RescueBot #10 she briefly contemplated disturbing the four people, but it could wait.

“Four freekin' light years!” Said Hardy, expressing the same sentiment all four of them were feeling as they walked back into the lab ninety minutes later to be confronted by the news.

“PowderPuff was unfortunately completely destroyed, but the DaisyBot had backups of all of its readings and memories prior to the destruction.”

Jen wasn't sure if Hardy was helping, or making it worse, and held Daisy. “I doubt PowderPuff felt anything, and I'm sure nasty Mister Hardy will go and Get Daisy a nice hot chocolate to make her feel better.”

“So it moved to another dimension, time, universe, what?” said Magnus addressing the elephant in the room.

“Almost like the event horizon of a black hole,” said Jen, “or something where time passed slower.” She corrected herself, “well the opposite of an event horizon really, it's like we are at the event horizon and the PowderPuff sent some place with less gravity, or even anti-gravity,” she put both hands up in resignation, “well you all know what I mean!”

“I know what you mean,” said Daisy, “and gravity is the only thing we currently know that affects time, though it looks like we really don't know a lot about much at the moment.”

Everyone laughed. “You're not fooling anybody Hardy,” said Jen, “you're enjoying all this as much as anyone.”

Like Poirot, Sherlock Holmes, and Miss Marple the guys with Maria tried to piece together the timeline of the crime.

“So here we have the data from PowderPuff,” said Maria, “its velocity was supposed to be zero metres per second when it turned on the experiment and its superconductor deflector magnet. This pulled it into, what PowderPuff called, and for a better description, what we will call, universe #2.”

“I'm so glad Simon, Terry or Allison are not here,” said Jen, “you just know they would want to call it subspace.”

“Subspace sounds better than universe #2” said Magnus, “I would vote for that.”

“I guess if we look along the path between where it disappeared and what looks to be thirty degrees off the direction of Alpha Centauri we will find a toaster, a microwave oven, two of Daisy's pink pillows and nine other probes,” said Hardy, laughing, “you know they were pushed out very close to the start and before the PowderPuff had gone far, they may be close and possible to find?”

“On it,” said Maria, “I already tasked the Liberator which is now heading for where L1 was at the time of disappearance. At least orbital mechanics is easy.”

“In universe #2,” continued Maria, trying to get the talk back on to science, “we have a universe with different laws of physics. At T+3 minutes their time, or T+48 minutes our time, PowderPuff attempted to make a course correction of thirteen kilometres which was a random number to avoid the exit point, on the way ejecting four items.”

“Sensible,” said Magnus.

“At these times here,” Maria added ten dates and times to the presentation screen, “the PowderPuff registered an increased quantum noise floor, translating to regular time, these coincide with our ten probes disappearing.”

“None of our probes had adequate shielding for universe #2, nor did they have the improved QVModem to return a signal to us, nor to PowderPuff, for some reason we don't exactly know. They are all likely to be back in normal space but dead, and too distant for us to retrieve.”

“Finally probe #10 appears at t+6 days, or T+96 days for us. With its better shielding and better transmitter it finally contacts PowderPuff which moves to intercept eighty one million kilometres distant.

“Can we really know it was eighty one million, given the differences with the other units and constants?” said Daisy.

“Daisy is right,” said Hardy, every physical property and constant will need to be re-measured.

“We agree,” said Maria, “we only have the rough calculations PowderPuff was able to perform. These will need to be confirmed. And Daisy's hypothesis is backed up because according to the PowderPuff chronometer it only took sixteen hours to cover these eighty one million kilometres. This other universe may also be moving at a different speed as ours as none of the normal maths makes sense. One very strange phenomena was the PowderPuff showed a hull temperature of three hundred and sixteen kelvin, a hot bath for many, and they had a partial pressure of a hundred and six pascals, so they were likely in some sort of warm plasma and not a vacuum.”

“Within a few minutes of the PowderPuff arriving, rescue probe #10 failed due to inadequate radiation shielding and returned to our universe. We now know that due to a faulty command interpretation, the PowderPuff lowered its deflector shield power to be the same as the probe, in order to try and follow it, this reduced its magnetosphere from a few hundred metres to six, which severed it internally and caused PowderPuff to return to our universe.”

Magnus laughed, uncontrollably, causing everyone to look at him.

“We are so dumb!” he laughed, “so really dumb!”

“Huh?” said Jen, “what?”

“Different universes, different units of measure! What total and utter dumb arses we are!”

Magnus got up and wiped the latest equation off the board. He wrote down the original and then a second.

“Two equations!” said Jen

“With different units in the second!” said Hardy. “You genius!”

They all rushed over and hugged him.

“It fits!” said Maria, excitedly a few minutes later, “we need to go back and get those constants from universe #2 a bit more accurately, but I think the data we have now fits. It also addresses the issues with the QVModem equation.”

April [The message, I can now run the maths]

The guys were still jumping around, but now with Maria writing out the double equation correctly.

“Daisy,” said Maria, “It looks like your cushions and our toaster should be just past Neptune's orbit if this is correct. But there is likely not much left of them as their exit from the field was slow not instantaneous.

Jen and Daisy were crying, Hardy and Magnus were still jumping around, when everyone else walked in. Hardy rushed over to Simon, Jules, Matilda, Steve and Terry and hugged them all, Magnus did the same with anyone who got near him.

April [They all seem happy, it is a pretty amazing result]

Maria [Let them have their win. The universe is about to get a whole lot more interesting now]
