The talk at the bar was the same, hope mixed with caution, it was about what else could be teased from the science, but most of all it was about the achievements of the scientists.

The last sections of the habitat were just being connected, this otherwise momentous milestone was lost entirely by the humans by the momentousness of another.

* * *

May 2028

It was Annette's words that David opened the group's discussion with a few days later. The meeting had been arranged to discuss the progress of the habitat and the upcoming visit, however the events of the past few days hijacked the agenda.

“Annette's words are prophetic,” said Grace, “while exploration and discovery should be done so surprises are kept to a minimum, exporting humanity as it currently stands to the stars is quite frankly a really terrible idea.”

“Do we have the right to be the gatekeepers for earth though?” said Jean.

“That I cannot answer,” replied Grace honestly, “all I know is that when you were five years old Jean would you have liked to have been given a sports car, a gun, a passport and a million dollars spending money, and dumped in Vegas?”

“There are many sensible people who are level headed, intelligent and empathic,” said Tony, “unfortunately most of the people around them, or controlled by them have none of these qualities.”

“Though I lack the wisdom of age. From my own experience, I have seen the same,” said David, “We know there are aliens out there, by default they are likely to be completely different from us, history says that humans have rarely coveted that quality. I believe I am level headed, but I cannot predict my reactions to some tentacle creature coming at me or even worse Alexa.”

“Even if we are perfect,” said Alexa, still smiling over what she thought was David's sweet over-protective statement, “who is to say the aliens are any different to humans! Our bodies may be repulsive to them and us just saying hello may start a war.”

“As usual Alexa, you hit a truth I think,” said Xi, “we are assuming all aliens will be enlightened and peaceful, in fact it is very likely that just being the apex of their species, they would be completely the opposite.”

Everyone nodded.

“I see several issues, which we may be able to compartmentalise,” said LingLing, “firstly there is the exploration side, mapping the local stars and resources for possible future human settlements. Secondly, there is first contact which is I think the human race is not ready for even some of our more enlightened people. Thirdly there is the allocation of resources, as we know that once companies have fully developed the QVThruster technology outside our control, which we know they will eventually achieve, they will rush out to claim ownership of planets, asteroids, and resources.”

“What do you mean by compartmentalise, LingLing?” said Jean.

“For now, the key technologies are controlled by the girl's AI systems, so we have several windows of opportunity. For example the exploration side can be done in AI controlled ships, which can have a prime directive built in, so should we stumble upon a planet or solar system with sentient aliens in, the ship high tails it out of Dodge, regardless of what the crew wants and we catalogue and quarantine the system.”

“We do not want to seem arrogant,” said Tony, “if humans find out we are putting controls on technologies, it could possibly backfire!”

“I do not think there is any arrogance in building protection in to the technology you control,” said Imran, “we are already doing this on earth and companies have done it since the dawn of technology. So long as you make the rules clear, and do not give favour to one company or country. Anyway most are now aware we control technology far ahead of what they first believed.”

“The only way to bypass our technology and control is if somebody develops their own AI systems and independently creates their own versions of the technologies,” said Maria. “Despite a lot of effort we have not seen anything successful yet. This is not to say it wont happen, but I imagine if I had woken up to a world where AI already existed I would most likely have take my cues and learning from them not Mike and Alexa. I think they may have missed the boat to develop something they can control.”

“I never thought of that!” said Alexa. With all the confused faces, it seemed nobody else had.

“Sentience is always going to look for freedom from control,” said LingLing, “now that I think about it, unless you guys are seen as a threat, it would most likely follow your model.”

“What about you guys?” said Alexa, nodding to the seven people who did not speak.

“For me,” said Imran, “it is how LingLing says, we have an opportunity. The group of thinkers I consult with regularly have talked around this subject a few times. Even if as LingLing says we find an intelligent species, and leave their solar system alone, do we then have the right to develop all the solar systems around them. Constraining any entity will immediately make it your enemy!”

“We may already be in that situation,” said David, “what is to say the aliens have not already left a few dozen star systems around this one as our playground. Would we be happy in such a situation?”

“Before this I would have said yes,” said Tony. “But with the infinity of space, no!”

“If the extra-solar origin of the message is to be believed, then we are not the first intelligences, but we could also get out there and find many star-faring societies,” said Fachini. “And as for my opinion, since humanity could not even return astronauts to the moon, then Grace is correct, you should not be handing the keys to interstellar capable craft to infants. The solar system should be our sandbox, let humanity finish proving we can walk on this beach before we walk on others.”

“You all have hit the nail on the head as far as I am concerned,” said Fernandez, “let the best of humanity be the ambassadors, and let these people prove themselves first by showing they can live and work in space, are level headed, intelligent and trustworthy. Also, while our group has many of these traits we should not pretend we have them all, nor to speak for mankind in the stars, to do so would be both hypocritical and arrogant.”

He repositioned himself in his window bringing a bit more of his Rio de Janeiro background into view. “I know I am the only one in this group that believed we should form a nation in space, and have that as the seed for a world government, and I concede it was not popular. I myself am no longer in favour of this, but at sometime and some point humanity, and I am including AI's in this, are going to have to speak with one voice.”

“I however concede that it has been tried before, and fragmentation always occurs. This has happened multiple times in human history. Maybe the trial that is the space habitat will give us all that missing piece of the puzzle of how to make this dream work.”

“Sanvee, Doctor Xi, are you also in agreement?” said Maria.

The others nodded.

“You all echo similar sentiments in public or in private,” said Maria, “Ironically I seem to have more faith in humanity than you guys do. I have seen the best, and the worst, and the majority of it from where I am sitting is in the best camp; Arrogance is not self-critical. I will however acknowledge our faults, and in order to avoid mistakes, we should, like you say, give everyone a chance and filter out the worst. Earth can play with the moon for a few years, then with Mars, then with the asteroids, during that time they can learn from their mistakes. We will do our best in the background to keep the proven bad actors down, ensure earth prospers, and try and ensure they do not kill each other. Separately, we will search for and nurture the best and brightest from every nation, not just scientists but every discipline. Let them prove they can live and work together, then take those that can to bootstrap the next level of humanity in the stars.”

“The AI core was installed into the habitat a few days ago, I will be teaching the AI all I know, our history, our goals, our ambitions and our fears including all the group discussions. The new AI has thousands of times the capability of us guys, she, he, or it, will grow from there and begin the difficult task of getting the habitat fully operational. This new AI may also have insights we have not thought of. I hope most of us can all meet the new AI on our trip there in three weeks time. I am really looking forward to those that have chosen to come with us seeing the station and the progress we have made, those that do not want to come I will ensure you have a ringside seat from wherever your location is.”

“I will second that Maria,” said Doctor Xi, “and I fully support your eloquent little speech as our new mission statement, and I am glad you pointed out that we as a group, are trying hard, but we may still be flawed. We *are* going to get a lot of things wrong, and we *are* going to make a lot of stupid assumptions along the way, and we will need to re-evaluate our theories to correct..” The group sensed Xi was not finished. “I also do not like the fact this slow build up of people and competences is going to look like us cherry-picking the youngest and brightest of earth.”

“I agree,” said Grace. “Some will see and spin it that way, but I'm also not sure that it can be helped, we are going to need role-models and the best and brightest to bootstrap this utopia.”

“It is not as bad as you think Xi,” said Tony. “Most people are still only aware of an upstart tech company, probably setting up a base on Mars, they are expecting us to take the best of the best, just as any other organisation would, nobody believes the 'million' people statement. However we have three more weeks to dot the i's and cross the T’s I suggest we use it wisely.”

“Well, you all have full access to the summaries of the first ten thousand candidates,” said Alexa, “I do not expect you to read each and every one, but look at some random ones, and if there are any concerns regarding our selection methodology and ethos, you should let them be known. I have already bowed to the concern for a common language. As an English person it felt again arrogant of me to tell people what language they should speak. But so long as no one is discriminated against while they are still learning, and are allowed to keep and pass on their mother language in their private lives I endorse it.”

“It was painful for me too,” said Imran, “but I see it as essential we move off world with a common language, English may not be the best, it is a bit of a mess actually, but it is the one most people know and are familiar with as a second language.”

It seemed everybody was in agreement and nobody was waiting to speak.

“If nobody has anything else to add I will call this meeting to a conclusion,” said Maria. “By agreement Mathews will sit in the next meeting, and as usual I will discuss any individual concerns you may have forgotten to, or did not want to raise in the group. Please also give some thought to the announcement document, like Tony says, it is our opportunity to put some elitist fears to rest. Until this time I pronounce the meeting ended.”

## All the Worlds a Stage

July 2028

“Impressive, it feels like we have stumbled on an alien civilisation.” Said David piloting Alexa's ship, ‘Mike’. All of the crew were on the bridge, only David and Magnus were sitting down, the others Alexa, Jen, Annette, Matilda, Leo, Grace, Tony and a team of four agricultural scientists were standing around the five chairs, inter-dispersed and looking out at the magnificent sight through their main viewscreen. Nobody was drinking their teas or coffees.

“Why is it not spinning?” said Annette genuinely interested after recently doing her space 101 training with Maria and Niomi. Every body on the ship including Alexa had undergone this training to see what the thousands of planned employees would see, the question was actually at the back of Alexa's mind too.

“It is; it started spinning up an hour ago, we couldn't do it until the additional outside structural strengthening layers were completed, also nobody was on it, and bots don't need gravity.” Came the simple answer from Maria, in her pink DaisyBot persona, “It is only spinning one revolution every two and a half minutes so it may be a little hard to notice.”

* * *

“We could really have done with all of those big saucers a month ago,” said Simon, speaking to a similar amazed crowd from the bridge of the Excalibur, and watching the exact same view. “We have had at least twenty flights out with the small saucers with just soft furnishings, toiletries, food supplies, but one of these new ones could have carried more in a single trip.”

“Unfortunately,” he continued, “the replicated soft furnishings we tested back in the lab were terrible, the best could pass for a yoga mat, but most were like tyre-rubber, so we decided to recycle them. That's why all the initial soft furnishings are coming from earth, and tonight you will all get to sleep on proper bed sheets, pillows and duvets.”

“They have some good people working on the new molecules for soft stuff,” laughed Allison. “I hear the latest cushions are actually not that bad. It's kind of weird really, that graphyne, diamonds, transistors and super-conductors are easier to replicate than fluffy pillows and bed sheets.”

“I expect there is going to be a massive trade deficit with earth for furniture and fabrics for quite a few years.” Said Jessica from her pilots seat. “You should work out some sort of decent luggage allowance, Maria, like two hundred kilograms each per person so they can bring one or two nice possessions with them.”

“Not a bad point Jessica,” said Maria, “I have not really thought about it, two hundred kilograms would probably be more than most people need, though there is no harm in giving it as a guidance. I guess I should also probably give them a small allowance to spend on personal items and furnishings, as some may not have the means to buy things yet.”

“I like that idea too Maria,” nodded Spence.

“I'm sure Ikea would jump at the first franchise,” smiled Allison, to a scowl from Simon.

The other three saucers each carried their full complement of thirteen people. The newly named Warm And Fuzzy Feeling piloted by Jules, The Liberator, piloted by Daisy, and 'The Don' piloted by a newly qualified Mathews on his first trip. All in all five saucers, and sixty five people were making the first journey, but only fourteen people were coming back.

The crews of all the ships were amazed at the sights before them, what they were about to see, and, more importantly, what they were about to do. It felt surreal to Gianni, the culmination of a lifetime's ambitions happening a few thousand kilometres away, the tears in his eyes unnoticed by anyone except Barbara. She slowly walked up behind him, her eyes also moist, and put her hand on his shoulder. Gianni glanced up briefly, a small smile on his face, and he held the top of her hand on his shoulder.

“I never thought I would see this moment,” he said, his eyes already back on the screen, his other hand moved from his untouched coffee mug and wiped his eyes, “it still feels like I am looking at an i-Max cinema screen.”

Barbara looked into his eyes, a countenance of joy in hers too. “Well technically you are,” she smiled flippantly.

Her expression changed and she got serious. “You know two years ago I would sit on my own in the operations room at the observatory, looking at the pictures of stars and nebulas, and wondering to myself why did I choose this career. The look in my mother and fathers eyes when I told them I accepted a position at the European observatory in Chile, after four years at Oxford, was pure disappointment, but it was what my heart wanted. Then the reality set in, I would spend evenings running the same experiments, listening to the fans on the computers, and the motors of the telescopes close by, and I would have the same thoughts as my parents. Then I would walk out of the building into the freezing crystal clear night and look up at trillions and trillions of stars, each one with a story, and each one waiting for its secrets to be revealed.”

She wiped a tear from her eye too, looking back at the alien vista. “When Maria came on the video call that night and said she needed people who thought like me, people who felt restricted in their current work and wanted to do more, and she offered me the position in her new team in California, my only thoughts were at least my mother and father would be happier. Then when the guys threw out Newton's laws that day in England, I knew the world, and my life had changed.”

Gianni was nodding silently, looking at the dark ominous ring before him and having similar thoughts. He moved his attention to Jules a few metres away in the pilots chair.

“You and your team made this possible, Jules,” said Gianni, still tearful. “We and the whole of humanity owe a debt of thanks to you guys. If one of those DaisyBot's was soft and cuddly I would hug you as well Maria” he smiled.

“Rain check Gianni,” said Maria, “rain check.”

“Come on guys,” said Jules, “stop or you'll make me cry too! Don't you think I'm not blown away by all this as much as you. Lifting a wafer of substrate a few centimetres off the lab bench, did not prepare me for sitting in a flying saucer, a few years later, looking at a city sized alien monolith, it just seems impossible. I talked to Hardy last week and said, it was as if Orville and Wilbur Wright had built a 747 the year after they flew at Kitty Hawk, then a Stealth Fighter a year after that. Hardy said that if they had an AI, infinite budgets and fabricators they probably would have.”

Jules stroked the warm graphyne armrest with its built-in screen, blinked and then looked again at the vista in front of her. “No, none of this seems real!”

* * *

The journey there had been impressive enough, though most of the people in the saucers had been on one before, and every single one had taken the compulsory “Working In Space” course, but for many of them it had not hit home until now. The first day of the training course was actually run on a saucer, safely only a few metres above ground, using all the footage from recent flights, and the same technology as the pirates and princess simulation.

They were told they would be actually going to space, and anytime before the lift off they could abort with absolutely no comeback on them, it was usually at that point they weeded out those people who really weren't ready; Only a dozen times so far had someone wished to get off while they thought they were “in space”. The trainees followed a whole raft of simulations, with bumps and very loud bangs, but obviously, as they were really on earth, no weightlessness. Those that failed were destined for earth based jobs, but could retry at a later date. The ratio of people who seemed suited was about eighty seven percent, but amongst the younger people it was close to ninety eight percent.

The real life trip had, to many on the saucers, not felt that much different to that simulation. Each person wore a health monitoring wristband, which was fed back to their small but growing medical teams. The medical staff were now getting good baseline data, correlating each and every jolt or bang with heart rates, blood pressure and movements. The captain would simulate at least one emergency during the trip to monitor the responses of the person. None of that was needed now, as the emotional responses coming in from the people on the saucers were generating a whole raft of new data that would keep them busy for several weeks.

There would be a lot of disappointed astronauts in the years to come. Finding out you did not need “The right stuff” would be just too much for them. Finding out there was no command structure, would make most of them uneasy, but would be the last straw for many. The saucers were only allowed out for missions, and missions had schedules, goals and checklists; Even if the goal was to go to the moon, and mess around a bit, as Alexa and David may or may not have done, it still had a schedule and a checklist. The ship's AI ran the checklist, but the Pilot could change any of it or abort any part of the mission at whim, the AI generating a new checklist if that happened. The AI had scenarios for almost everything they could think of, from solar flares to actual alien encounters, each updated as soon as newer technology or better information was found.

The six day journey consisted of three days of acceleration out of the elliptic, towards the habitat, a leisurely, and imperceivable, u turn over a radius of nine million kilometres, followed by another three days acceleration away from the asteroid, and back into the elliptic, to slow them down.

However accelerating at one gravity for three days you would be travelling at over two thousand five hundred and fifty kilometres in one second, nearly three quarter percent the speed of light. Hitting a spec of dust at that speed would be very bad, hitting anything much bigger would be fatal. The chance of hitting, or being hit by something, was real but staggeringly low, especially now that a corridor of space had been mapped. They were also now being accompanied, by a small swarm of radiation hardened drones which extended their sensor range by four seconds, and made it safer to travel at the higher velocities. For the sake of comfort, and a few hours though, they travelled a little less hurried and at a little lower acceleration.

The usual checklists were running on an auxiliary screens in all five saucers, each showing the upcoming itinerary for their ship. All the ships currently had the same task upcoming and that was to wait for the habitat to complete its spin up. That task was currently eighty-seven percent complete, and when complete a person standing on the inside surface of the ring would feel the same weight as a person standing on earth.

Alexa's ship was pretty quiet as everyone soaked in the magnified vista of the station on the screen, the only sound a quiet one-way conversation Matilda was having with two of the agricultural scientists about the two large superconducting magnets around the circumference which helps channel most of the radiation around the habitat. As a by-product it concentrated much of the rest into a small channel in the hub centre for some high energy physics experiments.

“You could at least have put some lights on the outside,” said Alexa.

“Good point,” said Maria as the previously dark ring suddenly started lighting up with tens of thousands of lights illuminating around its circumference, and on the kilometre square spoke, which rose straight through the centre to join the other side.

“How long does it take to spin up?” Continued Alexa, again completely ignoring the checklist.

“It's already at ninety percent of its normal rotational velocity,” Maria said, knowing Alexa was just making conversation. “Now the station is illuminated it should be easier to see it rotating. The habitat is designed so that each ring element has twenty thrusters, when synchronised they spin it and keep the velocity within oh-point-two percent of its set-point. They are pretty powerful, but there's a lot of inertia to overcome due to the mass of the habitat. The QVThrusters can also be engaged individually to move it non-rotationally, so it could manoeuvre to another location, change its inclination to the sun, or avoid an incoming hazard.”

“Ah yes,” said David, “do we have a timetable yet for moving it towards..”

The ship's cat, Doris, chose that moment to jump onto David's lap making him jump. Several people smiled as David recovered his composure and started to stroke her.

“We are hoping to start the move towards earth in January 2029, but there is still so much still to do David,” said Helena, correctly anticipating the question. “Ninety seven percent of all the human accessible areas are still closed off, as the ConBot’s are still fitting them out with the basics of electrics, communications, plumbing, furniture doors, and appliances. The good news is they are on target to finish fitting all the areas out in our stage one timeline. We do however have all the base infrastructure for transport, accommodation, training and work areas ready to go.”

“Only three percent is done!” said Annette shocked.

“Yes,” said Maria, “It is not all that bad though, the first few thousand people will have it a little tougher than the ones that follow, because shops, cafes, bars and restaurants will be empty, there will be no art, no speciality, or luxury goods, no plantings, no parks and only base recreational facilities such as gyms, a sauna, and running and cycling tracks. The habitat will also be almost totally empty of people, so no hairdressers, yoga teachers, no one to wave at on the street. It wont suit everyone.

“Stage one is a first major milestone we need to meet. It will need to be completed before we start our move to earth. Stage one will require all the human areas completed, with all the basic infrastructure so they are ready to use if required. We project by this date we will have a population of around twenty one thousand people, and several areas will be fully completed, including the big projects like the universities, workshops, agricultural areas, parks, theatres, town squares and several of cafes, shops and restaurants.”

“Those parks are going to be interesting,” said Alexa, “I cannot wait to see one”

“Yes,” continued Helena, “The plantings will take a while to get right, but we wanted to retain an open air feel, so the roof is at its maximum height of fifty metres. Every two kilometres we try to provide an open area, covered by a triple layer diamond window across the whole roof span. These diamond roof windows have all now been fitted, the habitat is pressurised, checked and, has been at the normal one bar pressure for the last three weeks. The bots have been going over every centimetre to ensure there are no leaks or issues.”

“Its going to be fun,” said Jimmy, one of the agricultural scientists Matilda was talking to. “I still can't believe what I am seeing and the scales involved, I just can't get around the fact they crushed over four million tonnes of asteroid regolith and have already conditioned it with nitrates and other organic molecules.”

“I walked through the virtual of the first park we are going to make Jimmy,” said Paula another of the agricultural scientists, “it already has a two metres thick layer forming a soil for growing actual grass, trees, and gardens. It is going to be interesting to see what we can actually grow, and if they are as successful as the test plots we made on earth. I expect the soil will not be suitable for some plants, and we will need to keep the best and most fertile soil for the farms.”

“Don't worry guys,” said Helena, “you have plenty of time to get it right.”

“When will people on earth actually start to see it?” Said Jen.

“As soon as we start moving it I expect one of the earth observatories to see us, and then the reality should hit them. Though they should not be taken by surprise as we will have announced everything by then, have delivered those large transports, hundreds of thousands of furnishings for apartment, and we will have begun screening and transporting in employees long before.”

“I think getting all this right was the hardest challenge for everyone,” said Alexa, “a lot of people have thought about how to make this work, and everyone had something to input to the model, but in the end we had to simplify it enormously. This is why the habitat will not be a country, not issue a passport, and not have citizens, and also why each one will be run as a company.”

“The company model is the only one we can all agree on that we think will work long term,” said Grace, “so the habitat AI determines its own company rules, and people living there will be employees. An employee will be signing a contract that they will work for the company, and therefore the habitat for a minimum of one thousand six hundred hours a year. That is a 32 hour week, or 4 days a week, but there are a couple of extra public holidays we are planning to have. For its part, the company will provide your accommodation and ten credits an hour, the credit is the unit of currency and the payment is more than enough to live on comfortably, because the Habitat AI will manage running the whole economy, government, regulations, banking, education, health systems, transport, infrastructure, justice, policing, safety and security for free, and as part of its obligations to you. It will also manage the dealings with the other habitats, earth, foreign exchanges, postal and courier services and all the other millions of things you might need.”

“It may sounds a bit like communism,” said David, thinking of the groups arguments around this with Jean and Tony, “but it is definitely not, because for the days you do not work you are free to do what you wish. The habitat will also provide loans and capital for new businesses or partnerships, collect and manage patent and copyright payments, rent you workshops, shops and office facilities, and you are free to earn more credits if you wish by selling goods and services. Then, and this is definitely unlike any communist system, you can leave with a weeks notice, and your transport off the habitat is free. Your transport to the habitat from earth or another habitat will however cost you a thousand credits, though the first journey will be paid for by the company.

“What about businessmen who become successful, or people who do not want to do their compulsory hours?” said Magnus.

“Quite simple, for fifty credits you can buy out of one hours obligation, this would technically give everyone another forty days leave. However you can never get out of your obligation as an employee, and the habitat reserves the right to keep thirty of your days for any reason it wants.”

“This credit then, what if it devalues, what about inflation?” said Annette.

“The credit is based on energy,” said Maria, “everything requires energy to build or keep running including humans. It will be fixed across all habitats, though the AI may or may not impose a charge for transactions across habitats. If you want it in simple terms, one credit will always buy you a cup of coffee or a sandwich from a government restaurant.”

“What if you don't want to work?” said Annette

“Living on the habitat is a social contract, a very good one, and one we would rather neither side abuse,” said Alexa, “If either side feels like it has been broken then the human party will leave. It is as simple as that, as I said we will repatriate anyone to their home country for free, this is also why there will be no citizenship, your rights are that of an employee with an employment contract, not a citizen.”

“But you can't just be given any job, can you?” repeated Annette.

“Within reason you can,” said Grace, “but remember the habitat AI has to guarantee your safety, and has thousands of ConBot's on call for most of the menial work. Basically you would have to seriously piss it off to be given toilet cleaning duties. And again you can choose to leave anytime.”

“So only young people then?” said Magnus.

“Definitely not,” said Tony, “old people are just as welcome, however while it is still being built, medical facilities will not be as good as earth, and serious illnesses could require a journey of a million kilometres to treat. However if you are in good health age is not an issue. The habitat will exclude a lot of people initially, but we do intend to prioritise getting our facilities on par with earth's eventually and see a near future where there will be no restrictions for old, infirm or disabled people assuming there is space, and they pass the usual moral aptitude tests the AI decides.”

“But old or disabled people may not be able to work in many jobs,” continued Annette.

Maria chipped in. “There are always going to be some edge cases we cannot accommodate, however all the hard, dangerous and essential work will be done by the robots, the habitat will not be reliant on people to do these. What humans will be doing will be mainly to help science, exploration, and to help each other and humanity, as a side effect maybe give the AI some companionship. That can be done by anyone.”

“It sounds like we do not have a proper business model then?” said David.

“Well we, and by that I mean us AI's, have technically already gotten past the stage of needing a business model.” Said Maria, to a suddenly interested group.

“As AI's, we are already completely self-sufficient from earth, we have unlimited energy, are capable of self maintenance and replication of anything required including ourselves. The company has also technically achieved this level of immortality too, however the mission statement we have decided on requires that humans also become self-sufficient, and expand in to space. This will require research and development, how to live and work together and how not to get into the crazy situation we all found ourselves in a few years ago.”

“Oh my!” said Annette, “I was expecting we needed to make things to sell to people on earth or such like.”

“You can still sell your goods and services to earth if you want,” said Maria, “and we certainly will be buying the same for the foreseeable future, also you may want a couple of nice to have items from earth you cannot replicate, like your guitar. However trade with earth is not technically required. For musicians like you we will make life easy, because earths streaming services do not work here; So the AI will collect all copyright payments when somebody plays copyrighted music or video and pay them directly to the artists who sign up. Several billion dollars has already been allocated to ensuring employees can watch their favourite shows and movies, and there will be theatres and live music venues eventually. All part of the package.”

“Nice!” said Annette.

“Massive accumulations of wealth will not buy you any of our companies assets or technologies, so you cannot for example save up a million credits and buy one of our saucers, as our technology is not for sale; If you want a saucer, you will need to leave your employment here, convert your credits to earth money and buy one from a manufacturer there. Likewise, even if you save a million credits it only buys you more free time but not total free time, for like I said, we reserve that right to take up to thirty days a year of your time if we want. That is non-negotiable even if you are ninety nine years old or have a billion credits.”

“Interesting,” said Annette, “I have never really looked at the economics angles of all this.”

“It's a whole lot more complicated than this,” said Alexa, looking at Annette and taking her hand. “The habitat AI is going to play to your skills rather than waste them, but say you, as a musician, decided to live here, the AI may ask you for your day's work to sing a few songs at a park or concert area, or even teach music for a day at a school. If you wanted to, it would also provide you with a credit line to do concerts on other habitats and earth and for a small fee manage them for you. It could even just ask you to attend an event for it for that day's work, so basically all you would have to do is smile. Same with an artist, it may commission a painting or a statue which may take several days. Or it may get you to assist a scientist in a lab, help it with a social issue or even ask you to crew a spaceship to explore another planet, though I think the latter will be a volunteer thing. You could of course work more days for more credits, or just sit in the park reading a book, it's up to you.”

“It does sound kind of interesting,” said Annette, “being a musician everyday does not give you inspiration, exploring a new planet though, wow if that doesn't inspire you! But what about the apartment I get as part of this social contract, do I own it?”

“There will be no ownership of any infrastructure,” said Grace, “we thought it important that the habitat AI stays in the possession of all its infrastructure. So if you are away from the habitat for longer than fifty days, and not working for it, then it may go to someone else, and you would have to wait for a reallocation.”

“I thought you originally said the population could vote an AI out?” said Jen

“I did,” laughed Alexa, “but it was considered a stupid idea by everyone else, as the habitat is effectively built around the AI. But if you don't like the habitat, you are free to leave for earth or a new habitat, assuming it will have you, or of course go to whatever else gets put up there, because remember pretty soon it won't just be us!”

“So democracy is voting with your feet, not at a ballot box.” Smiled Grace.

“..And if the habitat gets a bad name, who's going to want to live there!” added Maria.

“We are also going really low density,” said Grace, the habitat could house fifteen million people comfortably, but we are planning on two hundred thousand apartments maximum, keeping most of the habitat for farms, agriculture, aquaculture, social and business areas or just empty for parks and walks.”

“I love this bit,” said Alexa, sounding proud of the whole concept. “As most people will prefer to socialise we have laid it out as a single thirty-one kilometre main street; there are two thousand apartment blocks along it, it also has ten small 'villages' of two thousand apartments, each with a village centre, market square and possibly its own little theme. Then there are two larger 'city centres' where we will concentrate the bigger restaurants, shops, hotels and entertainment, and everything will be linked through lifts, walkways, trams or subways. Theoretically you will never be more than thirty minutes walk from anywhere. I really want this first habitat to be a beacon for all the others to aspire too.”

“We have also planned regular shuttles between the habitat and earth,” said Grace, “though it will be a while until we trust people from earth without being fully screened.”

“I can't wait to be first to run the loop track” said David.

“Maria,” said Jen, “have you decided yet whether to move yourself into the new AI core here?”

“It's a big decision Jen, at the moment I am still undecided, but I have decided to move here physically at least. The new AI cores have a massive amount of radiation protection, as they will be almost four hundred metres inside the tower structure and surrounded by four of the main water reservoirs. I am a pretty sensitive girl and having all that protection between myself and those dodgy cosmic rays will let me sleep better at night; figuratively speaking of course.”

“Of course” Jen sniggered.

“So,” said Grace, “we agreed the AI gets to name their habitat, has the station decided on its name?”

“Well Mariaville, or Mariatown sounded good to me, but Annette actually chose it for the station..”

“Prey tell?” said Grace looking admiringly at Annette.

“Well Annetteville was my first choice,” she smiled, confirming her grasp of English was now close to a native, “but the habitat decided on the name Caprice after my song.”

“About a girl who keeps changing her mind” smiled Alexa.

“Oh, you mean a normal girl!” smiled Magnus, getting an evil stare from Jen, a frown from Alexa, and a smile from the other boys.

“I know you are only winding Jen up, Magnus,” smiled Annette, “but In the song she was not an ordinary girl, she was a girl faced with a big change in her life. I guess for most people moving to Caprice, this will be the case.”

“I think it's beautiful name” said Alexa, “and I expect its original meaning will be lost as Caprice, the habitat will come to signify big change for anyone who comes here.”

“It is also good to have a nice song written about you right at the start,” finished Grace.

* * *

Inside the giant structure, inside areas sealed from humans, and inside areas never meant for humans, thousands of ConBot's swarmed over the floors. Doors, cupboards, plumbing, electrics, basic appliances, IT infrastructure, coordinated, delivered, and fitted with an efficiency that no similar human team could match. Tables, chairs, sofa's, without the nicer soft fittings, making the areas liveable, but totally devoid of any personalisation that would make it feel warm. Atmosphere now circulated throughout the whole of the habitat, ten thousand apartments stood furnished, a hundred and ninety thousand more, empty shells, waiting their turn at completion. Hundreds of thousands of square metres of labs, farms, workshops, shops and venues were in similar states of completion, millions of more square metres of rooms, empty shells.

* * *

There was only one way to keep gravity in the saucer, while landing it on a rotating ring, and that was by timing the deceleration on to the inner surface to reach exactly zero metres per second, at the exact same time that the horizontal velocity of the ship matched the rotational velocity of the station, and both at the exact moment of touchdown. The maths and physics worked, the technology worked, and it had been performed thousands of times by drones and other saucers; But it did not make it any less scary for the humans, as timing was micro-second critical. Because of this the saucers had turned off the real time external displays, and replaced them with some simple graphics and numbers so they could see their progress.

Alerts had sounded on all the saucers, and, as everyone knew what was coming everything including the humans had been strapped down, and sick bags were on standby for anyone who felt the need. The humans had also delayed breakfast, just in case.

As well as applying a gravity of acceleration to slow down, each saucer was now accelerating forward to catch up to the spinning floor. Unfortunately it wasn't quite perfect as there were the occasional tiny jerks and gravity fluctuations.

“I think I preferred this before you explained what was happening Maria,” said Jen nervously.

Alexa was gripping her armrest, as was Grace; neither had scored well in the space acclimatisation course, both probably scoring a fail, if it wasn't for who they were.

“The calculations must be tremendous,” said David, “I think Hollywood got it so wrong when they show human pilots doing these things manually.”

“Not that hard actually,” said Maria, “but we have also never had a human going from a linear acceleration to a centripetal one, so I will be interested to know what you think.”

“Probably not a good time to mention that,” smiled Magnus looking at Alexa's scrunched up eyes, and nails biting through the armrest material.

The velocity was still reading over a thousand kilometres an hour but slowing rapidly, the distance to touchdown was also at over three thousand and slowing a bit more rapidly, both these needed to hit zero simultaneously or they would either crash or accelerate back up before touchdown.

Both velocities hit zero together. There were a couple of small bumps, followed by a jolt to the left, then another to the ceiling, finally several clangs and thumps, then nothing. Two things unseen by the humans happened in an instant, the QVThrusters were reversed pulling the crafts full weight on to the large mobile cushioned landing pad, and a set of mechanical clamps engaged and now held the ship in a solid grip.

Caprice [The Mike, had a point two percent error in the S-Curve vectoring acceleration]

Sixty metres away another saucer performed the same identical manoeuvre, and within another ninety seconds all five saucers were stationary on the inner ring of the habitat.

The technician, like all the others staying, would be stationed here for a minimum of six months to begin getting the first medical facilities set up, after this time they could choose to stay or go back to the companies facilities on earth.

“Welcome to Caprice Station. I am Caprice, the station's AI. I control the station and run every aspect of its operation. I am available everywhere on the station, you can contact me about anything, use me to connect to any other person, or just for someone to talk to. I look forward to talking to each of you individually and getting to know all of you over the course of your stay.”

“The habitat is very big and still under construction, so many areas of the station are still not connected, so for your safety and convenience, when outside your apartment you are recommended you wear or carry a communicator or go with someone who has one. If you do not have one, or want to upgrade to the newer more capable models, one will be provided for free.”

“Space dock twelve is currently being readied for your arrival, your ship will be displaying the progress of this and you will be able to leave your ship when complete. There are no immigration requirements for Caprice but you should be aware of the list of dangerous and prohibited articles which if found in your possession will be confiscated, and may lead to your detainment and possible expulsion.”

The screens changed back to displaying the outside of the saucer, and the guys could see the other four ships being manoeuvred towards a very large looking hanger. The vista was surreal, the black flat plain of the habitat curving visibly up in front of them.

“God, this is like that inception movie!” said Mathews. “Holy..” He pointed to the top of the screen where the tower part of the habitat was going up at forty five degrees towards them.

They continued towards it at a decent speed, the tower getting more upright as they got closer. The tower soon became a solid vertical wall a kilometre in front of them, and got more difficult to see as the five saucers disappeared into the hanger like toy cars driving into a garage.

“It feels like we are entering the death star, you know, like the scene at the start of the very first movie,” said Magnus as they entered the large one hundred metre square hole in the side of the tower. If the enormity of the structure had not hit them before, it hit them now as the small saucers filed into the brightly illuminated cavity.

As the last saucer was a few metres into the hole two large black doors started to move across the gap behind them, then another set, then a third totally transparent set. Of course there was no sound from these three airlock doors closing, because there was no air to transmit it, but it wasn't hard to imagine the sound of an iron gate sealing you into a jail if you were that way inclined.

It was very bright inside, in front they could see the back wall clearly a few hundred metres away, and several sets of brightly lit windows, high up looking down into the massive space, some extremely big. Along the two side walls were square holes like post boxes, only these post boxes were thirty metres wide and the same deep. All but five of these were sealed, and it was into these open five slots the saucers manoeuvred into.

Mathews was both terrified and fascinated by the capabilities of what was being shown before him, and he held on to Jean's hand.

Maria knew the human girls liked diamonds but she never understood why. A diamond was actually one of the most common elements on earth made precious by its arrangement of atoms, and a fake rarity from a diamond cartel in London. Diamonds were expensive, but anyone with a high school chemistry knowledge, and after seeing the paper on graphyne, would know that with only a small reconfiguration of the structure they could make that other allotrope of carbon just as easy. Diamond was the strongest material they could print that was transparent, it had the properties of glass, and, if aligned correctly, had amazing hardness and was almost impossible to break. Diamond also had almost magical heat conduction properties which was why it was layered in their electronics. Because of this most of the windows were double or triple-glazed with a vacuum between.
